stories.title: The Creation
stories.summary:
The account begins with an unformed earth, darkness over deep waters, and God's Spirit hovering above them. God speaks light into being and separates day from night. On the second day, God makes the sky, dividing waters above from waters below. On the third, gathered seas reveal dry land, which produces plants and fruit trees.

The fourth day brings lights in the sky to govern day and night and mark seasons and years. On the fifth, God fills the waters with living creatures and the sky with birds, blessing them to multiply. Land animals appear on the sixth day. God then creates humanity, male and female, in God's image. They receive a blessing, authority over other creatures, and the command to multiply and fill the earth. Plants are provided as food for humans and animals.

God declares the completed creation very good. After six days of work, God rests on the seventh, blessing that day and setting it apart.

stories.title: The Fall of Man
stories.summary:
A serpent questions the woman's account of God's command about the forbidden tree. It denies that eating the fruit will bring death and promises knowledge of good and evil. Attracted by the fruit and the prospect of wisdom, she eats and gives some to her husband. Both become aware of their nakedness, make fig-leaf coverings, and hide when they hear God in the garden.

God questions them. The man points to the woman, and she points to the serpent. God pronounces hostility between the serpent and the woman's offspring. The woman faces pain in childbirth and her husband's rule. The man must work cursed ground that produces thorns, until he returns to the dust from which he came.

The man names his wife Eve, and God clothes them in animal skins. God then expels the man from Eden to prevent access to the tree of life. Heavenly guardians and a turning, flaming sword block the way back to that tree.

stories.title: Cain and Abel
stories.summary:
Eve gives birth to Cain and then Abel. Cain works the soil, while Abel tends sheep. Each brings an offering to God, but God favors Abel and his offering rather than Cain and his. The passage gives no explicit reason for this difference. Cain becomes angry, and God warns him that sin is waiting at the door and must be mastered.

Cain attacks and kills Abel in the field. When God asks where Abel is, Cain denies knowing and questions whether he must watch over his brother. God declares that Abel's blood cries from the ground. Cain is condemned to wander, and the soil will no longer yield its strength to him.

Cain protests that the punishment is unbearable and fears that someone will kill him. God warns against killing Cain and gives him a protective sign, without describing its appearance. Cain leaves God's presence and settles east of Eden in the land of Nod.

stories.title: The Line of Seth
stories.summary:
After Abel's death, Eve bears Seth and describes him as another child given in Abel's place. Seth later has a son named Enosh. The account connects this period with people beginning to call on God's name.

A family record then traces Adam's line through Seth, Enosh, Kenan, Mahalalel, Jared, Enoch, Methuselah, and Lamech to Noah. It recalls humanity's creation in God's likeness and describes Seth as born in Adam's likeness. Most entries give each father's age at his son's birth, mention other children, and close with his lifespan and death.

Enoch's entry breaks this repeated pattern. He walks with God and disappears because God takes him. Methuselah receives the longest lifespan listed, 969 years. Lamech names his son Noah, expressing hope for relief from painful work on the cursed ground. The record ends by naming Noah's three sons: Shem, Ham, and Japheth.

stories.title: Noah and the Flood
stories.summary:
In a world described as corrupt and violent, Noah is presented as righteous. God announces a flood and tells him to build a large, three-level vessel. Noah must preserve his household, animals, and food. The instructions include pairs of animals, with additional clean animals and birds. Noah obeys, entering with his wife, three sons, and their wives.

Waters burst from below and rain falls for forty days and nights. The rising flood covers the mountains, and all land-dwelling life outside the vessel dies. God remembers Noah and sends a wind as the waters recede. The vessel rests on the mountains of Ararat. Noah sends out a raven and later a dove. After returning once without a resting place, the dove brings an olive leaf, then eventually does not return.

When the ground is dry, God tells the family and animals to leave. Noah builds an altar and offers sacrifices. God promises continuing seasons and blesses Noah's family to multiply. Meat is permitted as food, but consuming blood is forbidden, and human life receives special protection.

God establishes a covenant, a binding promise, with Noah, his descendants, and every living creature. No flood will again destroy all life. The rainbow becomes the sign of that promise.

stories.title: The Family of Noah
stories.summary:
After the flood, Noah plants a vineyard, becomes drunk, and lies uncovered in his tent. Ham sees his father's nakedness and tells his brothers. Shem and Japheth carry a garment backward into the tent and cover Noah without looking at him. When Noah wakes, he curses Canaan, Ham's son, to serve his relatives. He also speaks blessings connected with Shem and Japheth. The account then records Noah's death at 950 years.

The narrative turns into a family list connecting the nations with Noah's three sons. Japheth's descendants are associated with coastal peoples. Ham's line includes Cush, Egypt, and Canaan, along with the peoples linked to those names. Nimrod receives particular attention as a powerful hunter and ruler associated with cities including Babel.

Shem's descendants include the line through Arpachshad, Shelah, and Eber. The list describes families spreading into their own lands, languages, and nations. It closes by tracing the division of the post-flood nations to these branches of Noah's family.

stories.title: The Tower of Babel
stories.summary:
People who share one language settle on a plain in Shinar. They make baked bricks and use tar as mortar. Together they plan a city and a tower reaching toward the sky. Their stated aims are to make a name for themselves and avoid being scattered across the earth.

God comes down to inspect the building. Observing their shared language and united effort, God says their plans will have no limit. God then confuses their speech so that they can no longer understand one another. The people stop building the city and are scattered across the earth.

The account connects the city's name, Babel, with the confusion of language. The unity the builders hoped to preserve gives way to the dispersal they had wanted to prevent.

stories.title: The Call of Abram
stories.summary:
The passage introduces Terah's family, including Abram, Nahor, and Haran. Haran dies in Ur, leaving his son Lot. Abram's wife Sarai has no children. Terah takes Abram, Sarai, and Lot toward Canaan, but they settle in Haran, where Terah dies.

God tells Abram to leave his country, relatives, and father's household for a land God will show him. The promise includes a great nation, a respected name, protection, and blessing extending to all the earth's families. Abram leaves Haran at seventy-five, taking Sarai, Lot, their possessions, and the people acquired there.

They enter Canaan and reach Shechem, where Canaanites already live. God promises the land to Abram's descendants, and Abram builds an altar. He later pitches his tent between Bethel and Ai, builds another altar, and calls on God's name. The passage ends with his journey continuing southward.

stories.title: Abram and Lot
stories.summary:
Abram returns from Egypt with Sarai, Lot, and considerable wealth. Near Bethel, their large herds strain the available land, and their herders quarrel. Abram proposes separating and lets Lot choose first. Lot selects the well-watered Jordan plain and settles near Sodom. God then renews the promise of land and countless descendants to Abram, who settles near Hebron.

A war between rival kings leads to Sodom's defeat. Lot and his possessions are carried away with other captives. After hearing the news, Abram pursues the attackers with 318 trained men from his household and allied forces. A night attack succeeds, and he recovers Lot, the other captives, and their goods.

On Abram's return, Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High, brings bread and wine and blesses him. Abram gives him a tenth of everything. The king of Sodom offers Abram the recovered goods, but Abram refuses personal profit. He allows only the food already consumed and his allies' shares, so the king cannot claim to have made him rich.

stories.title: Hagar and Ishmael
stories.summary:
Sarai has no children and gives her Egyptian servant Hagar to Abram as a wife, hoping to obtain children through her. Hagar becomes pregnant and begins to look down on Sarai. Sarai blames Abram, who leaves Hagar under her authority. Sarai treats Hagar harshly, and Hagar runs away.

An angel finds Hagar near a spring on the road to Shur and asks where she is going. After hearing that she has fled Sarai, the angel tells her to return and submit. The message also promises descendants too numerous to count. Her son is to be named Ishmael because God has heard her suffering. His future is described as independent and marked by conflict with others.

Hagar responds by naming God as the one who sees her. The well also receives a name connected with this encounter. The account ends with Hagar bearing Ishmael to Abram, who is eighty-six years old.

stories.title: Abraham and Sarah’s Covenant
stories.summary:
God appears to Abram at ninety-nine and promises a lasting covenant with him and his descendants. Abram receives the name Abraham and the promise that nations and kings will come from him. Canaan is promised to his descendants. Circumcision becomes the required sign for every male in his household, including servants and future children.

Sarai receives the name Sarah. God promises that she will bear a son named Isaac and that the covenant will continue through him. Abraham laughs at the prospect of a child being born to such elderly parents. He asks about Ishmael, and God promises to bless him with many descendants and twelve princes. Abraham then circumcises himself, Ishmael, and the males of his household.

Later, Abraham welcomes three visitors near his tent and provides a meal. They announce that Sarah will have a son within a year. Listening from the tent, she laughs privately because of their age. God questions her laughter and repeats the promise. Afraid, Sarah denies laughing, but the reply insists that she did.

stories.title: Lot Leaves Sodom
stories.summary:
Two angels arrive in Sodom, and Lot persuades them to stay in his house. The city's men surround it and demand the visitors for sex. Lot tries to protect his guests by offering his daughters instead. The crowd threatens him, but the visitors pull him inside and strike the attackers with blindness.

The angels announce the city's destruction and urge Lot to gather his family. His prospective sons-in-law dismiss the warning. At dawn, the angels lead Lot, his wife, and two daughters out by the hand. They order them to flee without looking back. Lot asks to shelter in nearby Zoar rather than the mountains, and his request is granted.

Fire and sulfur destroy Sodom, Gomorrah, and the surrounding plain. Lot's wife looks back and becomes a pillar of salt. Abraham sees smoke rising, and the account links Lot's rescue with God's remembrance of Abraham.

Lot later leaves Zoar for a cave with his daughters. Believing no men are available to continue the family, they get him drunk on successive nights and have sex with him. He is unaware of either encounter. Their sons, Moab and Ben Ammi, are identified as ancestors of the Moabites and Ammonites.

stories.title: Isaac and Ishmael
stories.summary:
Sarah gives birth to Isaac at the promised time, when Abraham is one hundred. Abraham names and circumcises the child as instructed. Sarah celebrates the unexpected laughter brought by having a son in old age. When Isaac is weaned, Abraham holds a feast.

Sarah sees Hagar's son mocking and demands that Hagar and the boy be sent away. She says he must not share Isaac's inheritance. Abraham is distressed, but God tells him to listen to Sarah. Isaac's line will carry the promised family name, while Hagar's son will also become a nation.

Abraham sends Hagar away with bread and water. In the wilderness near Beersheba, the water runs out. She places the boy under a shrub and withdraws, unable to watch him die. God hears the boy, and an angel reassures Hagar that he will have a future. She sees a well and gives him water. He grows up in the wilderness, becomes an archer, and receives an Egyptian wife chosen by his mother.

stories.title: The Binding of Isaac
stories.summary:
God tests Abraham by commanding him to offer Isaac as a burnt sacrifice in Moriah. Abraham leaves early with Isaac, two servants, a donkey, and wood. On the third day, he sees the place and leaves the servants behind. Isaac carries the wood while Abraham carries the fire and knife.

Isaac asks where the sacrificial lamb is. Abraham answers that God will provide it. At the appointed place, Abraham builds an altar, binds Isaac, and lays him on the wood. As he takes the knife to kill his son, an angel calls from heaven and orders him to stop. The angel says Abraham has shown that he fears God by not withholding his son.

Abraham sees a ram caught by its horns in a thicket and sacrifices it instead. He names the place for God's provision. A second message renews promises of countless descendants, victory over enemies, and blessing for the nations through his offspring. Abraham returns to his servants and travels with them to Beersheba.

stories.title: Isaac and Rebekah
stories.summary:
The elderly Abraham sends his senior servant to find Isaac a wife among his relatives rather than the Canaanites. Isaac must remain in Canaan. If the woman refuses to come, the servant will be released from his oath.

At a well near Nahor's city, the servant prays for a sign. The chosen woman will offer water both to him and to his camels. Rebekah arrives and does exactly that. She identifies herself as Abraham's relative and offers lodging. The servant gives her jewelry and thanks God for guiding him.

Rebekah's brother Laban welcomes the travelers. Before eating, the servant recounts his mission, prayer, and encounter with Rebekah. Her family agrees to the marriage, and he distributes gifts. The next morning, her relatives ask for a delay, but the servant wants to leave. Asked directly whether she will go, Rebekah agrees.

She departs with her nurse and attendants. As they approach Isaac, she learns who he is and covers herself with a veil. The servant reports what happened. Isaac marries Rebekah, loves her, and finds comfort after his mother's death.

stories.title: Jacob and Esau
stories.summary:
After Isaac prays for Rebekah to have children, she conceives twins who struggle within her. God tells her that two nations will emerge and the elder will serve the younger. Esau is born first, followed by Jacob, who grips his heel. Their parents favor different sons. Later, a hungry Esau sells Jacob his birthright, the privileges of the firstborn, for bread and lentil stew.

During a famine, Isaac stays in Gerar as God directs. He calls Rebekah his sister because he fears being killed, but Abimelech discovers their marriage and protects them. Isaac prospers, disputes arise over wells, and he moves repeatedly. At Beersheba, God renews the promises, and Isaac makes a peace agreement with Abimelech.

When Isaac grows old and loses his sight, he plans to bless Esau after eating game he has hunted. Rebekah prepares food and disguises Jacob with Esau's clothes and goatskins. Jacob claims to be Esau and receives a blessing of abundance and authority over his brothers. Esau returns too late and begs for another blessing. Isaac predicts a life of conflict and eventual release from his brother's rule.

Esau plans to kill Jacob. Rebekah urges Jacob to flee to Laban, while Isaac sends him there to marry within the family. Seeing his parents' disapproval of Canaanite wives, Esau adds a daughter of Ishmael to his marriages.

stories.title: Jacob’s Household
stories.summary:
Jacob reaches a well near Haran, where he meets Rachel and waters her father's flock. On learning that he is Rebekah's son, Laban welcomes him into the household. Jacob loves Rachel and agrees to work seven years to marry her.

At the wedding, Laban substitutes his older daughter Leah. Jacob discovers the deception the next morning. Laban appeals to local marriage customs and offers Rachel after Leah's wedding week, in return for seven more years of work. Jacob marries both sisters but loves Rachel more.

God sees Leah's rejection, and she bears Reuben, Simeon, Levi, and Judah. Rachel, still childless, gives her servant Bilhah to Jacob; Bilhah bears Dan and Naphtali. Leah then gives him Zilpah, who bears Gad and Asher. The sisters' rivalry continues through the children's names and their struggle for Jacob's attention.

Rachel trades a night with Jacob for mandrake plants found by Leah's son. Leah later bears Issachar, Zebulun, and a daughter, Dinah. Finally, God answers Rachel, and she gives birth to Joseph. His name expresses her hope for another son.

stories.title: Jacob Returns to Canaan
stories.summary:
As relations with Laban worsen, God tells Jacob to return to his homeland. Rachel and Leah support leaving, saying their father has treated them as outsiders. Jacob departs secretly with his family and possessions. Unknown to him, Rachel takes Laban's household gods.

Laban pursues them but receives a divine warning before confronting Jacob. His search fails because Rachel hides the objects beneath her seat. Jacob protests his years of hard service and repeated changes to his wages. The men establish a boundary marked by stones and promise not to cross it to harm one another. Laban says farewell and returns home.

Jacob learns that Esau is approaching with four hundred men. Afraid, he divides his camp, prays for protection, and sends livestock ahead as gifts. That night, after taking his household across the Jabbok, he wrestles alone with a man until dawn. His hip is injured, but he refuses to let go without a blessing. He receives the name Israel and calls the place Peniel, saying he has seen God and survived.

Esau runs to embrace Jacob, and both weep. He accepts Jacob's gift after initial resistance. They part peacefully, with Esau returning to Seir. Jacob travels through Succoth to Shechem, where he buys land and builds an altar.

stories.title: Dinah at Shechem
stories.summary:
Dinah, Jacob and Leah's daughter, visits the women of the region. Shechem, a local ruler's son, seizes and sexually violates her. He then declares his attachment to her and asks his father Hamor to arrange a marriage. Jacob waits for his sons to return before responding; they are furious when they hear what happened.

Hamor proposes intermarriage, trade, and shared settlement between the families. Shechem offers any marriage payment they demand. Jacob's sons answer deceptively, requiring every male in the city to be circumcised before they will agree. Hamor and Shechem persuade the townsmen, also suggesting that Jacob's possessions will eventually benefit them.

On the third day, while the men are still in pain, Simeon and Levi attack the unsuspecting city. They kill its males, including Hamor and Shechem, and take Dinah from Shechem's house. Jacob's sons plunder the city and seize its women and children.

Jacob condemns Simeon and Levi for putting his small household at risk of retaliation from neighboring peoples. They answer by asking whether their sister should have been treated as a prostitute. The passage closes without resolving the dispute.

stories.title: The Death of Rachel
stories.summary:
God tells Jacob to return to Bethel and build an altar. Jacob orders his household to remove foreign gods, purify themselves, and change clothes. He buries their gods and earrings near Shechem. They travel safely because surrounding communities are afraid to pursue them.

At Bethel, Jacob builds the altar. Rebekah's nurse Deborah dies and is buried there. God again names Jacob Israel and promises nations, kings, and the land given to Abraham and Isaac. Jacob marks the encounter with a stone pillar, oil, and a drink offering.

On the journey toward Ephrath, also called Bethlehem, Rachel experiences severe childbirth. She bears a son but dies, naming him Benoni before her death. Jacob calls him Benjamin and marks Rachel's roadside grave with a pillar.

The account also records Reuben having sex with Bilhah, his father's concubine, and notes that Jacob hears of it. After listing Jacob's twelve sons, it describes his return to Isaac at Hebron. Isaac dies at 180, and Esau and Jacob bury him together.

stories.title: Joseph and His Brothers
stories.summary:
Seventeen-year-old Joseph tends flocks with his brothers and brings their father a bad report about them. Jacob favors Joseph and gives him a special tunic, increasing their hostility. Joseph then tells dreams in which his brothers' grain bundles, and later the sun, moon, and eleven stars, bow before him. His brothers resent these claims, while Jacob both rebukes him and remembers them.

Sent to check on the brothers, Joseph finds them near Dothan. They plot to kill him, but Reuben persuades them to leave him in an empty pit instead. Reuben intends to rescue him later. They strip off Joseph's tunic and throw him into the pit.

When a trading caravan appears, Judah proposes selling Joseph rather than killing him. Joseph is taken from the pit and sold for twenty pieces of silver. The account refers to both Midianite traders and Ishmaelites in this transfer. Reuben returns to find Joseph gone and tears his clothes.

The brothers dip the tunic in goat's blood and show it to Jacob. He concludes that a wild animal killed Joseph and refuses comfort. Meanwhile, Joseph reaches Egypt and is sold to Potiphar, an official of Pharaoh.

stories.title: Judah and Tamar
stories.summary:
Judah marries a Canaanite woman and has three sons: Er, Onan, and Shelah. Er marries Tamar, but God kills him for wickedness. Judah tells Onan to father a child for his dead brother. Onan deliberately prevents conception because the child would not count as his own. God kills him too.

Judah sends Tamar to her father's home, promising Shelah when he grows up, but does not fulfill the promise. After Judah's wife dies, Tamar hears he is traveling to shear sheep. She removes her widow's clothes, veils herself, and waits beside the road. Judah mistakes her for a prostitute and has sex with her. As security for payment, she receives his seal, cord, and staff.

When Tamar's pregnancy becomes known, Judah orders her burned. She produces the objects and says the owner is the father. Recognizing them, Judah acknowledges that she is more righteous than he is, because he withheld Shelah. He does not have sex with her again.

Tamar gives birth to twins. A hand appears first and receives a scarlet thread, but the other child emerges before him. The sons are named Perez and Zerah.

stories.title: Joseph in Egypt
stories.summary:
Potiphar buys Joseph, and the account attributes Joseph's success to God's presence with him. Potiphar places him over his household. Potiphar's wife repeatedly demands sex, but Joseph refuses. When she grabs his clothing, he escapes, leaving it behind. She uses it to support a false accusation, and Potiphar has Joseph imprisoned.

In prison, Joseph again gains responsibility. He interprets dreams for Pharaoh's cupbearer and baker, attributing interpretation to God. He predicts the cupbearer's restoration and the baker's execution within three days. Both happen, but the cupbearer forgets Joseph's request for help.

Two years later, Pharaoh dreams of thin cattle consuming healthy cattle and thin grain consuming full heads of grain. When others cannot explain the dreams, the cupbearer remembers Joseph. Joseph says they announce seven years of abundance followed by seven years of severe famine. He recommends collecting a fifth of the produce during the good years.

Pharaoh appoints Joseph to oversee Egypt, gives him signs of authority, and arranges his marriage to Asenath. Joseph stores vast quantities of grain and becomes father to Manasseh and Ephraim. When the famine arrives, Egypt has reserves. Joseph opens the storehouses, and people from other lands come to buy food.

stories.title: Joseph Reunites His Family
stories.summary:
Famine sends Jacob's sons to Egypt for grain, while Benjamin stays home. Joseph recognizes them, but they do not recognize him. He accuses them of spying and demands that they bring their youngest brother. Simeon remains detained while the others return with grain and money secretly restored to their sacks.

As food runs out again, Judah guarantees Benjamin's safety, and Jacob reluctantly lets him go. Joseph receives the brothers, releases Simeon, and hosts a meal. He weeps privately at seeing Benjamin. Before their departure, he has his silver cup hidden in Benjamin's sack. When it is discovered, all the brothers return. Joseph proposes keeping Benjamin as a slave. Judah offers himself instead, describing how losing Benjamin would devastate their father.

Joseph dismisses his attendants and reveals his identity through tears. His brothers are frightened, but he tells them that God has used his arrival in Egypt to preserve life. Five years of famine remain, so he invites the whole family to live nearby. Pharaoh supports the move and provides wagons and supplies.

Jacob initially cannot believe Joseph is alive. After seeing the wagons, he sets out. At Beersheba, God reassures him about entering Egypt. The family travels together, and Joseph embraces his father in Goshen. Pharaoh grants them land, Jacob blesses Pharaoh, and Joseph supplies the household with food.

stories.title: Jacob Blesses His Family
stories.summary:
As Jacob grows ill, Joseph brings Manasseh and Ephraim to him. Jacob adopts both grandsons into his own family and recalls God's promises and Rachel's death. He deliberately crosses his hands, giving the younger Ephraim the leading blessing. Despite Joseph's objection, Jacob says Ephraim's descendants will become greater than Manasseh's.

Jacob gathers his sons and speaks about their futures. Reuben loses his leading position because Jacob accuses him of defiling his father's bed. Simeon and Levi face scattering because of their violence. Judah receives images of kingship and abundance, while Joseph receives an extended blessing of strength and fruitfulness. Each of the twelve sons receives a distinct saying.

Jacob requests burial in the family cave at Machpelah and dies. Joseph has him embalmed, and Egypt mourns. With Pharaoh's permission, a large company travels to Canaan. The sons bury Jacob beside his ancestors, then return to Egypt.

Afterward, the brothers fear Joseph will retaliate. He reassures them, distinguishing their harmful intentions from the life-preserving outcome he attributes to God. He promises to provide for them and their children. Joseph later dies at 110, after making the family swear to carry his bones away when God brings them out of Egypt. His embalmed body remains in a coffin there.

stories.title: Israel Oppressed in Egypt
stories.summary:
The generation of Joseph and his brothers dies, but their descendants multiply throughout Egypt. A new king who does not know Joseph regards the growing Israelite population as a threat. He fears they might join Egypt's enemies in war and leave the country.

The Egyptians impose forced labor, making the Israelites build storage cities and work with bricks, mortar, and crops. Harsh treatment does not stop their growth. Pharaoh then orders the Hebrew midwives Shiphrah and Puah to kill boys at birth while allowing girls to live.

The midwives fear God and spare the boys. When Pharaoh questions them, they say Hebrew women give birth before a midwife arrives. The account says God treats the midwives well and gives them families, while Israel continues to grow. Pharaoh escalates the order, commanding all his people to throw newborn boys into the river and preserve the girls.

stories.title: The Birth and Rescue of Moses
stories.summary:
A Levite couple has a son, and his mother hides him for three months. When she can no longer conceal him, she waterproofs a papyrus basket with tar and pitch. She places the baby inside and sets it among reeds at the riverbank. His sister watches from a distance.

Pharaoh's daughter comes to bathe and notices the basket. A servant retrieves it, and she finds a crying baby. Recognizing him as a Hebrew child, she feels compassion for him. His sister approaches and offers to find a Hebrew woman to nurse him.

With permission, the girl brings the baby's own mother. Pharaoh's daughter agrees to pay her to nurse the child. When he grows older, his mother brings him to Pharaoh's daughter, and he becomes her son. She names him Moses, explaining the name through her act of drawing him from the water.

stories.title: Moses Flees to Midian
stories.summary:
As an adult, Moses visits his fellow Hebrews and sees their forced labor. He finds an Egyptian beating a Hebrew, looks around, and kills the Egyptian. He hides the body in the sand. The next day, he tries to stop two Hebrews fighting. One challenges his authority and mentions the killing, making Moses realize it is known.

Pharaoh seeks to kill him, so Moses escapes to Midian. At a well, he helps seven daughters of the local priest when shepherds drive them away. He also waters their flock. Their father Reuel invites Moses to eat, and Moses stays with the family. He marries Zipporah, and their son Gershom receives a name connected with Moses' life as a foreigner.

Back in Egypt, the king dies, but Israel's enslavement continues. The people cry out under their burdens. God hears them, remembers the covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and takes notice of their suffering.

stories.title: The Burning Bush
stories.summary:
While tending his father-in-law's flock near Horeb, Moses sees a bush burning without being consumed. He approaches, and God calls his name. Moses must remove his sandals because he stands on holy ground. God identifies himself with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob and says he has heard Israel's suffering in Egypt.

God sends Moses to Pharaoh to bring the people out and lead them toward a fertile land. Moses questions his suitability and asks what name to give the Israelites. God answers with the declaration “I AM WHO I AM” and identifies himself as their ancestors' God. Moses must gather the elders and ask Pharaoh for leave to worship in the wilderness. God predicts resistance, signs against Egypt, and an eventual departure with Egyptian valuables.

Moses fears people will not believe him. God gives signs involving a staff becoming a snake, a diseased hand restored, and water turning to blood. Moses then objects that he speaks poorly. God promises help, but Moses asks for someone else. Angered, God appoints Aaron as his spokesman. Moses is to take the staff for the signs.

stories.title: Moses Returns to Egypt
stories.summary:
Moses asks Jethro's permission to visit his people in Egypt and receives a peaceful farewell. God tells him that those who wanted to kill him are dead. He sets out with his wife, sons, and the staff associated with God's signs.

God warns that Pharaoh will resist despite the wonders Moses performs. Moses must describe Israel as God's firstborn son and demand the people's release for worship. Pharaoh's refusal will bring the death of his own firstborn.

At a lodging place, the journey is interrupted by a brief account of a divine threat to kill Moses. Zipporah circumcises her son with a flint and speaks of a “bridegroom of blood.” The threat ends. The passage does not fully explain the episode.

Aaron meets Moses in the wilderness, and Moses tells him about the commission and signs. Together they gather Israel's elders. Aaron delivers the message, and the signs are performed. Hearing that God has seen their suffering, the people believe and bow in worship.

stories.title: Moses and Aaron Before Pharaoh
stories.summary:
Moses and Aaron ask Pharaoh to let Israel hold a festival for God in the wilderness. Pharaoh rejects God's authority and refuses to release them. He accuses the people of idleness and orders an increased burden: they must gather their own straw while producing the same number of bricks.

Workers scatter to find material, and Israelite foremen are beaten when the quotas are missed. Their appeal to Pharaoh fails. They blame Moses and Aaron for making their situation worse. Moses then questions God, asking why his mission has brought trouble rather than rescue.

God promises that Pharaoh will eventually drive the people out. Recalling the covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, God promises freedom from slavery, a renewed relationship, and possession of the promised land. Moses repeats this assurance, but the people cannot listen because of their distress and harsh labor.

When God sends him back to Pharaoh, Moses again doubts that he will be heard and objects to his speaking ability. The passage ends with God charging both Moses and Aaron to bring Israel out of Egypt.

stories.title: The Plagues of Egypt
stories.summary:
Moses and Aaron repeatedly demand Israel's release for worship. When Pharaoh refuses, Egypt's water turns to blood, killing fish and making the river undrinkable. Frogs then overrun the country. Pharaoh promises freedom when asking for relief, but reverses himself once the frogs die.

Further plagues bring lice, swarms of flies, livestock disease, and painful boils. Egypt's magicians initially imitate signs but fail to produce lice and acknowledge divine power. They later cannot stand before Moses because of the boils. Several plagues explicitly spare Israel or the land of Goshen.

A warning of devastating hail allows those who heed it to shelter people and animals. Hail and lightning destroy crops and kill those left outside. Pharaoh admits wrongdoing, but again refuses release when the storm ends. Locusts consume what remains, despite his officials urging him to let the people go.

Three days of thick darkness follow, while Israelites have light. Pharaoh offers increasingly limited permissions, first excluding families and later requiring livestock to stay. Moses insists that everyone and their animals must leave. The narrative attributes Pharaoh's resistance both to his own hardening and to God hardening him. It ends with Pharaoh threatening Moses against returning and Moses accepting the break.

stories.title: The Passover and the Death of the Firstborn
stories.summary:
God announces one final plague after which Pharaoh will drive Israel out. Moses warns that Egypt's firstborn will die at midnight, from the royal household to the lowest ranks, including livestock. The Israelites are also told to request silver and gold from their neighbors.

God gives instructions for a household meal. An unblemished young sheep or goat is to be killed, with its blood placed on the doorposts and doorway beam. Its meat is roasted and eaten with unleavened bread and bitter herbs. The people must eat ready to travel and remain inside until morning. The marked houses will be spared when destruction passes through Egypt.

Passover and the following festival of unleavened bread are established as lasting observances. Parents must explain to children that the meal recalls God's protection of Israel's households. The people carry out the instructions.

At midnight, the firstborn die throughout Egypt, and mourning fills the country. Pharaoh summons Moses and Aaron and tells the Israelites to leave with their livestock. The Egyptians press them to depart quickly. Israel takes unrisen dough, along with silver, gold, and clothing obtained from the Egyptians.

stories.title: The Exodus from Egypt
stories.summary:
The Israelites travel from Rameses to Succoth with their families, livestock, and a mixed company of other people. The account numbers the men on foot at about six hundred thousand. Their dough has not risen because they were driven out quickly, so they bake unleavened bread. Their departure is placed at the end of a 430-year stay in Egypt.

Instructions establish how Passover is to be observed and who may share the meal. A foreign resident may participate after the required circumcision, under the same rule as a native Israelite. The festival of unleavened bread is also to preserve the memory of release from slavery.

The firstborn of people and animals are set apart for God. Firstborn sons must be redeemed, meaning released from this claim rather than sacrificed. These practices are to prompt explanations to future children about the departure from Egypt.

God leads the people by a wilderness route rather than the shorter road through Philistine territory, lest war send them back. Joseph's remains leave Egypt with Moses, fulfilling the oath Joseph had required. A pillar of cloud guides them by day, and a pillar of fire gives light at night.

stories.title: Crossing the Sea
stories.summary:
God directs Israel to camp beside the sea, where Pharaoh will think them trapped. Regretting the loss of their labor, Pharaoh pursues with chariots and troops. The Israelites panic and accuse Moses of bringing them into the wilderness to die. Moses tells them to stand firm and see God's rescue.

The cloud moves behind Israel, separating the two camps during the night. At God's command, Moses stretches his hand over the sea. A strong east wind drives the water back, opening dry ground with water on either side. Israel crosses, and the Egyptian force follows.

God throws the pursuers into confusion and disrupts their chariots. As they try to escape, Moses stretches out his hand again. The water returns and covers the army. Israel reaches safety and sees the dead Egyptians on the shore. The account describes a renewed fear of God and trust in Moses.

Moses and the Israelites sing of God's victory, portraying God as a warrior who defeats the enemy and leads the rescued people toward a sanctuary. Miriam leads women with tambourines and dancing, repeating the celebration of horse and rider thrown into the sea.

stories.title: Bitter Water, Manna and Quail
stories.summary:
After three days without water, Israel reaches Marah, where the water is too bitter to drink. The people complain to Moses. God shows him a piece of wood, which he throws into the water, making it drinkable. God links obedience with protection from disease. The people then camp at Elim, among springs and palms.

In the next wilderness, hunger prompts complaints about leaving Egypt. God promises meat in the evening and bread in the morning. Quail cover the camp, and a fine substance appears after the dew lifts. The people call it manna. Moses tells each household to gather its daily share.

Ordinary leftovers spoil when kept overnight, but a double portion gathered on the sixth day remains usable for the seventh. No manna appears on that Sabbath, the day of rest. Some still go looking and find nothing, bringing another rebuke for disobedience.

Moses orders a portion preserved so later generations can see the food supplied in the wilderness. The account describes manna's appearance and taste and states that Israel eats it for forty years, until reaching Canaan's border.

stories.title: Water from the Rock and the Battle with Amalek
stories.summary:
At Rephidim, the people find no drinking water and quarrel with Moses. They accuse him of bringing their families and animals out of Egypt to die of thirst. Moses fears they may stone him and asks God what to do. God tells him to take the elders and strike a rock at Horeb with his staff. Water comes out. The place receives names recalling Israel's testing and quarrelling.

Amalek then attacks Israel. Joshua leads chosen men into battle while Moses stands on a hill with the staff. When Moses raises his hand, Israel gains ground; when he lowers it, Amalek gains ground. As Moses tires, Aaron and Hur seat him on a stone and support his hands until sunset.

Joshua defeats the attackers. God orders the victory recorded and tells Moses to repeat to Joshua a promise to erase Amalek's memory. Moses builds an altar named for God as Israel's banner. The passage ends by declaring continuing conflict between God and Amalek.

stories.title: Jethro Advises Moses
stories.summary:
Jethro, Moses' father-in-law and a priest of Midian, brings Zipporah and her two sons to Israel's camp. Moses welcomes him and recounts the departure from Egypt, the hardships of the journey, and God's rescues. Jethro praises God, offers sacrifices, and shares a meal with Aaron and Israel's elders.

The next day, he watches Moses hear disputes from morning until evening. Moses explains that people come to seek God's judgment and learn the laws. Jethro warns that this arrangement will exhaust both Moses and those waiting for him.

He proposes that Moses continue representing the people before God and teaching them, while appointing reliable judges for ordinary cases. These leaders should fear God, tell the truth, and reject dishonest gain. They will oversee groups of different sizes, bringing only difficult matters to Moses.

Moses accepts the advice and appoints leaders over thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens. They share the judging work, while difficult cases still reach him. Jethro then leaves for his own country.

stories.title: The Covenant and Ten Commandments at Sinai
stories.summary:
Three months after leaving Egypt, Israel camps before Mount Sinai. God tells Moses that obedience to the covenant will make the people God's special possession, a kingdom of priests, and a holy nation. The people agree. They wash their clothes and prepare for an encounter, with strict boundaries around the mountain.

Thunder, lightning, cloud, smoke, fire, and a loud trumpet accompany God's descent. The people tremble below while Moses goes up and receives further warnings against crossing the boundary.

God identifies himself as the one who brought Israel out of slavery and gives the commandments. They forbid other gods, worship of images, and misuse of God's name. The Sabbath requires rest for the whole household, servants, resident foreigners, and livestock. The commands also require honoring parents and prohibit murder, adultery, theft, false testimony, and coveting a neighbor's household or possessions.

Terrified by the sounds and smoke, the people ask Moses to speak for God rather than hear God directly. Moses explains the encounter as a test intended to keep them from wrongdoing. They remain at a distance as he approaches the darkness.

stories.title: The Covenant Is Sealed at Sinai
stories.summary:
Moses reports God's words and rulings to the people, who promise to obey. He writes the words down and builds an altar below the mountain, with twelve pillars representing Israel's tribes. Young men offer sacrifices. Moses places some of the blood in basins and sprinkles the rest on the altar.

He reads the covenant document aloud, and the people again pledge obedience. Moses then sprinkles blood on them, identifying it as the blood of the covenant. This ceremony marks the agreement between God and Israel concerning the words they have heard.

Moses, Aaron, Nadab, Abihu, and seventy elders ascend. The passage says they see Israel's God, with something like a clear sapphire pavement beneath his feet. They are not struck down and share food and drink.

God calls Moses higher to receive stone tablets containing the law. Moses leaves Aaron and Hur responsible for disputes and goes up with Joshua. Cloud covers the mountain, and God's glory appears to the people like consuming fire. Moses enters the cloud and remains forty days and nights.

stories.title: The Golden Calf
stories.summary:
When Moses is delayed on the mountain, the people ask Aaron for gods to lead them. He collects gold earrings and fashions a calf. The people identify it with their escape from Egypt. Aaron builds an altar and announces a festival, followed by sacrifices, eating, drinking, and celebration.

God tells Moses what has happened and proposes destroying the people and making a nation from him instead. Moses appeals to God's reputation before Egypt and the promises to Abraham, Isaac, and Israel. God relents from destroying them all.

Descending with the stone tablets, Moses sees the calf and dancing. He breaks the tablets, destroys the calf, grinds it into powder, and makes the people drink water containing it. Aaron blames the people and describes the calf as emerging from the fire. Moses then summons those loyal to God. The Levites gather and, at his command, kill about three thousand people in the camp.

The next day, Moses seeks forgiveness, offering to be erased from God's book if forgiveness is refused. God says those who sinned will bear responsibility and tells Moses to continue leading. The account closes with a plague against the people because of the calf.

stories.title: Moses Sees God's Glory
stories.summary:
God orders the journey toward the promised land to continue but initially says an angel will lead instead of God's own presence. The people mourn and remove their ornaments. Moses meets God at a tent outside the camp, where a pillar of cloud descends. The account describes their conversation as direct, like that between friends.

Moses insists that God's presence must accompany the people, and God agrees. Moses then asks to see God's glory. God promises to pass by but says no one can see God's face and live. Moses will be sheltered in a rock opening and allowed a limited view afterward.

Moses cuts new stone tablets and returns to Sinai. God proclaims mercy, patience, forgiveness, and judgment that reaches across generations. Moses asks for pardon and God's continuing presence. A renewed covenant includes commands against other gods and instructions concerning festivals, firstborn offerings, Sabbath rest, and worship.

After forty days and nights without food or water, Moses descends with the tablets. His face shines, frightening Aaron and the people. He calls them near and delivers the commands. He then covers his face, removing the covering when speaking with God and when reporting God's words to Israel.

stories.title: Building the Tabernacle
stories.summary:
Moses first restates the Sabbath command, then invites voluntary gifts for the tabernacle, a portable sanctuary. Men and women bring metals, cloth, skins, wood, precious stones, oil, and spices. Skilled workers contribute weaving and other crafts. Bezalel and Oholiab lead the work, with abilities the account attributes to God's Spirit. Contributions become so abundant that Moses orders the people to stop bringing them.

The workers make curtains, coverings, wooden frames, and a dividing veil. They construct the gold-covered ark and its lid with winged figures, a table, a lampstand, and an incense altar. A bronze altar, washing basin, and courtyard complete the main furnishings. The account records the quantities of donated metals and their uses.

Special clothing is made for Aaron and his sons. Aaron's garments include engraved stones naming Israel's tribes, a jeweled breastpiece, and a gold plate declaring dedication to God. Moses inspects the completed work and blesses the workers.

On the appointed day, Moses assembles the sanctuary and places its furnishings. The covenant tablets go inside the ark. When the work is finished, cloud covers the tent and God's glory fills it, preventing Moses from entering. Thereafter, the cloud's movement governs Israel's journeys, with fire visible by night.

stories.title: Aaron and His Sons Are Ordained
stories.summary:
God directs Moses to gather the community for the installation of Aaron and his sons as priests. Moses washes them, dresses Aaron in the special priestly garments, and anoints the sanctuary, furnishings, altar, and Aaron with oil. He also clothes Aaron's sons.

A bull and two rams are offered in a sequence of sacrifices. Blood is applied to the altar, and portions of the animals are burned as instructed. For the installation offering, Moses places blood on Aaron's right ear, thumb, and big toe, then does the same for his sons. Oil and blood are sprinkled on them and their clothing. They eat the prescribed meal and remain at the sanctuary entrance for seven days.

On the eighth day, Aaron begins offering sacrifices for himself and the people, assisted by his sons. Moses says God's glory will appear. Aaron blesses the people, then enters the meeting tent with Moses. When they emerge and bless the assembly, God's glory appears. Fire comes from God's presence and consumes the offering on the altar. The people shout and fall facedown.

stories.title: Nadab and Abihu
stories.summary:
Aaron's sons Nadab and Abihu bring incense with fire that God has not commanded. Fire comes from God's presence and kills them. Moses tells Aaron that God will be shown holy among those who approach and honored before the people. Aaron remains silent.

Relatives carry the bodies outside the camp. Moses tells Aaron and his surviving sons, Eleazar and Ithamar, not to leave their duties or use the usual signs of mourning. The wider community may mourn. God then forbids priests from drinking wine or strong drink when entering the meeting tent. They must distinguish sacred from ordinary things, determine ritual cleanness, and teach the people.

Moses gives further directions about the priests' portions of offerings. Discovering that a sin offering was burned rather than eaten, he becomes angry with the surviving sons. Aaron replies that, after the day's losses, eating it would not have seemed right before God. Moses hears the explanation and accepts it.

stories.title: The Blasphemer Stoned
stories.summary:
A man with an Israelite mother and Egyptian father fights with another man in the camp. During the dispute, he curses God's name. He is brought to Moses and held in custody while the community waits for a ruling. His mother is identified as Shelomith of the tribe of Dan, but he is not named.

God directs that he be taken outside the camp. Those who heard him must place their hands on his head, and the congregation must stone him. The accompanying rule applies the same death penalty for cursing God's name to foreign residents and native Israelites.

The passage also sets out penalties for killing and injury. Killing a person requires death, while killing an animal requires compensation. Bodily injury is answered with equivalent injury, expressed as eye for eye and tooth for tooth. One standard is stated for native and foreign residents. Moses communicates the ruling, and the community takes the man outside and stones him.

stories.title: Counting the Camp
stories.summary:
In the second year after leaving Egypt, God directs Moses and Aaron to count Israel's men who are at least twenty and eligible for war. A named leader from each tribe helps conduct the census at Sinai. Families declare their ancestry, and the men are registered by tribe and household.

The passage lists each tribe's total, counting Joseph's descendants separately as Ephraim and Manasseh. Judah has the largest recorded force. The combined total is 603,550 men. This is a count of fighting-age males, not the entire population.

The Levites are excluded from this military registration. They receive responsibility for the tabernacle, its equipment, and its transport. They must dismantle it when the camp moves and assemble it when the people stop. Their tents surround the sanctuary, while the other Israelites camp by their tribal divisions. Unauthorized approach to these duties carries a death penalty. The chapter closes by saying Israel follows the instructions.

stories.title: Offerings and the Passover at Sinai
stories.summary:
After the sanctuary is set up and dedicated, Israel's leaders bring wagons and oxen for transporting its parts. Moses distributes these according to the Levite groups' duties. The Kohathites receive none because they carry the sacred furnishings on their shoulders. Over twelve days, each tribal leader brings the same set of vessels, grain, incense, and animals to dedicate the altar.

The account describes Moses hearing God's voice from above the ark. Aaron arranges the seven lamps as instructed. The Levites undergo cleansing, wash their clothing, and are publicly presented for service. They are assigned to assist Aaron's household in place of Israel's firstborn. Rules also set the ages for their active work and later assistance.

Israel observes Passover at Sinai. Men prevented from participating because of contact with a corpse ask for a remedy. God permits a later observance for those ritually unclean or away on a distant journey, while holding eligible people responsible for keeping it.

The closing section describes the cloud over the sanctuary, appearing fiery at night. Whether it remains briefly or for a long period, Israel stays in camp. When it rises, the people travel.

stories.title: Leaving Sinai and the Complaints
stories.summary:
The cloud rises from the sanctuary, and Israel leaves Sinai in ordered groups, with the Levites carrying its parts. Moses asks Hobab to remain as a guide because he knows the wilderness. The ark travels ahead, and Moses speaks set words when it starts and when it rests.

Complaints soon bring fire at the camp's edge. Moses prays, and the fire stops. Another wave of dissatisfaction centers on food: people remember Egypt's fish and vegetables and reject the daily manna. Moses tells God that leading them alone has become unbearable.

God appoints seventy elders to share his burden and places the Spirit on them. They prophesy. Two registered elders, Eldad and Medad, do so inside the camp rather than at the tent. Joshua asks Moses to stop them, but Moses wishes all the people could receive God's Spirit.

God also promises meat in overwhelming abundance. A wind brings quail, and the people spend two days and a night gathering them. While the meat is still being eaten, a severe plague strikes. The place receives a name recalling the graves of those who craved meat. Israel then moves to Hazeroth.

stories.title: Miriam and Aaron Speak Against Moses
stories.summary:
Miriam and Aaron criticize Moses over his Cushite wife and challenge his special authority. They ask whether God has spoken only through him rather than through them as well. The narrator describes Moses as exceptionally humble. God summons all three to the meeting tent.

Speaking from the cloud, God distinguishes Moses from other prophets. Others receive dreams and visions, but Moses receives direct, clear speech and is trusted throughout God's household. God rebukes Miriam and Aaron for speaking against him.

When the cloud leaves, Miriam has a severe skin condition described as white as snow. Aaron admits their wrongdoing and asks Moses not to let her remain in that state. Moses immediately prays for her healing.

God requires Miriam to remain outside the camp for seven days, comparing the exclusion to the shame of a father's public rebuke. The whole community waits rather than traveling without her. After she returns, they leave Hazeroth and camp in the wilderness of Paran.

stories.title: The Twelve Spies
stories.summary:
At God's command, Moses sends twelve tribal leaders to inspect Canaan. They are to assess its people, defenses, soil, and trees, and bring back fruit. After forty days, they return with grapes, figs, and pomegranates. They confirm the land's richness but describe powerful inhabitants and fortified cities. Caleb urges immediate action, while the others spread a frightening report.

The people weep and propose choosing another leader to return to Egypt. Joshua and Caleb tear their clothes and insist that God can give them the land. The assembly threatens to stone them. God then proposes destroying the people, but Moses appeals to God's mercy and reputation among the nations.

God grants pardon while declaring that the complaining adult generation will die in the wilderness. Caleb and Joshua are named as exceptions. Their children will enter the land, after forty years of wandering corresponding to the spies' forty days. The spies responsible for the discouraging report die in a plague.

On hearing the sentence, the people mourn and decide to advance after all. Moses warns that God will not accompany them, but they proceed without him or the ark. Amalekite and Canaanite forces defeat them and drive them back.

stories.title: Korah's Rebellion
stories.summary:
Korah and other leaders challenge Moses and Aaron, arguing that the whole community is holy and questioning their elevated authority. Moses proposes a test with incense offerings so God can identify the chosen priest. Dathan and Abiram refuse his summons and accuse him of bringing them out of Egypt without delivering the promised land.

As the confrontation develops, Moses and Aaron plead against punishment of the whole assembly. The people are warned away from the rebels' tents. The ground opens and swallows the rebellious households and possessions. Fire kills the 250 men offering incense. Their bronze firepans are made into an altar covering, a warning against unauthorized priestly service.

The next day, the people blame Moses and Aaron for the deaths. A plague begins. At Moses' direction, Aaron carries incense into the assembly and stands between the dead and living. The plague stops after 14,700 further deaths.

A second test places twelve named tribal staffs in the sanctuary. Aaron's staff sprouts, flowers, and produces almonds. It is preserved as a sign intended to end the complaints. The people respond with fear that approaching the sanctuary will bring death.

stories.title: Water from the Rock at Meribah
stories.summary:
Israel reaches Kadesh in the wilderness of Zin, where Miriam dies and is buried. A water shortage brings another confrontation with Moses and Aaron. The people wish they had died earlier and accuse their leaders of bringing them to a place without crops, fruit, or water.

Moses and Aaron fall facedown at the meeting tent, and God's glory appears. God tells Moses to take the staff, gather the community, and speak to the rock. Water is to come out for both the people and their livestock.

Moses gathers the assembly and addresses them as rebels, asking whether he and Aaron must bring water from the rock. He then strikes it twice with his staff. Abundant water flows, and the people and animals drink.

God tells Moses and Aaron that they failed to trust him and uphold his holiness before Israel. They therefore will not lead the people into the promised land. The water is named Meribah, recalling the community's quarrel with God.

stories.title: Edom Refuses Passage and Aaron Dies
stories.summary:
From Kadesh, Moses sends messengers to Edom's king, appealing to kinship and recounting Israel's suffering and release from Egypt. He asks permission to use the main road through Edom. Israel promises to avoid fields and vineyards and not take well water. Edom refuses and threatens armed resistance.

The Israelites repeat that they only want to pass through, offering payment for any water used by people or livestock. Edom again refuses and comes out with a large force. Israel turns away instead of crossing the border.

The people then reach Mount Hor. God tells Moses and Aaron that Aaron will die without entering the promised land because of their rebellion at Meribah. Moses must take Aaron and his son Eleazar up the mountain and transfer Aaron's priestly garments to Eleazar.

The three ascend before the community. Moses carries out the transfer, and Aaron dies on the summit. Moses and Eleazar return without him. When the people learn of his death, they mourn for thirty days.

stories.title: The Bronze Serpent
stories.summary:
As Israel travels around Edom, the people become impatient with the journey. They speak against God and Moses, complaining that they have been brought from Egypt to die. They say they lack bread and water and despise the food available to them.

God sends venomous snakes among them, and many people die from bites. The people acknowledge that they have sinned by speaking against God and Moses. They ask Moses to pray for the snakes to be removed, and he prays on their behalf.

God tells Moses to make a serpent and place it on a pole. Anyone bitten can look at it and live. Moses makes the figure from bronze and raises it as instructed. The passage ends by describing bitten people surviving when they look toward the bronze serpent.

stories.title: Victories over Sihon and Og
stories.summary:
Israel travels through a series of camps along the edges of Moab and Amorite territory. The account includes fragments of songs about the landscape and a well where God provides water. The people celebrate the well and continue toward Pisgah.

Israel asks Sihon, king of the Amorites, for peaceful passage along the main road. They promise not to enter fields or vineyards or use the wells. Sihon refuses and brings his forces out to fight at Jahaz. Israel defeats him and takes his territory between the Arnon and Jabbok, occupying Heshbon and surrounding towns.

The narrative explains that Sihon had previously taken Heshbon from Moab and includes a poem recalling those conflicts. Israel also captures the settlements around Jazer and drives out their Amorite inhabitants.

When Israel advances toward Bashan, King Og comes out to battle at Edrei. God tells Moses not to fear and promises the same outcome as against Sihon. Israel defeats Og, his sons, and his people, leaving no survivors according to the account, and takes the land.

stories.title: Balaam and Balak
stories.summary:
Alarmed by Israel's numbers and victories, Balak of Moab sends for Balaam to curse them. God initially forbids Balaam to go because Israel is blessed. A second delegation offers greater honor. God permits the journey with a restriction: Balaam must speak only what God commands.

During the journey, God becomes angry, and an armed angel blocks the road. Balaam cannot see the angel, but his donkey does. She turns aside, presses against a wall, and finally lies down. Balaam strikes her each time. God enables the donkey to speak, then opens Balaam's eyes. The angel says the donkey has saved his life and repeats the restriction on his words.

Balak brings Balaam to successive viewpoints overlooking Israel and arranges sacrifices. Instead of curses, Balaam repeatedly announces blessings. His speeches describe Israel's numbers, strength, divine protection, and future prosperity. Balak becomes furious and withdraws his promised reward, but Balaam insists that payment cannot change God's words.

Before leaving, Balaam gives further sayings about the future. A star and scepter from Israel signify a ruler who will defeat Moab and Edom. Other sayings announce trouble for Amalek, the Kenites, and further nations. Balaam and Balak then depart separately.

stories.title: Baal of Peor
stories.summary:
While Israel camps at Shittim, men become sexually involved with Moabite women and join meals and worship connected with their gods. The people attach themselves to Baal of Peor, provoking God's anger. God orders punishment, and Moses instructs Israel's judges to kill those under their authority who have joined this worship.

As the assembly weeps at the meeting tent, an Israelite man brings a Midianite woman into the camp in public view. Phinehas, Aaron's grandson, takes a spear, follows them into a tent, and kills them both. The account links this act with the end of a plague that has killed twenty-four thousand people.

God says Phinehas has turned away divine anger and grants him a covenant of peace and an enduring priesthood for his descendants. The dead pair are identified as Zimri, a Simeonite leader, and Cozbi, the daughter of a Midianite leader. The passage closes with God's order to attack the Midianites for their role in the events at Peor.

stories.title: A New Census and Joshua Appointed
stories.summary:
After the plague, Moses and Eleazar count Israel's men aged twenty and older who can serve in war. The census takes place on Moab's plains near the Jordan. It lists tribal families and totals 601,730 men. Land is to be distributed according to tribal numbers, with allocation by lot. The Levites are counted separately and receive no tribal land inheritance. The account notes that, apart from Caleb and Joshua, the earlier census generation has died.

Zelophehad's five daughters ask for their father's inheritance because he left no sons. Moses brings their case to God, who upholds their claim. The ruling establishes an inheritance order beginning with a daughter when no son exists, then other close relatives.

God tells Moses to view the land from the mountains of Abarim before his death. He will not enter because of his conduct at Meribah. Moses asks for a successor so the people will not be like sheep without a shepherd.

God chooses Joshua and directs Moses to commission him publicly before Eleazar and the assembly. Joshua will seek guidance through the priest. Moses lays his hands on Joshua and gives him authority as instructed.

stories.title: Vengeance on Midian
stories.summary:
God commands a campaign against Midian before Moses' death. Moses sends twelve thousand armed men, one thousand from each tribe, with Phinehas and sacred equipment. They kill Midianite males, including five kings and Balaam, burn settlements, and bring women, children, livestock, and goods back as captives and plunder.

Moses is angry that the women were spared. He attributes Israel's wrongdoing at Peor to their involvement under Balaam's advice. He orders the killing of the boys and of women who have had sex, while permitting girls who have not had sex to remain alive as captives.

Soldiers and captives must remain outside camp and undergo purification. Clothing and equipment also require cleansing, with fire used for metals that can withstand it. The captives and animals are counted and divided between the soldiers and the wider community. Portions from each share are assigned to the priest and Levites.

The commanders report that none of their soldiers is missing. They bring captured gold ornaments as an offering to make atonement, seeking to address guilt before God. Moses and Eleazar place the gold in the meeting tent as a memorial.

stories.title: Tribes Settle East of the Jordan
stories.summary:
The tribes of Reuben and Gad see that land east of the Jordan suits their large herds. They ask Moses, Eleazar, and the leaders to grant it to them rather than send them across the river. Moses objects that their brothers would have to fight while they remain behind. He compares their request with the spies' discouraging report and warns against renewing that failure.

They propose building protected settlements for their families and pens for their animals, then crossing armed with the others. They promise not to return home until the rest of Israel has received its inheritance. Their own land will remain east of the river.

Moses accepts on those terms and warns them that failing to keep the agreement will make them guilty before God. He states the conditions publicly to Eleazar, Joshua, and the tribal leaders. Reuben and Gad reaffirm their commitment.

Moses assigns the conquered kingdoms of Sihon and Og to them and half the tribe of Manasseh. The closing list describes towns rebuilt, fortified, captured, or renamed, including settlements taken by descendants of Manasseh.

stories.title: Moses Recalls the Wilderness Years
stories.summary:
Speaking east of the Jordan in the fortieth year, Moses recalls the journey from Horeb. God had commanded Israel to move toward the land promised to their ancestors. As the people grew, Moses appointed tribal leaders and judges, instructing them to hear cases fairly and bring him the difficult ones.

At Kadesh Barnea, the people proposed sending scouts into Canaan. The scouts brought fruit and called the land good, but reports of strong inhabitants frightened the community. Moses recalls urging trust, yet the people refused to advance. God barred that generation from the land, with named exceptions. Their later attempt to invade against God's warning ended in defeat.

Moses then recounts the long journey around Seir and past Moab and Ammon. God prohibited attacks on these peoples because their lands had been assigned to Esau's and Lot's descendants. The earlier fighting generation died during the years of wandering.

Israel defeated Sihon and Og after confrontations east of the Jordan. Moses describes the destruction of their towns and inhabitants, including women and children, and the taking of livestock and goods. Their territories were assigned to Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh, whose fighters still had to help the other tribes. Moses encouraged Joshua, then asked to cross the Jordan himself. God refused, allowing him only to view the land and directing him to strengthen Joshua.

stories.title: Moses Sets Apart Three Cities of Refuge
stories.summary:
Moses designates three cities east of the Jordan as places of refuge. A person who kills someone unintentionally, without previous hatred, may flee to one of them and preserve his life.

The cities are Bezer in the wilderness plateau for Reuben, Ramoth in Gilead for Gad, and Golan in Bashan for Manasseh. This brief passage names the locations and the kind of killing covered by the protection. It does not describe a particular fugitive or an individual case.

stories.title: Moses Recalls the Golden Calf
stories.summary:
Moses urges Israel to remember its repeated rebellion rather than forget it. He recalls spending forty days and nights without food or water on Horeb, receiving the stone tablets of the covenant. God then told him to descend because the people had made an image and abandoned the commanded way. God proposed destroying them and making a greater nation from Moses.

Moses came down carrying the tablets and saw the calf. He broke the tablets before the people. He recounts another period of fasting and pleading because he feared God's anger would destroy them. He also prayed for Aaron, whom God threatened to destroy. Moses burned the calf, ground it to dust, and threw the dust into the stream flowing from the mountain.

He names other places where the people provoked God, including Kadesh Barnea, where they refused to enter the land. The passage closes with his appeal for mercy. Israel remained God's people, rescued from Egypt, and God's promises to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob still mattered. Moses also argued that destruction would give Egypt grounds to misunderstand God's power and purpose.

stories.title: Moses Recalls the Second Tablets
stories.summary:
Moses recalls God's command to cut two new stone tablets and make a wooden ark, or chest. He made the chest from acacia wood and carried the tablets up the mountain. God wrote the same ten commandments spoken from the fire and gave the tablets back to him. Moses then placed them inside the ark.

The passage interrupts this recollection with a short travel account. It locates Aaron's death and burial at Moserah and says Eleazar succeeded him as priest. Further stages lead to Jotbathah, a place with streams. It also describes the Levites' appointment to carry the ark, serve before God, and pronounce blessings. Their service to God replaces a territorial inheritance among the tribes.

Moses returns to his forty-day stay on the mountain and says God again listened rather than destroying Israel. The account ends with God's instruction that he resume leading the people toward possession of the land promised to their ancestors.

stories.title: Joshua Commissioned and the Law Entrusted
stories.summary:
Moses tells Israel that he is 120 and will not cross the Jordan. Joshua will lead them, and God will go before them as in the victories over Sihon and Og. Moses urges the people to be courageous and publicly gives Joshua the same encouragement.

He writes the law and entrusts it to the priests and elders. Every seventh year, during the festival of booths, it must be read to the gathered community. Men, women, children, and foreign residents are to hear it, learn its commands, and pass that knowledge to the next generation.

God then summons Moses and Joshua to the meeting tent. Appearing in a cloud, God predicts that Israel will turn to other gods after Moses dies. Prosperity will be followed by betrayal of the covenant and suffering. Moses is told to write and teach a song that will remain as a witness against the people.

Joshua receives his commission and God's promise of presence. Moses orders the completed law placed beside the ark as another witness. He warns the leaders about future rebellion, calls heaven and earth as witnesses, and recites the song to the assembly. Its words follow beyond this passage.

stories.title: The Death of Moses
stories.summary:
Moses climbs Mount Nebo from the plains of Moab and reaches the summit of Pisgah, opposite Jericho. God shows him the land stretching across the regions named for Israel's tribes, toward the sea and the southern plain. God identifies it as the land promised to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Moses may see it but will not cross into it.

He dies in Moab at 120. The account says his sight and strength have not failed. He is buried in a valley opposite Beth Peor, and the location of his grave remains unknown. Israel mourns for thirty days.

Joshua, on whom Moses had laid his hands, is described as filled with wisdom. The people listen to him and follow the commands given through Moses. The closing assessment presents Moses as unmatched among Israel's prophets. It recalls his direct relationship with God, the signs performed in Egypt, and the powerful deeds witnessed by the whole people.

stories.title: Joshua Commissioned
stories.summary:
After Moses dies, God directs Joshua to lead Israel across the Jordan and into the land promised to their ancestors. God promises to remain with him as he was with Moses and repeatedly calls him to courage. Joshua must study and follow Moses' law rather than turn away from it. The commission connects his leadership with both the coming conquest and obedience to those instructions.

Joshua orders the camp to prepare food because the crossing will begin within three days. He also addresses Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh, whose land lies east of the river. Their families and livestock may remain there, but their fighting men must help the other tribes secure their own territory. Only then may they return home. They pledge to follow Joshua's commands, call for punishment of anyone who rebels, and urge him to be strong and courageous.

stories.title: Rahab and the Spies
stories.summary:
Joshua secretly sends two men to inspect Jericho, where they lodge at the house of Rahab, a prostitute. When the king demands their surrender, she hides them beneath flax on her roof. She tells the king's men that the visitors have already left, sending the search in the wrong direction.

Rahab tells the spies that reports of Israel's escape from Egypt and victories beyond the Jordan have terrified the inhabitants. She acknowledges Israel's God and asks them to spare her family because she has protected them. They agree, provided she keeps their mission secret and gathers her relatives inside her house. A scarlet cord in the window will identify it; anyone outside will not be covered by their promise.

She lowers the men through a window in the city wall and advises them to hide in the hills for three days. They evade their pursuers and return to Joshua. Their report emphasizes the fear they have found and their confidence that Israel will gain the land.

stories.title: Crossing the Jordan
stories.summary:
Israel camps beside the Jordan while officers explain how to follow the priests carrying the covenant ark. Joshua tells the people to prepare themselves for what God will do. God promises that the crossing will establish Joshua's standing as Moses' successor.

The river is overflowing its banks when the priests step into the water. The upstream flow stops, and the water below drains away. The priests remain on dry ground in the riverbed while the people cross opposite Jericho. Armed men from the eastern tribes join the crossing ahead of the others.

At Joshua's direction, twelve representatives carry stones from the riverbed to the new campsite. Joshua also sets up twelve stones where the priests have stood. When the priests finally leave the river, its waters return to their former level.

The people camp at Gilgal, where Joshua arranges the stones as a lasting reminder. Future generations are to hear how Israel crossed on dry ground, just as their ancestors crossed the Red Sea. The account presents the crossing as a display of God's power and a confirmation of Joshua's leadership.

stories.title: Circumcision and Passover at Gilgal
stories.summary:
Reports of the Jordan crossing leave the neighboring kings afraid. At Gilgal, God orders Joshua to circumcise the Israelite males born during the wilderness journey. The account explains that the men who left Egypt had been circumcised, but the generation born afterward had not. The earlier fighting generation died in the wilderness after refusing to obey God.

The people remain in camp until they recover. God declares that the reproach of Egypt has been removed, and the passage connects this declaration with the place's name, Gilgal. Israel then celebrates Passover on the plains near Jericho. After they eat bread and roasted grain from the land, the manna stops. From that point, they eat Canaan's produce.

Near Jericho, Joshua encounters a man holding a drawn sword. Asked which side he supports, the figure identifies himself as commander of God's army. Joshua bows and asks for instructions. The commander tells him to remove his sandals because the ground is holy, and Joshua obeys.

stories.title: The Fall of Jericho
stories.summary:
Jericho closes its gates against Israel. God tells Joshua that the city will fall and gives instructions for a procession around its walls. For six days, soldiers and priests carrying the covenant ark circle the city once. Seven priests sound ram's horns, while the people remain silent.

On the seventh day, they circle seven times. At Joshua's command, the people shout as the horns sound, and the walls collapse. Israel enters the city and kills its inhabitants, including young and old, along with its livestock. Joshua has forbidden taking goods for private use. Gold, silver, bronze, and iron are reserved for God's treasury, and the rest of the city is burned.

The two spies bring Rahab and her relatives out of her house, honoring the promise made when she sheltered them. They survive and are brought outside Israel's camp; the narrator later describes Rahab as living among Israel. Joshua pronounces a curse on anyone who rebuilds Jericho, linking its foundations and gates with the loss of that person's sons. His reputation spreads throughout the land.

stories.title: Achan's Sin and Ai
stories.summary:
