Israel's first attack on Ai fails, and about thirty-six men die. Joshua mourns before the covenant ark, fearing that surrounding peoples will destroy Israel. God attributes the defeat to a violation of the command concerning Jericho's goods and orders an inquiry.

The selection narrows from tribe to household until Achan is identified. He admits taking a robe, silver, and gold and hiding them beneath his tent. Messengers recover the objects. Achan, his children, animals, and possessions are taken to the Valley of Achor, where the account describes stoning and burning. A stone heap marks the place, and God's anger subsides.

God then directs another attack on Ai, this time allowing Israel to keep livestock and goods. Joshua sets an ambush and draws the defenders away by pretending to retreat. The hidden force enters and burns the city, trapping its people between Israel's forces. Ai's inhabitants are killed, and its king is executed and buried beneath stones.

Afterward, Joshua builds an altar on Mount Ebal and copies Moses' law onto stones. With the people gathered near Mounts Ebal and Gerizim, he reads its blessings and curses. Women, children, and resident foreigners hear the entire reading alongside the rest of Israel.

stories.title: The Gibeonite Deception
stories.summary:
While neighboring kings prepare to fight Israel, the people of Gibeon seek protection through deception. Their representatives arrive wearing worn clothing and carrying damaged wineskins and moldy bread. They claim to have traveled from a distant country and ask Joshua for a treaty.

Israel's leaders question their origins but accept the apparent evidence without consulting God. Joshua makes peace with them, and the leaders swear to let them live. Three days later, Israel learns that these visitors belong to nearby towns within the land. The people complain, but the leaders insist that their oath still prevents an attack.

Joshua confronts the Gibeonites, who explain that they feared destruction after hearing of God's command to Moses. He spares their lives but assigns them permanent labor cutting wood and drawing water. Their work serves the community and God's altar. The passage ends with the agreement preserved, though the deception leaves the Gibeonites in a subordinate position.

stories.title: The Sun Stands Still
stories.summary:
Five Amorite kings attack Gibeon after it makes peace with Israel. The Gibeonites appeal to Joshua, who marches overnight from Gilgal to help them. God promises victory, and the attackers flee before Israel. During the pursuit, large hailstones kill more of the enemy than Israel's weapons do.

Joshua calls for the sun to stand over Gibeon and the moon over the Valley of Aijalon. The account says daylight is prolonged until Israel defeats its enemies. Citing the Book of Jashar, it presents this as an unmatched day when God answered a human voice and fought for Israel.

The five kings hide in a cave at Makkedah. Joshua seals its entrance while the pursuit continues, then brings the captured kings before his commanders. They place their feet on the kings' necks before Joshua executes them. Their bodies are later placed inside the cave, which is blocked with stones.

The narrative continues through a southern campaign against several cities, describing the killing of their inhabitants and rulers. It attributes the victories to God's support and ends with Joshua and Israel returning to Gilgal.

stories.title: Northern Campaign and the Land Taken
stories.summary:
Jabin of Hazor assembles northern kings and a large army with horses and chariots near the waters of Merom. God tells Joshua not to fear them and orders him to disable their horses and burn their chariots. Israel attacks suddenly, defeats the coalition, and pursues the fleeing forces.

Joshua captures Hazor, kills its ruler and inhabitants, and burns the city. Other captured cities are not burned, although their inhabitants are killed and their goods and livestock taken. The account describes these actions as fulfillment of commands given through Moses. It also says that God hardened the opposing peoples' hearts so that they fought rather than sought peace.

The narrative summarizes a lengthy campaign across the land and the removal of the Anakim from Israel's hill country. Some remain in Gaza, Gath, and Ashdod. Joshua distributes territory among the tribes, and the land rests from war.

A closing list distinguishes earlier victories under Moses east of the Jordan from Joshua's victories in the west. It names Sihon and Og in the east and counts thirty-one defeated kings in the west.

stories.title: Caleb Receives Hebron
stories.summary:
Caleb approaches Joshua at Gilgal and recalls the promise made to him when Moses sent scouts into Canaan. He says that he gave an honest report while the other scouts frightened the people. Because he followed God wholeheartedly, Moses promised that the land he had explored would belong to him and his descendants.

Forty-five years have passed, and Caleb is now eighty-five. He declares that he remains strong enough for battle and asks for the hill country containing Hebron. He acknowledges that the Anakim and fortified cities are still there, but expresses confidence that, with God's help, he can drive them out.

Joshua blesses Caleb and grants him Hebron as his inheritance. The narrator again connects this grant with Caleb's loyalty to God. The passage notes Hebron's earlier name, Kiriath Arba, and ends by saying that the land has rest from war.

stories.title: The Altar by the Jordan
stories.summary:
Joshua releases the warriors of Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh to return to their land east of the Jordan. He praises their service, urges them to keep God's commands, and tells them to share their wealth with those at home.

On their journey, they build a large altar beside the Jordan. The other tribes interpret it as a rival place of sacrifice and gather for war. Before attacking, they send the priest Phinehas and ten leaders to investigate. The delegation warns that rebellion could bring punishment on all Israel and offers land on the western side instead.

The eastern tribes explain that the altar is not intended for offerings. They fear that future generations might treat the river as a religious boundary and deny their descendants a place among God's people. Their altar copies the authorized one as a witness to their shared worship, rather than replacing it.

Phinehas and the leaders accept the explanation. When they report back, the threatened war is abandoned. The altar stands as a witness that the tribes on both sides acknowledge the same God.

stories.title: Joshua's Farewell and Covenant at Shechem
stories.summary:
Near the end of his life, Joshua gathers Israel's leaders and recalls their victories. He urges them to follow Moses' law and remain loyal to God. He warns that alliances, intermarriage, and worship of neighboring gods will endanger their place in the land. Just as the promised benefits have arrived, he says, the threatened consequences can follow disobedience.

At Shechem, Joshua recounts Israel's story in God's voice, beginning with Abraham's family beyond the Euphrates. He recalls the departure from Egypt, the wilderness journey, and the occupation of towns and fields they did not create. Joshua asks the people to abandon other gods and choose whom they will serve. He declares that his own household will serve God.

The people repeatedly pledge the same loyalty, despite Joshua's warnings about the seriousness of their commitment. He establishes a covenant, records its terms, and sets up a large stone as a witness. The assembly then returns home.

Joshua dies at 110 and is buried in his inheritance. The closing notices describe Israel's loyalty during his lifetime and that of the surviving elders. They also record the burial of Joseph's bones at Shechem and the death and burial of Eleazar the priest.

stories.title: Incomplete Conquest
stories.summary:
After Joshua's death, Judah and Simeon join forces to fight the remaining inhabitants of their territories. They defeat Adoni-Bezek and cut off his thumbs and big toes. He describes this as repayment for his own treatment of captured kings. The account then follows attacks on Jerusalem and several southern towns.

At Debir, Caleb offers his daughter Achsah in marriage to the man who captures the town. Othniel succeeds, and Achsah later asks Caleb for springs to accompany her land. The house of Joseph also captures Bethel after a resident shows its entrance. That man and his family are spared.

The account repeatedly notes places where Israel does not remove the existing population. Some groups remain independent, while others are subjected to forced labor. Judah cannot dislodge the inhabitants of the plain with their iron chariots, and Dan is confined to the hills.

God's messenger confronts Israel at Bochim for making agreements with local peoples and failing to destroy their altars. He announces that these peoples and their gods will remain a danger. The people weep and offer sacrifices.

stories.title: The Cycle of the Judges
stories.summary:
The passage returns to Joshua's lifetime, when Israel settles its allotted territories and serves God under leaders who witnessed the earlier victories. Joshua dies at 110, and eventually that entire generation passes away. A later generation does not know God or the deeds associated with Israel's past.

The narrator describes a recurring pattern. Israel turns to the gods of neighboring peoples, especially Baal and the Ashtaroth. God then allows raiders and enemies to overpower them. In response to their suffering, God raises judges, leaders who rescue the people and govern them. Relief lasts during a judge's lifetime, but after the leader dies, the people return to practices the narrator condemns.

God declares that the remaining nations will no longer be driven out. Their presence will test whether Israel follows the commands given through Moses. The passage also says that these conflicts teach warfare to generations without experience of it. It ends with Israelites living among neighboring peoples, marrying into their families, and worshiping their gods.

stories.title: Othniel, Ehud and Shamgar
stories.summary:
After Israel turns to other gods, Cushan-Rishathaim of Mesopotamia rules over them for eight years. When the people call for help, God raises Othniel. Empowered by God's spirit, he defeats the king and leads Israel through forty years of peace.

After Othniel's death, renewed wrongdoing is followed by eighteen years under Eglon of Moab. Ehud, a left-handed Benjaminite, carries Israel's tribute to him with a short sword concealed on his right thigh. After delivering the tribute, Ehud returns and requests a private audience, claiming a secret message. Alone with Eglon, he draws the sword with his left hand and kills him.

Ehud locks the room and escapes while the servants delay entering. He then summons Israelites from Ephraim's hills and leads them to seize the Jordan crossings. They prevent the Moabites from escaping and kill about ten thousand of their fighting men. Moab's domination ends, followed by eighty years of peace.

A brief final notice introduces Shamgar, who kills six hundred Philistines with an ox goad, a tool used to drive cattle. The narrator also credits him with rescuing Israel.

stories.title: Deborah and Barak
stories.summary:
Israel suffers twenty years under Jabin of Hazor and his commander Sisera, whose army has nine hundred iron chariots. Deborah, a prophet and judge, summons Barak to gather troops from Naphtali and Zebulun. She announces that God will draw Sisera to the Kishon River and defeat him. Barak agrees to go only if Deborah accompanies him. She consents but says that a woman will receive the honor of overcoming Sisera.

Barak descends from Mount Tabor with ten thousand men, and Sisera's army is thrown into confusion. While Barak pursues and destroys the force, Sisera escapes on foot to Jael's tent. She welcomes him, gives him milk, and covers him. When he sleeps, she kills him with a tent peg and shows his body to Barak.

A song attributed to Deborah and Barak celebrates the victory through images of storm, stars, and the rushing Kishon. It praises those who joined the battle and criticizes those who stayed away. Jael's killing of Sisera receives particular praise. The song also imagines his mother waiting for his return and expecting plunder. The account ends with forty years of peace.

stories.title: Gideon and the Midianites
stories.summary:
Midianite raids destroy Israel's crops and livestock, driving people into hiding. A divine messenger calls Gideon while he threshes wheat in a winepress. Gideon questions why Israel is suffering and doubts his own standing, but God promises to be with him. Fire consuming an offering confirms the encounter. Gideon then destroys his father's altar to Baal at night and survives the townspeople's demand for his death.

After gathering fighters, Gideon asks for two signs involving dew and a fleece. God grants both, then reduces his force to three hundred so Israel cannot claim victory through its own strength. Gideon gains further confidence after overhearing an enemy soldier's dream. His men surround the camp with trumpets, jars, and concealed torches. Their sudden noise and lights accompany confusion in which the enemy turns its weapons against itself.

Other Israelites join the pursuit. Gideon captures the kings Zebah and Zalmunna and kills them after learning they killed his brothers. He also punishes Succoth and Penuel for refusing supplies to his exhausted men.

Gideon refuses an offer of hereditary rule, saying that God should rule Israel. Yet he collects gold and makes an ephod, a sacred object that becomes a focus of improper worship. Israel rests for forty years during his lifetime. After his death, the people return to Baal worship and fail to show loyalty to his household.

stories.title: Abimelech
stories.summary:
Abimelech persuades his mother's relatives in Shechem to support him as ruler rather than the other sons of Gideon. With money from Baal-Berith's temple, he hires followers and kills his brothers at Ophrah. Only the youngest, Jotham, escapes. Shechem then makes Abimelech king.

From Mount Gerizim, Jotham tells a fable in which useful trees reject kingship, leaving a thornbush to accept it and threaten fire. He challenges Shechem's treatment of Gideon's family and predicts mutual destruction between the city and its new ruler. Jotham then flees.

After three years, the alliance breaks down. The narrator attributes the hostility to God as repayment for the brothers' deaths. Gaal challenges Abimelech, but the city's official Zebul secretly alerts the king. Abimelech defeats Gaal, destroys Shechem, and burns a stronghold containing about a thousand men and women.

He next attacks Thebez, where the inhabitants shelter in a tower. As he approaches to burn it, a woman drops a millstone onto his head. Mortally injured, he orders his armor-bearer to kill him so people will not say a woman did it. His army disperses. The narrator presents these deaths as the fulfillment of Jotham's curse.

stories.title: Jephthah's Vow
stories.summary:
After years of oppression, Israel abandons foreign gods and asks for rescue. Gilead's leaders recruit Jephthah, a fighter whose mother was a prostitute. His half-brothers had expelled him and denied him an inheritance as another woman's son. He agrees to lead them against Ammon on condition that he remain their chief afterward.

Jephthah first exchanges messages with the Ammonite king, disputing his claim to the contested land. He recounts Israel's journey and argues that the territory was taken from the Amorites, not Ammon. The king refuses his explanation. Before battle, Jephthah vows to offer as a burnt offering whatever comes from his house to meet him if he returns victorious.

After defeating Ammon, Jephthah comes home to find his only child, a daughter, celebrating his return. He grieves but says he cannot withdraw his vow. She asks for two months with her companions to mourn her unmarried life. When she returns, the narrator says he carries out the vow. Israelite women subsequently commemorate her for four days each year.

A dispute with Ephraim then becomes civil war. Jephthah's men seize the Jordan crossings and identify fleeing Ephraimites by their pronunciation of the word Shibboleth. Thousands are killed. Jephthah leads Israel for six years before his death.

stories.title: Samson
stories.summary:
During Philistine domination, a divine messenger announces Samson's birth to Manoah's childless wife. He is to be a Nazirite, a person specially dedicated to God, with uncut hair. His parents receive instructions, and the messenger ascends in the flame of their offering. Samson grows up, and God's spirit begins to move him.

Samson seeks a Philistine wife at Timnah. A lion he kills and the honey later found in its carcass inspire a wedding riddle. Threatened guests pressure his wife to obtain its answer. Samson kills thirty men to pay his wager and leaves in anger. After learning that his wife has been given to another man, he burns Philistine crops using animals carrying torches. Retaliation and further killings follow. When Judah hands him over bound, he breaks free and kills a thousand Philistines with a donkey's jawbone.

Later, Samson escapes a trap in Gaza by carrying away its gates. Philistine rulers then pay Delilah to discover the source of his strength. After several false answers, he tells her about his uncut hair. While he sleeps, his hair is shaved; the Philistines capture, blind, and imprison him.

At a celebration for Dagon, Samson is brought out for entertainment. He asks God for strength and vengeance, then pushes against the supporting pillars. The building collapses, killing him and the people gathered there. His family retrieves and buries his body. The account credits him with twenty years as Israel's judge.

stories.title: Micah's Idols and the Danites
stories.summary:
Micah admits taking silver from his mother and returns it. She dedicates silver for sacred images, which are placed in his house. He establishes a private shrine and later hires a wandering Levite as priest, expecting this arrangement to bring God's favor.

Meanwhile, Danite scouts seek territory for their tribe. They visit Micah's house and ask the priest about their journey; he gives an encouraging response. They then find Laish, whose inhabitants live securely and are isolated from potential allies. The scouts recommend taking the town.

Six hundred armed Danites set out. Passing Micah's house, they seize his images and other sacred objects. They persuade the priest to join them by offering service to an entire tribe rather than one household. Micah pursues them with neighbors, but their threats force him to turn back.

The Danites attack Laish, kill its inhabitants, burn it, and rebuild it under the name Dan. They install Micah's image and establish a priestly line there. The narrative frames these events with the observation that Israel has no king and people act according to their own judgment.

stories.title: The Levite and Gibeah
stories.summary:
A Levite travels to Bethlehem to bring back his concubine, a woman in a secondary marital relationship. On their return, they lodge with an older man in Gibeah. A mob surrounds the house and demands the Levite for sexual assault. The host offers women instead, and the Levite sends his concubine outside. The men rape and abuse her throughout the night. She collapses at the doorway and does not answer when he finds her.

Back home, the Levite cuts her body into twelve pieces and sends them throughout Israel. An assembly demands that Benjamin surrender the perpetrators, but the tribe refuses. Civil war follows. Israel suffers two major defeats before an ambush destroys Gibeah and routs Benjamin. Only six hundred Benjaminite men escape to the wilderness, while Israel devastates their towns.

The victors then mourn the possible disappearance of an entire tribe. Their oath not to give daughters to Benjamin creates another crisis. They attack Jabesh-Gilead for failing to join the assembly, killing its inhabitants except four hundred unmarried women. These women are given to the surviving Benjaminites.

When more wives are needed, the leaders authorize the remaining men to seize women dancing at a festival in Shiloh. The survivors return to rebuild their towns. The book ends by repeating that Israel has no king and everyone does what seems right to them.

stories.title: Naomi and Ruth Return to Bethlehem
stories.summary:
A famine drives Elimelech, Naomi, and their two sons from Bethlehem to Moab. Elimelech dies there. The sons marry Moabite women, Orpah and Ruth, but both men also die, leaving three widows. After hearing that food is again available in Judah, Naomi prepares to return home.

Her daughters-in-law begin the journey with her, but Naomi urges them to return to their mothers' households and seek new marriages. She says she cannot provide other sons for them to marry and describes her losses as God's hand against her. All three weep. Orpah eventually leaves, while Ruth refuses to separate from Naomi.

Ruth pledges to share Naomi's home, people, God, and burial place. Seeing her determination, Naomi stops urging her to go back. They reach Bethlehem as the barley harvest begins. When the townspeople recognize Naomi, she asks to be called Mara, meaning bitter, rather than Naomi. She says she left with a full household and has returned empty, with Ruth beside her.

stories.title: Ruth Gleans in Boaz's Field
stories.summary:
Ruth asks Naomi's permission to gather grain left behind by harvesters. She happens to enter a field belonging to Boaz, a wealthy relative of Naomi's late husband. When Boaz asks about her, his supervisor identifies her as the Moabite woman who returned with Naomi.

Boaz tells Ruth to remain in his fields beside his female workers. He has ordered the men not to harm her and allows her to drink their water. Ruth asks why he is treating a foreigner so kindly. He explains that he has heard of her loyalty to Naomi and her departure from her own family and homeland.

At mealtime, Boaz offers her food. He also privately tells the workers to let her gather among the bundles and deliberately leave extra grain. Ruth returns home with a substantial amount of barley and food saved from the meal.

Naomi learns whose field Ruth visited and explains that Boaz is a close relative. She encourages Ruth to remain where she will be safe. Ruth continues gathering through both barley and wheat harvests while living with Naomi.

stories.title: The Threshing Floor
stories.summary:
Naomi seeks a secure future for Ruth and devises a plan involving Boaz, their close relative. She tells Ruth to wash, dress, and go to the threshing floor, where Boaz is processing barley. Ruth must wait until he finishes eating and lies down, then uncover his feet and lie there.

At midnight, Boaz wakes and discovers her. Ruth identifies herself and asks him to spread his garment over her because he is a relative able to protect the family's interests. Boaz praises her choice not to pursue younger men and promises to act for her. However, another relative has a prior claim. He will first give that man the opportunity, then take responsibility himself if the man declines.

Ruth remains until early morning and leaves before she can be recognized. Boaz gives her six measures of barley so she will not return to Naomi empty-handed. After hearing Ruth's report, Naomi tells her to wait. She expects Boaz to settle the matter that day.

stories.title: Boaz Redeems and Marries Ruth
stories.summary:
Boaz meets the closer relative at Bethlehem's gate and gathers ten elders as witnesses. He explains that Naomi is selling land associated with Elimelech's family. The man initially agrees to buy it, but Boaz links the transaction with Ruth and preserving her dead husband's name through an heir. The man then withdraws, saying the arrangement could damage his own inheritance.

Following the custom described in the passage, the relative removes his sandal to confirm the transfer of his right. Boaz publicly declares that he is acquiring the family's property and taking Ruth as his wife. The elders and gathered people witness the agreement and pronounce blessings on their household.

Ruth and Boaz marry, and she gives birth to a son. Bethlehem's women celebrate with Naomi, saying that Ruth's love and the child's birth will sustain her in old age. Naomi takes the baby into her care. The child is named Obed, and the closing genealogy identifies him as Jesse's father and David's grandfather.

stories.title: Hannah and the Birth of Samuel
stories.summary:
Hannah travels with her husband Elkanah's household to worship at Shiloh each year. She has no children, while his other wife, Peninnah, has several and repeatedly taunts her. During one visit, Hannah prays in deep distress and promises that a son, if granted, will be dedicated to God throughout his life.

The priest Eli sees her moving lips without hearing words and assumes she is drunk. Hannah explains that she is pouring out her grief, not drinking. Eli responds with a blessing, and she leaves able to eat again.

Hannah later bears Samuel and keeps him at home until he is weaned. She then brings him to Shiloh with offerings and tells Eli that this is the child for whom she prayed. She presents him for lifelong service as promised.

Her prayer celebrates God as one who reverses human fortunes, weakening the powerful and raising the poor. It describes life, death, wealth, and strength as subject to God's authority and ends with a reference to God's king. Samuel remains to serve under Eli while his family returns home.

stories.title: Eli's Sons and Samuel's Call
stories.summary:
Eli's sons misuse their priestly positions at Shiloh. Their servants take meat from sacrifices and demand portions before the fat is offered, threatening force when worshipers object. Eli also hears that his sons sleep with women serving at the sanctuary. He rebukes them, but they refuse to listen.

Meanwhile, Samuel serves there as a child. Hannah brings him a robe each year and later has other children. An unnamed man of God tells Eli that his household will lose its privileged position because he has honored his sons above God. Both sons will die on the same day, and a faithful priest will replace their line.

One night, Samuel repeatedly hears his name called and goes to Eli. After the third time, Eli realizes that God is calling and tells Samuel how to respond. God announces judgment on Eli's family because its wrongdoing has not been restrained.

Samuel fears telling Eli, but the older priest insists on hearing everything and accepts the message. As Samuel grows, his words are reliable. The passage ends with Israel recognizing him as a prophet through whom God speaks at Shiloh.

stories.title: The Ark Captured and Returned
stories.summary:
After a defeat by the Philistines, Israel brings the covenant ark from Shiloh into battle, expecting it to secure victory. Instead, the army suffers a greater defeat, the ark is captured, and Eli's sons are killed. Hearing the news, Eli falls from his seat and dies. His daughter-in-law dies after childbirth, naming her son Ichabod to express the loss of Israel's glory.

The Philistines place the ark beside Dagon's image in Ashdod. On successive mornings, the image is found fallen, then broken before it. Tumors and death strike the population. The ark is moved to Gath and then Ekron, but suffering follows, and the people demand its removal.

After seven months, Philistine religious advisers recommend returning it with gold models of tumors and mice as an offering. They place it on a cart pulled by cows separated from their calves. The cows travel directly to Beth-shemesh, which the advisers have proposed as a test of God's involvement.

Harvesters rejoice at its arrival and offer sacrifices. Yet deaths follow when people look into the ark. Frightened, the inhabitants ask Kiriath-jearim to take it. The ark is placed in Abinadab's house, with his son Eleazar appointed to guard it.

stories.title: Samuel Judges Israel
stories.summary:
After the ark has remained at Kiriath-jearim for twenty years, Israel turns toward God in grief. Samuel tells the people that a full return requires abandoning foreign gods and serving God alone. They remove the Baals and Ashtaroth and gather at Mizpah, where they fast, pour out water, and confess wrongdoing.

The Philistine rulers hear of the gathering and advance against it. Afraid, the Israelites ask Samuel to keep praying for their rescue. He offers a lamb and calls on God. As the Philistines approach, thunder throws them into confusion, and Israel pursues and defeats them.

Samuel raises a stone between Mizpah and Shen and calls it Ebenezer, marking the help received from God. The account describes Philistine pressure easing, captured towns being restored, and peace with the Amorites.

Samuel continues judging Israel throughout his life. Each year he travels a circuit through Bethel, Gilgal, and Mizpah, then returns to Ramah. His home and an altar he builds are there.

stories.title: Israel Demands a King
stories.summary:
As Samuel grows old, his sons accept bribes and distort justice. Israel's elders ask for a king who will govern and fight for them like rulers in other nations. God tells Samuel to allow the request but to warn of its costs. Samuel describes military service, forced labor, taxation, and royal seizure of land. The people remain determined.

Saul, a tall young Benjaminite, encounters Samuel while searching for his father's missing donkeys. God has identified him as Israel's future ruler. Samuel honors him at a meal, privately anoints him, and gives signs confirming the appointment. Saul later joins a group of prophets as God's spirit comes upon him.

At a public assembly, Saul is selected but found hiding among the baggage. The people acclaim him, though some question his ability. His standing strengthens when Nahash of Ammon threatens Jabesh-gilead. Saul gathers an army, defeats the attackers, and refuses demands to execute his earlier critics. The kingship is renewed at Gilgal.

Samuel then reviews his own public service and Israel's history. He warns that both king and people remain accountable to God. Thunder and rain during the harvest frighten the assembly, which asks him to pray. He promises continued prayer and instruction while urging loyalty rather than further wrongdoing.

stories.title: Saul Rejected
stories.summary:
Facing a large Philistine force, Saul waits at Gilgal as his troops begin to scatter. Before Samuel arrives, he offers the sacrifice himself. Samuel says that Saul has disobeyed and that his dynasty will not continue. Israel remains badly outmatched, with few weapons available.

Jonathan and his armor-bearer attack a Philistine outpost, setting off panic that spreads through the enemy camp. Saul's forces join the pursuit. However, Saul has forbidden eating until evening. Jonathan, unaware of the oath, eats honey; later, exhausted soldiers eat captured animals without properly draining the blood. When Jonathan's action is discovered, Saul declares that he must die, but the people intervene and save him.

Samuel next conveys a command to destroy Amalek completely, including its people and livestock. Saul defeats the Amalekites but spares King Agag and the best animals. Confronted by Samuel, he says the livestock was saved for sacrifice. Samuel replies that obedience matters more than offerings and announces Saul's rejection as king.

Saul admits wrongdoing and asks Samuel to honor him publicly. As Samuel turns away, Saul tears his robe, which Samuel interprets as a sign of the kingdom's removal. Samuel later kills Agag. The two men separate, and Samuel continues to mourn Saul while the account describes God's regret over making him king.

stories.title: David Anointed
stories.summary:
God directs Samuel to stop mourning Saul and go to Jesse in Bethlehem, where a new king has been chosen. Samuel fears Saul's reaction, so the visit is arranged around a sacrifice. Jesse and his sons are invited.

Samuel first assumes that Eliab's appearance marks him as the choice. God rejects that judgment, distinguishing outward appearance from the heart. Seven sons pass before Samuel without being chosen. He asks whether another remains, and Jesse sends for David, the youngest, who is tending sheep. At God's instruction, Samuel anoints him among his brothers. God's spirit comes upon David from that day.

The narrative then turns to Saul, from whom God's spirit has departed. He is troubled by a harmful spirit described as coming from God. His servants recommend a skilled musician to bring relief, and one recommends Jesse's son.

David enters Saul's service with gifts from his father. Saul grows fond of him and makes him an armor-bearer. Whenever the troubling spirit comes, David plays the harp, and Saul finds relief.

stories.title: David and Goliath
stories.summary:
Israel and the Philistines face each other across the Valley of Elah. For forty days, the heavily armed Goliath challenges Israel to send one fighter against him. Saul and his army are afraid. David arrives with food for his older brothers and hears the challenge, along with reports of the king's promised reward.

Despite his brother's anger and Saul's doubts about his youth, David volunteers. He recalls defending his father's sheep against a lion and a bear and says God can deliver him again. He tries Saul's armor but removes it because he is not accustomed to it. Instead, he carries his staff, sling, and five smooth stones.

Goliath mocks and threatens him. David replies that he comes in the name of Israel's God and that victory does not depend on swords or spears. He runs forward, slings a stone into Goliath's forehead, and brings him down. He then takes Goliath's sword and cuts off his head.

The Philistines flee, and Israel pursues them and plunders their camp. David keeps the armor and brings the head to Jerusalem. The passage closes with Saul asking about David's family, and David identifying himself as Jesse's son.

stories.title: Saul's Jealousy and David's Flight
stories.summary:
David forms a close bond and covenant with Jonathan while gaining success in Saul's service. Songs crediting David with greater victories anger Saul, who begins to view him as a rival. Saul attacks him with a spear and later seeks to expose him to death through dangerous military service. David survives and marries Saul's daughter Michal after fulfilling a violent bride-price demand against the Philistines.

Jonathan briefly persuades Saul to stop threatening David, but another attack forces David to escape. Michal lowers him through a window and places a household image in his bed to delay pursuit. David seeks Samuel at Ramah. Saul's messengers, and eventually Saul himself, are overcome by prophetic activity rather than capturing him.

David and Jonathan arrange a test of Saul's intentions at the new-moon meal. Saul's rage and attack on Jonathan confirm the danger. Jonathan signals David with arrows, and the two part in tears after reaffirming loyalty between their families.

At Nob, David tells Ahimelech that he is on secret royal business. The priest gives him sacred bread and Goliath's sword. David then goes to Gath, where recognition makes him afraid. He feigns madness, and King Achish rejects his presence.

stories.title: David in the Wilderness
stories.summary:
David gathers relatives and distressed men around him at Adullam, then moves through Judah's wilderness. Saul learns that the priest Ahimelech helped him and orders the priests' deaths. When the royal guards refuse, Doeg kills them and attacks Nob's inhabitants. Abiathar escapes to David, who accepts responsibility for exposing his family to danger and offers protection.

David rescues Keilah from Philistine raiders but leaves after learning that its leaders would surrender him to Saul. Jonathan visits and encourages him. Saul nearly traps David in the wilderness, but news of a Philistine raid forces him away.

At En-gedi, Saul enters a cave where David and his men are hiding. David cuts his robe but refuses to kill the anointed king. From a safe distance, he shows the cloth as evidence of restraint. Saul acknowledges David's conduct and asks protection for his descendants.

After Samuel's death, Nabal refuses David's request for supplies. David prepares to kill his household, but Nabal's wife Abigail brings food and persuades him to stop. Nabal later dies, and Abigail becomes David's wife.

When Saul again pursues him, David enters his sleeping camp with Abishai. He refuses another opportunity to kill Saul and takes only his spear and water jar. Saul again admits wrongdoing after David reveals what happened. They separate rather than returning together.

stories.title: Saul and the Medium at Endor; Saul's Death
stories.summary:
As the Philistines prepare for battle, Saul receives no answer from God through dreams, priests, or prophets. Though he has expelled mediums, he secretly visits one at Endor and asks her to summon Samuel. The figure identified as Samuel announces that Saul's kingdom has passed to David and that Saul and his sons will soon die. Saul collapses in fear, then accepts food before leaving.

Meanwhile, Philistine commanders refuse to let David fight beside them, despite Achish's trust. David returns to Ziklag and finds it burned, with the families carried away by Amalekite raiders. After consulting God, he pursues them. An abandoned Egyptian servant guides him to their camp, and David recovers the captives and goods. He requires equal shares for fighters and men who guarded the baggage, then sends gifts to communities in Judah.

On Mount Gilboa, the Philistines kill Saul's sons, including Jonathan. Under attack from archers, Saul asks his armor-bearer to kill him. When the man refuses, Saul falls on his own sword, and the armor-bearer follows. Israel's defeat leads people to abandon nearby towns.

The Philistines display Saul's body and armor as trophies. Men from Jabesh-gilead retrieve the bodies of Saul and his sons, burn them, and bury their bones. They mourn with a seven-day fast.

stories.title: David Becomes King
stories.summary:
An Amalekite brings David Saul's crown and bracelet, claiming that he killed Saul at the king's request. David mourns Saul, Jonathan, and Israel's losses, then orders the messenger's execution for claiming to have killed God's anointed king. His lament honors Saul and Jonathan and expresses deep grief for Jonathan.

Following divine guidance, David moves to Hebron, where Judah anoints him king. Meanwhile, Abner establishes Saul's son Ish-bosheth as ruler over the other tribes. Fighting breaks out between their forces. During a pursuit, Abner kills Asahel after repeatedly warning him to turn aside, beginning a deadly feud with Asahel's brother Joab.

As David's position strengthens, Abner quarrels with Ish-bosheth and offers to bring Israel over to David. David requires the return of Michal, who is taken from her husband. Abner then negotiates with Israel's leaders, but Joab kills him without David's knowledge. David publicly mourns and rejects responsibility.

Two of Ish-bosheth's officers murder him in his bed and bring his head to David. Rather than rewarding them, David orders their execution. Finally, Israel's elders come to Hebron, make a covenant with David, and anoint him king over all Israel. The passage summarizes his reign as forty years, first in Hebron and then Jerusalem.

stories.title: Jerusalem and the Ark
stories.summary:
David captures Jerusalem's Jebusite stronghold despite its defenders' confidence that he cannot enter. He makes it his residence and calls it the City of David. Hiram of Tyre supplies materials and workers for a royal house. David's household expands, and two victories over the Philistines follow instructions received when he consults God.

David then organizes a procession to bring the covenant ark to Jerusalem on a new cart. Music and celebration stop when the oxen stumble and Uzzah touches the ark. God strikes him dead. Angry and afraid, David leaves the ark at Obed-Edom's house rather than continuing.

Three months later, reports of blessing on that household prompt David to resume the journey. Sacrifices accompany the procession, and David dances wearing a linen priestly garment. The ark is installed in a tent, offerings are made, and food is distributed to the people.

Michal watches David's dancing with contempt and later accuses him of undignified exposure before the servants. David answers that his celebration was before God, who chose him over her father's household. The passage ends by stating that Michal has no children throughout her life.

stories.title: The Davidic Covenant
stories.summary:
Settled in a cedar house and enjoying relief from enemies, David tells Nathan that God's ark still rests in a tent. Nathan initially supports his wish to build a permanent sanctuary. That night, however, God gives Nathan a different message.

God reminds David that no cedar house was requested during Israel's travels. The message reviews David's rise from shepherd to ruler and promises security for Israel and a lasting name for him. Instead of David building God a house, God will establish David's house, meaning his royal line.

A son will succeed David and build the sanctuary. God promises a father-and-son relationship with this ruler. Wrongdoing will bring discipline, but divine loyalty will not be withdrawn as it was from Saul. The message promises that David's house, kingdom, and throne will endure.

David responds by sitting before God in prayer. He expresses astonishment that such promises concern his family and praises God's actions for Israel. He asks that the announced future be confirmed and that his household continue under God's blessing.

stories.title: David and Mephibosheth
stories.summary:
The passage first surveys David's victories over neighboring kingdoms, including the Philistines, Moab, and Zobah. It records tribute, captured wealth, garrisons, and the killing of defeated soldiers. The narrator attributes David's success to God and lists officials serving his expanding kingdom.

David then asks whether anyone from Saul's family remains to whom he can show kindness for Jonathan's sake. Ziba tells him about Jonathan's son Mephibosheth, who has disabilities affecting both feet. David summons him, reassures him, and restores Saul's land to him. Ziba's household is assigned to work the property, while Mephibosheth receives a permanent place at the royal table like a king's son.

A separate attempt at kindness ends differently. David sends condolences to Hanun after the death of his father, Ammon's king. Suspecting espionage, Hanun humiliates the messengers by cutting their beards and clothing. Ammon then hires Aramean forces for war.

Joab and Abishai divide Israel's army to face the two forces and drive them back. When the Arameans regroup, David defeats them again. Their subordinate kings make peace, and they stop supporting Ammon.

stories.title: David, Bathsheba and Uriah
stories.summary:
While Israel's army besieges Rabbah, David remains in Jerusalem. He sees Bathsheba bathing, learns that she is Uriah's wife, and sends for her. After they have sex, she returns home and later reports that she is pregnant.

David summons Uriah from the battlefield and urges him to go home. Uriah refuses to enjoy domestic comforts while his fellow soldiers remain in camp. Even after David makes him drunk, he does not visit his wife. David then sends Joab a letter, carried by Uriah himself, ordering his placement in deadly fighting. Uriah is killed. After Bathsheba's mourning, David takes her as his wife.

Nathan confronts David through a story about a rich man taking a poor man's cherished lamb. When David condemns the man, Nathan identifies him as the offender. He announces violence within David's household and the death of the child. David admits his wrongdoing. Although Nathan says he will not die, the child becomes ill and dies despite David's fasting and prayer.

David resumes eating after the death, explaining that continued fasting cannot bring the child back. Bathsheba later bears Solomon, whom the account describes as loved by God. The passage closes with David joining the capture of Rabbah, taking its crown and wealth, and imposing labor on its people.

stories.title: Amnon, Tamar and Absalom
stories.summary:
Amnon desires his half-sister Tamar and follows his cousin Jonadab's plan to feign illness. At his request, David sends Tamar to prepare food. Amnon dismisses everyone else, draws her into his room, and rapes her despite her protests. He then rejects her and orders her expelled. Tamar tears her royal garment, mourns openly, and lives desolate in her brother Absalom's house.

David is angry when he hears what happened, but the passage records no punishment from him. Absalom says nothing to Amnon while nursing hatred. Two years later, he invites the royal sons to a sheep-shearing celebration and orders servants to kill Amnon. The other princes flee. An initial report that all have died is corrected, but the household mourns Amnon.

Absalom escapes to Geshur and remains there for three years. Joab uses a woman from Tekoa to tell David a staged story about a surviving son threatened with execution. She urges the king to apply his mercy to his own banished son.

David permits Absalom's return but refuses to see him for two more years. Absalom burns Joab's field to compel his attention. Joab finally arranges an audience, and David receives Absalom with a kiss.

stories.title: Absalom's Rebellion
stories.summary:
Absalom cultivates support by greeting people seeking justice and suggesting that he would hear their cases better than David's administration. He then goes to Hebron under a religious pretext and launches a claim to kingship. As support grows, David leaves Jerusalem with his household and loyal followers, leaving ten concubines behind.

David sends the ark back and arranges for priests and their sons to relay information. He also sends Hushai to counter Ahithophel's advice. During the flight, Ziba accuses Mephibosheth of disloyalty, while Shimei curses David. David grants Ziba the disputed property but prevents retaliation against Shimei.

In Jerusalem, Absalom publicly has sex with David's concubines on Ahithophel's advice. Hushai then persuades him to delay pursuit and gather a larger army, giving David time to cross the Jordan. Ahithophel, seeing his counsel rejected, kills himself.

David's troops defeat Absalom's forces in the forest. Although David has ordered his son spared, Joab and his men kill Absalom after his head becomes caught in a tree. David's grief overshadows the victory until Joab urges him to acknowledge the soldiers who saved him.

On his return, David pardons Shimei, hears Mephibosheth's competing account of Ziba's conduct, and thanks Barzillai for support. Yet arguments between Judah and the other tribes accompany the restoration, leaving political divisions unresolved.

stories.title: Sheba's Revolt and the Gibeonites
stories.summary:
Sheba, a Benjaminite, calls on Israel to abandon David, while Judah remains loyal. David returns to Jerusalem and places the concubines left during his flight in permanent seclusion. He orders Amasa to assemble troops against Sheba. When Amasa is late, another force departs, and Joab kills him during a deceptive greeting.

Joab pursues Sheba to Abel Beth-maacah and besieges the city. A wise woman negotiates with him, asking why an entire community should be destroyed. Joab agrees to withdraw if Sheba is surrendered. The townspeople kill Sheba and throw his head over the wall, ending the siege.

A separate episode connects a three-year famine with Saul's attack on the Gibeonites, who had treaty protection. At their request, David hands over seven of Saul's descendants for execution, sparing Jonathan's son because of his oath. Rizpah guards the exposed bodies against birds and animals until rain comes. After hearing of her vigil, David arranges burial of the remains along with Saul and Jonathan's bones. The narrator then reports that God answers prayer for the land.

The passage ends with battles against Philistine champions. After Abishai saves an exhausted David, his men insist that he no longer accompany them into battle.

stories.title: The Exploits of David's Mighty Men
stories.summary:
This collection recalls exceptional fighters associated with David. Josheb-basshebeth is credited with killing eight hundred opponents in one encounter. Eleazar stands against the Philistines until his hand becomes exhausted and clings to his sword. Shammah holds a field of lentils after others flee. The narrator attributes the resulting victories to God.

Another episode begins when David longs for water from Bethlehem's well while a Philistine garrison occupies the town. Three warriors break through enemy lines, draw the water, and bring it back. David refuses to drink what they obtained at such risk. Comparing it with their blood, he pours it out as an offering to God.

The passage also honors Abishai for killing three hundred men and describes Benaiah's exploits against Moabite fighters, a lion in a snowy pit, and an Egyptian. Benaiah takes the Egyptian's spear and uses it against him. Both men gain distinction, though the account differentiates their standing from the leading three. David appoints Benaiah over his guard.

stories.title: The Census and the Plague
stories.summary:
The account opens with God angry at Israel and prompting David to count the people. David orders Joab and the army commanders to conduct the census despite their objections. They travel throughout the land and return after more than nine months with totals for Israel and Judah.

David then confesses that he has acted foolishly. Through the prophet Gad, God offers three consequences: famine, flight before enemies, or plague. David asks to fall into God's hands rather than human hands, appealing to divine mercy. A plague kills seventy thousand people.

As the destroying angel approaches Jerusalem, God orders it to stop near Araunah's threshing floor. David acknowledges his own wrongdoing and asks why the people should suffer. Gad instructs him to build an altar at that location.

Araunah offers the site, oxen, and equipment freely. David insists on paying because he will not offer sacrifices that cost him nothing. He buys the threshing floor and animals, builds the altar, and makes offerings. The chapter ends with God answering prayer for the land and the plague ending.

stories.title: Solomon Becomes King
stories.summary:
As David grows old, Adonijah gathers supporters and holds a feast to present himself as the next king. Joab and the priest Abiathar support him, but Nathan, Zadok, Benaiah and Solomon are excluded. Nathan urges Bathsheba to remind David of his promise that Solomon will succeed him. David confirms that promise and orders Solomon's public anointing at Gihon.

The city celebrates as Solomon takes the throne. Adonijah's guests scatter when they hear the news. Adonijah seeks protection at the altar, and Solomon initially spares him on condition that he behaves loyally. Before dying, David tells Solomon to follow the law of Moses. He also directs him to reward Barzillai's sons and deal with Joab and Shimei.

After David's death, Adonijah asks through Bathsheba to marry Abishag, who had cared for David. Solomon treats the request as a renewed claim to kingship and orders Benaiah to kill him. He removes Abiathar from the priesthood but spares his life because of his service to David. Joab takes refuge at the altar, yet Solomon orders his execution for killing Abner and Amasa.

Solomon appoints Benaiah over the army and Zadok as priest. He requires Shimei to remain in Jerusalem under threat of death. Three years later, Shimei leaves to retrieve runaway slaves. Solomon has him killed for breaking the agreement. The account closes with Solomon firmly in control of the kingdom.

stories.title: Solomon's Wisdom
stories.summary:
Solomon marries Pharaoh's daughter and continues the building work in Jerusalem. He worships the LORD, though sacrifices still take place at local shrines because the temple has not yet been built. At Gibeon, God appears to him in a dream and invites him to make a request. Solomon asks for understanding to judge the people and distinguish right from wrong.

God approves his request for wisdom rather than wealth, long life or the death of enemies. Solomon receives the wisdom he asks for, along with riches and honor. A longer life is promised if he follows God's commands.

Two women then bring a dispute before the king. Each claims that the living baby is hers and the dead baby belongs to the other woman. Solomon calls for a sword and orders the living child divided between them. One woman begs him to give the child to the other rather than kill him. Solomon identifies her as the mother and gives her the baby. Israel hears the judgment and recognizes his ability to administer justice.

The account also describes Solomon's officials, twelve districts supplying his court, and the wealth and security of his reign. His household requires large daily supplies of food and fodder. His wisdom includes proverbs, songs and knowledge of plants and animals. Rulers from other lands send people to hear him.

stories.title: The Temple Built
stories.summary:
With peace around his kingdom, Solomon arranges to build the temple that David had wanted to construct. Hiram, king of Tyre, supplies cedar and cypress from Lebanon in return for food for his household. Solomon organizes forced labor, stonecutters, carriers and overseers. Large dressed stones and timber form the building, which takes seven years to complete.

The temple has an inner sanctuary for the ark, carved wooden walls and gold-covered surfaces. Winged figures called cherubim stand over the ark's place. During construction, God ties his promise to dwell among Israel to Solomon's obedience. The account also describes Solomon's palace buildings, completed over thirteen years. A bronze craftsman named Hiram makes pillars, a great basin supported by twelve oxen, wheeled stands and other temple vessels.

At the dedication, priests bring the ark into the inner sanctuary. It holds the stone tablets associated with the covenant at Horeb. A cloud fills the temple, and the priests cannot continue their work because of the LORD's glory. Solomon tells the assembled people that the building fulfills God's promise to David.

In prayer, Solomon acknowledges that even the heavens cannot contain God, much less this house. He asks God to hear prayers directed toward it and to judge fairly, forgive and restore. His requests cover defeat, drought, hunger, sickness and captivity. He also asks that foreigners who come to pray be heard. After blessing the people, he calls them to remain faithful to God's commands. Large sacrifices and an extended festival mark the dedication, and the people return home rejoicing.

stories.title: The Queen of Sheba and Solomon's Decline
stories.summary:
After Solomon finishes the temple and palace, God appears to him again. The temple is accepted, but the promise to preserve his throne is tied to obedience. God warns that worshiping other gods will bring the loss of the land and the temple. The account then describes Solomon's towns, building projects, forced labor, trade and fleet.

The queen of Sheba comes with gifts and difficult questions after hearing of Solomon's fame. He answers her questions, and she is overwhelmed by his wisdom, buildings and royal household. She praises the God who placed him on the throne to do justice. Solomon gives her gifts before she returns home. Descriptions of gold, an ivory throne, imported goods, horses and chariots show the scale of his wealth.

Yet Solomon's later years take a different course. The account says his many foreign wives turn his heart toward other gods. He follows their worship and builds shrines for them. God announces that most of the kingdom will be taken from his family. For David's sake, this will happen under Solomon's son rather than during Solomon's life, and part of the kingdom will remain.

Hadad of Edom and Rezon of Damascus become adversaries. Jeroboam, an official overseeing labor, also rises against Solomon. The prophet Ahijah tears a new garment into twelve pieces and gives Jeroboam ten, announcing his future rule over ten tribes. He promises lasting support if Jeroboam obeys God. Solomon tries to kill Jeroboam, who escapes to Egypt. After forty years of rule, Solomon dies, and Rehoboam succeeds him.

stories.title: The Kingdom Divides
stories.summary:
At Shechem, Jeroboam and the assembled people ask Rehoboam to lighten the heavy service imposed by Solomon. Rehoboam asks for three days to consider his reply. The older advisers urge him to serve the people and answer kindly. He rejects their advice and follows the younger men who grew up with him, promising harsher treatment instead.

The northern tribes refuse the rule of David's family. When Rehoboam sends his forced-labor official, the people stone the official to death. Rehoboam escapes to Jerusalem, while the assembly makes Jeroboam king of Israel. Rehoboam gathers troops from Judah and Benjamin to recover the kingdom. The prophet Shemaiah tells them not to fight their fellow Israelites because the division comes from God. They abandon the campaign.

Jeroboam strengthens Shechem and Penuel, but fears that worship in Jerusalem will restore the people's loyalty to Rehoboam. He makes two golden calves and places them at Bethel and Dan. He presents these as the gods who brought Israel out of Egypt, and the account condemns the resulting worship.

Jeroboam also establishes shrines and appoints priests who are not Levites. He creates a festival on a date of his own choosing, modeled on the feast in Judah. The chapter ends with him approaching the altar at Bethel to burn incense.

stories.title: The Man of God from Judah
stories.summary:
An unnamed man of God comes from Judah to confront Jeroboam at the altar in Bethel. He announces that a future king named Josiah will sacrifice its priests there and burn human bones on it. He predicts that the altar will split and spill its ashes. Jeroboam's hand becomes powerless when he orders the prophet seized. The altar splits, and the king's hand is restored after the prophet prays.

The visitor refuses the king's hospitality because God has forbidden him to eat, drink or return by the same road. An older prophet then follows him and falsely claims that an angel has given different instructions. The man accepts a meal. During it, the older prophet announces judgment for his disobedience. A lion later kills him on the road but does not eat his body or harm his donkey. The older prophet retrieves and buries him, mourning him and affirming his message about Bethel.

Jeroboam continues appointing priests for the shrines. When his son becomes ill, he sends his wife in disguise to consult Ahijah. Though blind, Ahijah recognizes her because God has warned him. He announces the destruction of Jeroboam's family and Israel's future removal from the land. The child dies as his mother returns home, and Israel mourns him.

The account also turns to Rehoboam's reign in Judah. It condemns Judah's worship practices and reports that Shishak of Egypt takes the temple and palace treasures. Rehoboam replaces Solomon's gold shields with bronze ones. The two kingdoms remain at war. Both kings die, and their sons succeed them.

stories.title: Zimri's Coup and Omri's Rise
stories.summary:
While King Elah is drinking in Tirzah, Zimri, an officer commanding half his chariots, kills him and takes the throne. Zimri then destroys Baasha's male descendants, relatives and supporters. The account connects the fall of Baasha's family with a warning previously spoken by the prophet Jehu.

Zimri's reign lasts only seven days. Israel's army is besieging the Philistine town of Gibbethon when it hears of the coup. The soldiers make their commander Omri king, and he leads them to Tirzah. When the city falls, Zimri retreats into the palace stronghold, sets it on fire and dies inside. The narrator links his downfall to the same condemned worship associated with Jeroboam.

Israel then divides between supporters of Omri and supporters of Tibni. Omri's side prevails, Tibni dies, and Omri secures the kingdom. He buys a hill from Shemer, builds a city there and names it Samaria. Despite this achievement, the account judges his conduct more harshly than that of the kings before him. After Omri dies and is buried in Samaria, his son Ahab becomes king.

stories.title: Elijah and the Drought
stories.summary:
Elijah tells King Ahab that neither dew nor rain will fall except at his word. God directs him to hide beside the brook Cherith, where ravens bring bread and meat morning and evening. He drinks from the brook until it dries up in the drought.

God then sends him to a widow in Zarephath. Elijah asks her for water and bread, but she has only enough flour and oil for one last meal with her son. He tells her to make a small loaf for him first. He promises that her supplies will last until rain returns. She follows his instructions, and the flour and oil continue to feed the household.

Later, the woman's son becomes so ill that he stops breathing. She accuses Elijah of bringing her sins to notice and causing the child's death. Elijah carries the boy upstairs, lays him on his bed and cries out to God. He stretches himself over the child three times and asks for his life to return.

The account says God hears Elijah, and the boy revives. Elijah brings him back to his mother alive. She responds that she now knows Elijah is a man of God and that the LORD's word spoken through him is true.

stories.title: Elijah on Mount Carmel
stories.summary:
During the drought's third year, God sends Elijah back to Ahab with a promise of rain. Elijah first meets Obadiah, a royal official who has hidden a hundred prophets from Jezebel. Obadiah fears being killed if he announces Elijah's arrival and Elijah disappears. Elijah assures him that he will meet the king that day.

Ahab blames Elijah for Israel's trouble. Elijah instead accuses Ahab's family of abandoning God's commands and following Baal. He calls the people and the rival prophets to Mount Carmel. There, he challenges the people to choose whom they will follow. Two bulls are prepared on separate altars without fire. The god who answers with fire will be acknowledged as God.

Baal's prophets call out for hours, but receive no answer. Elijah repairs the LORD's altar with twelve stones, arranges his offering and has it soaked repeatedly with water. He prays that the people will recognize the LORD and know that he has acted at God's command. Fire consumes the offering, wood, stones, dust and water. The people fall down and acknowledge the LORD. Elijah orders Baal's prophets seized and kills them at the Kishon brook.

Elijah then tells Ahab that rain is coming. He bows on the mountain while his servant watches the sea. On the seventh visit, the servant sees a small cloud. The sky darkens, heavy rain falls, and Ahab rides toward Jezreel. The account ends with Elijah, strengthened by the LORD, running ahead of the king's chariot.

stories.title: Elijah at Horeb
stories.summary:
After Ahab reports the killing of the prophets, Jezebel threatens Elijah's life. Elijah flees to Beersheba, leaves his servant there and goes alone into the wilderness. Exhausted, he asks God to let him die. An angel wakes him and provides food and water twice. Strengthened by the food, he travels forty days and nights to Horeb, the mountain of God.

At a cave, Elijah tells God that Israel has abandoned the covenant, destroyed the altars and killed the prophets. He says he alone remains and is being hunted. God tells him to stand on the mountain. A powerful wind, an earthquake and a fire pass, but the account says the LORD is not in them. A quiet voice follows. Elijah covers his face and comes to the cave's entrance, where he repeats his complaint.

God sends him back toward Damascus with instructions to appoint Hazael as king of Syria, Jehu as king of Israel and Elisha as his successor. God also says that seven thousand in Israel have not bowed to Baal. Elijah then finds Elisha plowing and places his cloak over him. Elisha says farewell to his parents, kills his oxen and feeds the people with their meat. He leaves to follow Elijah and serve him.

stories.title: Naboth's Vineyard
stories.summary:
Ahab wants the vineyard beside his palace in Jezreel for a vegetable garden. He offers Naboth money or a better vineyard in exchange. Naboth refuses to surrender his family's inherited land. Ahab returns home angry, lies down and refuses to eat.

Jezebel promises to obtain the vineyard. Using Ahab's name and seal, she sends orders to the city's leaders. They must hold a public fast, give Naboth a prominent place and arrange two false accusations that he has cursed God and the king. The leaders obey. Naboth is taken outside the city and stoned to death. Once Jezebel hears the news, she tells Ahab to take the land, and he goes to claim it.

God sends Elijah to confront Ahab in the vineyard. Elijah accuses him of killing and taking possession, then announces judgment on him and his family. He predicts that dogs will lick Ahab's blood and that Jezebel will also meet a violent end. The account condemns Ahab's worship of idols and describes Jezebel's influence on his conduct.

Ahab responds by tearing his clothes, wearing sackcloth and fasting. God tells Elijah that Ahab has humbled himself. The destruction announced against his household is therefore postponed until his son's reign.

stories.title: Ahab and Micaiah
stories.summary:
Ahab asks Jehoshaphat of Judah to help recover Ramoth-gilead from Syria. Jehoshaphat agrees but asks them first to seek God's word. About four hundred prophets promise victory. At Jehoshaphat's request, Ahab also summons Micaiah, whom he dislikes because his messages are unfavorable.

Micaiah first repeats the promise of success. When pressed for the truth, he describes Israel scattered like sheep without a shepherd. He then tells of a heavenly council in which a spirit offers to deceive Ahab through his prophets. The LORD authorizes the spirit to do so. Micaiah says their promises conceal the disaster awaiting the king. The prophet Zedekiah strikes him, and Ahab orders him imprisoned on meager rations until the king returns safely. Micaiah replies that a safe return would show his message to be false.

Ahab enters battle in disguise while Jehoshaphat wears royal robes. Syrian commanders briefly pursue Jehoshaphat, then turn away when they realize he is not Ahab. An arrow shot at random strikes Ahab between the joints of his armor. He remains propped up in his chariot and dies that evening. The army disperses. When the chariot is washed in Samaria, dogs lick his blood, as the account connects his death with God's earlier warning.

The chapter closes with notices about Jehoshaphat and Ahab's son Ahaziah. Jehoshaphat is praised for following his father Asa's ways, though local shrines remain. His ships are wrecked before their voyage, and his son Jehoram succeeds him. Ahaziah becomes king of Israel and continues the worship of Baal, which the narrator condemns.

stories.title: Elijah Taken Up
stories.summary:
After an injury, King Ahaziah sends messengers to consult Baal-zebub of Ekron. Elijah intercepts them and announces that the king will die because he has sought another god. Two detachments sent to seize Elijah are consumed by fire. A third captain pleads for mercy, and Elijah accompanies him to repeat the warning. Ahaziah dies without a son to succeed him.

Elisha then follows Elijah from Gilgal through Bethel and Jericho, refusing repeated requests to remain behind. Prophetic groups warn him that Elijah will be taken away that day. At the Jordan, Elijah strikes the water with his cloak, and the two cross on dry ground.

Elisha asks for a double portion of Elijah's spirit. Elijah says this will depend on whether Elisha sees his departure. Fiery horses and a chariot separate them, and Elijah ascends in a whirlwind. Elisha sees it, mourns, and retrieves the fallen cloak. He uses it to divide the Jordan again, and other prophets recognize him as Elijah's successor.

After an unsuccessful search for Elijah, Elisha heals Jericho's water by throwing salt into its spring. On the road to Bethel, youths mock his baldness. He curses them, and two bears maul forty-two. He then travels to Carmel and Samaria.

stories.title: Elisha and Moab
stories.summary:
Mesha of Moab stops paying tribute after Ahab's death. Israel's king Jehoram forms an alliance with Jehoshaphat of Judah and the king of Edom to attack Moab. Their roundabout march through the wilderness leaves the army and animals without water.

At Jehoshaphat's suggestion, they consult Elisha. He rebukes Jehoram but agrees to speak because of his regard for Judah's king. After a musician plays, Elisha announces that the valley will fill with water despite no visible wind or rain. He also predicts victory and the destruction of Moab's towns, trees, springs, and fields.

Water arrives the next morning. Seeing its red appearance in the sunlight, the Moabites mistake it for blood and assume the allied kings have killed one another. They rush toward the camp for plunder but meet Israel's army and flee. The allies devastate the countryside and press the siege of Kir-hareseth.

Unable to break through, Mesha sacrifices his eldest son and heir on the city wall. The passage then reports great wrath against Israel without identifying its source. The allied force withdraws, and the campaign ends.

stories.title: The Widow's Oil and the Shunammite's Son
stories.summary:
A prophet's widow tells Elisha that a creditor threatens to take her two sons as slaves. Her only remaining resource is a jar of oil. Elisha tells her to borrow empty containers and pour behind closed doors. The oil continues until every vessel is full. She can sell it to repay the debt and support her family.

At Shunem, a woman regularly provides Elisha with meals and a furnished room. Learning that she has no son, he promises a child, who is born the following year. Later, the boy becomes ill in the fields and dies in his mother's arms. She lays him on Elisha's bed and travels urgently to find the prophet.

Gehazi goes ahead with Elisha's staff, but laying it on the child does not revive him. Elisha arrives, prays privately, and stretches himself over the boy. The child's body warms, and after Elisha repeats the action, he opens his eyes. His mother receives him alive.

Two shorter accounts follow during famine. Elisha makes a harmful stew safe by adding flour, then directs that twenty barley loaves feed a hundred men. Despite the servant's doubts, everyone eats and food remains.

stories.title: Naaman Healed
stories.summary:
Naaman, an honored Aramean commander, has a serious skin disease. An Israelite girl captured in a raid serves his wife and recommends the prophet in Samaria. Naaman travels with gifts and a royal letter asking Israel's king for healing. The king fears a diplomatic trap, but Elisha invites Naaman to his house.

Rather than greeting him personally, Elisha sends instructions to wash seven times in the Jordan. Naaman is angry because he expected a dramatic healing and considers Damascus's rivers better. His servants persuade him to try the simple command. He immerses himself seven times, and his skin is restored.

Naaman returns, acknowledges Israel's God, and offers a gift, which Elisha refuses. He asks for earth to take home and forgiveness when his duties require accompanying his king into Rimmon's temple. Elisha sends him away in peace.

Gehazi secretly follows Naaman and invents a request for silver and clothing on Elisha's behalf. After hiding the gifts, he denies having gone anywhere. Elisha reveals that he knows what happened and declares that Naaman's disease will attach to Gehazi and his descendants. Gehazi leaves visibly afflicted.

stories.title: Elisha and the Arameans
stories.summary:
While a prophetic community enlarges its quarters, a borrowed iron axe head falls into the Jordan. Elisha throws a stick into the water, and the iron floats so its user can recover it.

Elisha also repeatedly warns Israel's king of Aramean military plans. The Aramean king sends troops to seize him at Dothan. Elisha prays that his frightened servant can see the fiery horses and chariots surrounding them. He then asks that the attackers be blinded and leads them into Samaria. Once their sight returns, he prevents their execution, orders a meal for them, and sends them home.

Later, an Aramean siege brings extreme famine to Samaria. A woman's account of eating her child horrifies the king, who threatens Elisha. The prophet predicts plentiful, inexpensive food the next day. A skeptical officer is told he will see it but not eat it.

Four men with skin disease venture into the enemy camp and find it deserted. The account explains that God made the Arameans hear an approaching army, causing them to flee. After eating and taking goods, the men report the discovery. Scouts confirm it, and the city plunders the camp. Food prices fall as predicted, while the skeptical officer is trampled at the gate.

stories.title: Jehu's Revolt
stories.summary:
The passage begins with the Shunammite woman's property being restored after seven years away during famine. It then follows Elisha to Damascus, where he foretells Hazael's rise and weeps over the violence Hazael will inflict on Israel. Hazael kills Ben-hadad and becomes king. Notices about Judah's rulers establish their close ties with Ahab's dynasty.

Elisha sends a young prophet to anoint the commander Jehu as Israel's king and charge him with destroying Ahab's household. Jehu's officers proclaim him king, and he rides to Jezreel. He kills Joram and orders his body thrown onto Naboth's land. Judah's king Ahaziah also dies after Jehu orders an attack on him. At Jezreel, attendants throw Jezebel from a window, and dogs consume most of her body.

Jehu pressures the guardians of Ahab's seventy sons into killing them and sending their heads. He destroys further members and supporters of the royal household, including relatives of Ahaziah. Then, pretending devotion to Baal, he gathers Baal's worshipers into their temple. His men kill them and destroy the sanctuary.

The narrator credits Jehu with ending Baal worship but condemns his continued support of the calf shrines at Bethel and Dan. His dynasty is promised four generations. Meanwhile, Hazael takes Israelite territory east of the Jordan. Jehu dies after twenty-eight years, and Jehoahaz succeeds him.

stories.title: Athaliah and Joash
stories.summary:
After Ahaziah's death, his mother Athaliah kills the royal descendants and takes power in Judah. Jehosheba rescues the infant Joash and his nurse, hiding them in the temple for six years.

In the seventh year, the priest Jehoiada brings military officers into a secret agreement. He arranges armed protection, presents Joash, and has him crowned and anointed. Athaliah hears the celebration, enters the temple, and cries treason. Jehoiada orders her removed so she will not be killed in the sanctuary. She is executed near the palace, and Joash takes the throne at seven years old.

Jehoiada establishes commitments between God, king, and people. The population destroys Baal's temple and kills its priest. Joash later directs repairs to God's temple. When the original collection system produces no repairs, money is placed in a chest and paid directly to supervisors and skilled workers.

When Hazael of Aram threatens Jerusalem, Joash sends him sacred gifts and gold from the temple and palace, and he withdraws. Joash's reign ends when his servants conspire against and kill him. He is buried in the City of David, and his son Amaziah becomes king.

stories.title: Elisha's Death and Israel's Victories
stories.summary:
Israel suffers severe losses under Aramean pressure during Jehoahaz's reign. He appeals to God, and the narrator describes relief, though Israel continues the religious practices it condemns. His son Jehoash later visits the dying Elisha and weeps over the loss of Israel's protector.

Elisha directs the king to shoot an arrow eastward, declaring it a sign of victory over Aram. He then tells him to strike the ground with arrows. When Jehoash stops after three strikes, Elisha says he will win only three victories rather than destroy the enemy completely. Elisha dies and is buried. In a later incident, a dead man placed hurriedly in his tomb revives after touching his bones. Jehoash subsequently recovers captured towns through three victories.

The account turns to Amaziah of Judah, who executes his father's killers but spares their children under Moses' law. After defeating Edom, he challenges Israel. Jehoash warns him against overconfidence, then defeats and captures him, damages Jerusalem's wall, and takes treasure and hostages. Amaziah later dies in a conspiracy.

In Israel, Jeroboam succeeds Jehoash and restores territory as foretold through Jonah. Although his worship is criticized, the narrator presents these gains as God's response to Israel's suffering.

stories.title: The Fall of Samaria
stories.summary:
The passage traces instability in Israel alongside successive reigns in Judah. Israel's kings fall through repeated coups, while Assyria gains influence and territory. Menahem taxes wealthy Israelites to secure Assyrian support. Later, Tiglath-pileser captures northern districts and deports their inhabitants. Hoshea then kills Pekah and takes the throne.

In Judah, Ahaz faces attacks from Israel and Aram and asks Assyria for help, sending temple and palace treasure. Assyria captures Damascus. Ahaz copies an altar seen there and changes the arrangements for worship in Jerusalem, alongside practices the narrator strongly condemns.

Hoshea initially pays tribute to Assyria but seeks Egyptian help and stops payment. He is imprisoned, and Assyria besieges Samaria for three years. The city falls, and Israelites are deported. The narrator explains the catastrophe through rejection of the covenant, worship of other gods, child sacrifice, and refusal to heed prophetic warnings. Judah is also criticized.

Assyria settles other populations in Samaria's towns. After lion attacks, a deported priest is returned to teach them the worship of the land's God. Yet the settlers retain their own gods as well. The closing account describes this mixed worship continuing among their descendants.

stories.title: Hezekiah and Sennacherib
stories.summary:
Hezekiah removes local shrines, sacred pillars, and the bronze serpent associated with Moses, which people have begun honoring with incense. The narrator praises his loyalty to God. He breaks with Assyria, but Sennacherib later captures Judah's fortified cities. Hezekiah pays a heavy tribute, even stripping gold from the temple, yet Assyrian forces still threaten Jerusalem.
