An Assyrian spokesman publicly challenges confidence in Egypt, Hezekiah, and God. Speaking so the people on the wall can understand, he urges surrender and promises food before resettlement elsewhere. The people remain silent under Hezekiah's orders.

Hezekiah mourns and seeks Isaiah's help. Isaiah announces that the Assyrian king will return home and die there. When further threats arrive, Hezekiah spreads the letter before God and prays for deliverance. Isaiah replies that God has heard. His message challenges Sennacherib's arrogance, promises Judah's recovery, and declares that the enemy will not enter Jerusalem or build siege works against it.

That night, the account says God's angel kills 185,000 in the Assyrian camp. Sennacherib returns to Nineveh. The narrative closes with his murder while worshiping in his god's temple and the accession of his son Esarhaddon.

stories.title: Hezekiah's Illness and the Babylonian Envoys
stories.summary:
Hezekiah becomes gravely ill, and Isaiah tells him to arrange his affairs because he will die. The king turns toward the wall, weeps, and asks God to remember his faithful conduct. Before Isaiah has gone far, God sends him back with a new message. Hezekiah will recover, receive fifteen additional years, and see Jerusalem protected from Assyria.

A fig preparation is applied to his boil. When Hezekiah asks for a confirming sign, Isaiah offers a choice involving a shadow's movement. Hezekiah requests that it move backward rather than forward. Isaiah prays, and the shadow reverses ten steps on Ahaz's sundial.

Babylon's king later sends letters and a gift after hearing of the illness. Hezekiah shows the envoys his treasures, supplies, and armory. Isaiah questions him, then announces that these possessions will eventually be carried to Babylon. Some of Hezekiah's descendants will also serve there as palace eunuchs.

Hezekiah accepts the message while reflecting on peace during his own lifetime. A closing notice credits him with bringing water into Jerusalem through a conduit. He dies, and Manasseh succeeds him.

stories.title: Manasseh, Amon and Josiah
stories.summary:
Manasseh reverses Hezekiah's religious changes, rebuilds local shrines, and installs altars and an Asherah image in the temple. The account condemns his worship of heavenly bodies, divination, burning of his son, and extensive killing of innocent people. Prophets announce that Jerusalem will face destruction like Samaria. His son Amon continues these practices but is killed by servants. After the conspirators are executed, Josiah becomes king at eight years old.

During temple repairs in Josiah's eighteenth year, Hilkiah discovers a book of the law. Hearing it read, Josiah tears his clothes and sends officials to consult the prophet Huldah. She confirms coming disaster because the people have abandoned God, but says Josiah will not live to see it because he has humbled himself.

Josiah gathers the people, reads the book publicly, and renews the covenant. He removes objects associated with other gods, destroys shrines in Judah and former northern territory, and desecrates sites of child sacrifice. At Bethel, he burns human bones on the altar but preserves the tomb of the prophet who foretold its destruction. He also kills priests of northern shrines and organizes a major Passover celebration.

The narrator praises his unmatched commitment but says judgment remains because of Manasseh's offenses. Josiah dies confronting Pharaoh Neco at Megiddo. His body is returned to Jerusalem, and Jehoahaz succeeds him.

stories.title: The Fall of Jerusalem
stories.summary:
After Josiah's death, Egypt removes Jehoahaz and installs Jehoiakim, who taxes Judah to pay tribute. Babylon later gains control. Jehoiakim serves Nebuchadnezzar for three years and then rebels. The narrator links the resulting attacks with Judah's wrongdoing, especially Manasseh's shedding of innocent blood.

Jehoiachin succeeds him but soon surrenders Jerusalem during a Babylonian siege. The king, royal household, officials, soldiers, and skilled workers are deported, along with palace and temple treasures. Babylon installs his uncle Zedekiah, who also rebels.

A renewed siege brings severe famine. When Jerusalem's defenses are breached, Zedekiah flees but is captured near Jericho. His sons are killed before him, then he is blinded and taken to Babylon. Babylonian troops burn the temple, palace, and major houses, demolish the walls, and carry away sacred metalwork. More people are deported, while some of the poorest remain to cultivate the land.

Gedaliah is appointed governor and urges the remaining population to accept Babylonian rule. His assassination by Ishmael prompts the survivors to flee to Egypt in fear of retaliation.

The book closes many years later in Babylon. King Evil-merodach releases Jehoiachin from prison, grants him an honored position, and provides meals and a continuing allowance for the rest of his life.

stories.title: The Death of Saul
stories.summary:
The Philistines defeat Israel on Mount Gilboa and kill Saul's sons Jonathan, Abinadab and Malchishua. Archers overtake Saul, and he asks his armor bearer to kill him before the enemy can abuse him. The armor bearer refuses out of fear. Saul falls on his own sword, and the armor bearer follows his example. When Israelites in the valley hear that Saul and his sons are dead, they abandon their towns. The Philistines move into them.

The next day, the Philistines find Saul's body while stripping the dead. They remove his head and armor and spread news of their victory. They place his armor in a temple and fasten his head in the temple of Dagon. Men from Jabesh Gilead recover the bodies of Saul and his sons. They bury their bones beneath an oak and fast for seven days. The account closes by interpreting Saul's death as judgment for disobeying the LORD and consulting a medium instead of seeking God. It says the LORD transfers the kingdom to David.

stories.title: David Takes Jerusalem and Gathers His Warriors
stories.summary:
Israel's elders gather at Hebron and recognize David as the leader who guided them even during Saul's reign. David makes an agreement with them before the LORD, and they anoint him king. He then attacks Jerusalem, whose inhabitants insist that he cannot enter. David captures its stronghold, while Joab wins command of the army by leading the attack. David settles there and strengthens the city.

The account names the warriors who support his rule and describes their deeds. Three men risk their lives to bring him water from Bethlehem, then occupied by the Philistines. David refuses to drink it because they obtained it at such risk, and pours it out to the LORD. Other episodes describe fighters defending a barley field, defeating enemy warriors and killing a lion.

The narrative then looks back at those who joined David while he was still fleeing Saul. They include skilled archers from Saul's own tribe, fighters from Gad and men from Manasseh. David questions one arriving group about its intentions, and Amasai pledges loyalty to him. The account ends with troops from across Israel gathering at Hebron to make him king. Their families and neighbors supply food for three days of shared celebration.

stories.title: The Ark Brought to Jerusalem
stories.summary:
David consults Israel's leaders and gathers the people to bring God's ark from Kiriath Jearim. They place it on a new cart and celebrate with music. When the oxen stumble, Uzzah reaches out to steady the ark. The account says God strikes him dead for touching it. David becomes angry and afraid, and leaves the ark at Obed-edom's house. It remains there for three months, during which the household prospers.

The narrative also describes David's growing family and a palace built with help from Hiram of Tyre. When the Philistines attack, David asks God how to respond. He follows the instructions he receives and defeats them twice. David then prepares a tent for the ark in Jerusalem. He tells the priests and Levites to prepare themselves, explaining that the earlier attempt failed because proper instructions were not followed.

This time, Levites carry the ark on their shoulders using poles, as Moses commanded. Singers and musicians accompany them, and David dances in celebration. Watching from a window, Michal despises him. The ark is placed in its tent, sacrifices are offered, and David distributes food to the people. He appoints Levites to lead worship before the ark, while priests continue sacrifices at Gibeon. A song recalls God's promises to Israel and calls the nations to praise. The people return home, and David goes to bless his household.

stories.title: God's Covenant with David and His Wars
stories.summary:
Living in a cedar palace, David tells Nathan that God's ark still stands in a tent. Nathan initially supports his wish to build a house for God. That night, however, God tells Nathan that David is not to build it. Instead, God promises to establish David's royal family. A son will build the house, and his throne will endure. David responds with a prayer of thanks, asking God to fulfill this promise.

The account next describes campaigns that extend David's rule. He defeats Philistine, Moabite and Aramean forces, receives tribute and places troops in conquered territory. Abishai also defeats Edom. David dedicates captured gold, silver and bronze to the LORD. The text credits God with his victories and describes David as administering justice throughout Israel.

A further war begins after David sends men to comfort Hanun following his father's death. Hanun's advisers accuse them of spying, and he humiliates them by shaving them and cutting their clothes. The Ammonites hire allied forces, but Joab and Abishai drive them back. David defeats the Aramean reinforcements, who then stop helping Ammon. Joab later captures Rabbah, and David takes its crown and plunder. The cited account describes him cutting its people with saws, iron picks and axes. It closes with battles in which David's warriors kill formidable Philistine opponents, including Goliath's brother Lahmi.

stories.title: The Census and the Temple Site
stories.summary:
The account begins with Satan urging David to count Israel. Joab objects that the order will bring guilt on the people, but David insists. Joab reports the number of fighting men, leaving Levi and Benjamin uncounted. David then admits that he has sinned. Through the prophet Gad, God offers a choice of famine, military defeat or plague. David asks to fall into God's hands rather than human hands, trusting in divine mercy.

A plague kills seventy thousand Israelites. As an angel threatens Jerusalem, God orders the destruction to stop near Ornan's threshing floor. David sees the angel with a drawn sword and pleads that he and his household bear the punishment instead of the people. Gad directs him to build an altar there. Ornan offers the site and supplies freely, but David insists on paying the full price. He offers sacrifices, and the account says God answers with fire. The angel puts away his sword.

David identifies the place as the site for God's house and begins gathering stone, timber and metals. He tells Solomon that God has barred him from building the temple because he has shed much blood in war. Solomon is to build it during a time of peace. David urges his son to obey God's law and act with courage. He also commands Israel's leaders to help Solomon complete the work.

stories.title: David's Last Charge and Death
stories.summary:
David gathers Israel's leaders in Jerusalem and explains why Solomon will build the temple. He says God prevented him from doing so because he had fought wars and shed blood. David urges the people to keep God's commands and tells Solomon to serve with a willing heart. He warns that seeking God and abandoning God have different consequences.

David gives Solomon plans for the temple, its courts, storerooms, furnishings and priestly duties. He describes the plans as instructions received from God. He also points to the workers, priests and leaders available to support the project. David adds gold and silver from his own wealth to the materials already collected. Leaders and people contribute willingly, and the assembly rejoices.

In his prayer, David says that wealth, power and honor belong to God. He acknowledges that even their gifts came from God in the first place. He asks that the people remain willing and that Solomon carry out the work faithfully. The assembly offers sacrifices and shares a feast. Solomon is made king a second time, and Zadok is anointed as priest. The leaders and David's other sons accept Solomon's rule. David dies in old age after forty years as king, including seven at Hebron and thirty-three in Jerusalem.

stories.title: Solomon Builds the Temple
stories.summary:
Solomon gathers Israel's leaders at Gibeon, where the tent of worship and bronze altar stand. After he offers sacrifices, God appears to him and invites him to ask for a gift. Solomon requests wisdom and knowledge to govern the people. God grants this request and also promises wealth and honor.

Solomon arranges to build both the temple and a royal palace. Huram of Tyre supplies timber and a skilled craftsman, while Solomon assigns foreign residents to carry loads and cut stone. Construction begins on Mount Moriah, at the threshing floor David had chosen. The account describes the temple's gold-covered rooms, carved winged figures, pillars, lamps and tables. A large bronze basin and smaller basins provide water for the priests and sacrifices.

When the work is complete, priests bring the ark into the inner room beneath the winged figures. Singers and trumpeters praise God, and a cloud fills the building so densely that the priests cannot continue serving. Solomon addresses the people and kneels to pray. He says that even heaven cannot contain God, much less this building. He asks God to hear prayers offered toward the temple, including prayers from foreigners and from Israelites facing defeat, drought, illness or exile.

After the prayer, fire descends and consumes the offerings, and God's glory fills the temple. The people bow down and celebrate with sacrifices and a feast. God later appears to Solomon again, promising to hear people who humble themselves and turn from wrongdoing. The same message warns that abandoning God for other gods will bring removal from the land and the rejection of the temple.

stories.title: Solomon's Reign and the Queen of Sheba
stories.summary:
After completing the temple and his palace, Solomon develops towns, defenses and storage centers across his territory. He uses surviving non-Israelite communities for forced labor, while Israelites serve as soldiers and officers. He moves Pharaoh's daughter to a separate residence because he regards places associated with the ark as holy. He also maintains sacrifices and assigns priests, Levites and gatekeepers according to David's arrangements. Ships supplied by Huram bring gold from Ophir.

The queen of Sheba arrives in Jerusalem with a large caravan carrying gold, spices and precious stones. She tests Solomon with difficult questions, and he answers them all. His wisdom, buildings, food and court arrangements leave her astonished. She says the reports she heard did not describe even half his greatness. She praises Israel's God for appointing him to rule justly. The two exchange gifts before she returns to her country.

The account describes Solomon's wealth through gold shields, an ivory throne overlaid with gold and rich imports brought by sea. Foreign rulers visit to hear his wisdom and bring gifts. His horses, chariots and trade networks further display his power. After ruling Israel from Jerusalem for forty years, Solomon dies and is buried in David's city. His son Rehoboam succeeds him.

stories.title: Rehoboam and the Division
stories.summary:
At Shechem, Jeroboam and the people ask Rehoboam to reduce the harsh labor imposed by Solomon. Rehoboam consults older advisers, who recommend kindness, then turns to the men who grew up with him. He follows their advice and threatens an even heavier burden. The northern people reject David's royal line. They stone the official sent to oversee forced labor, and Rehoboam escapes to Jerusalem.

Rehoboam gathers troops from Judah and Benjamin to recover the kingdom. The prophet Shemaiah tells them not to fight their fellow Israelites, and they return home. Rehoboam strengthens fortified towns and supplies them with weapons and food. Priests and Levites move south after Jeroboam excludes them from service. Other northerners who seek the LORD also come to Jerusalem, strengthening Rehoboam's kingdom during its early years.

Once secure, Rehoboam abandons God's law. In his fifth year, Shishak of Egypt captures Judah's fortified towns and advances on Jerusalem. Shemaiah presents the attack as a consequence of abandoning God. Rehoboam and the leaders humble themselves, and the prophet announces that they will survive but remain subject to Shishak. The invader takes treasures from the temple and palace, including Solomon's gold shields. Rehoboam replaces those shields with bronze ones. The account ends by judging his rule unfavorably and recording his death after seventeen years as king.

stories.title: Abijah and Asa
stories.summary:
Abijah faces Jeroboam with a smaller army and defends the rule of David's family. He contrasts Judah's priests and temple worship with Jeroboam's calf images and appointed priests. Jeroboam places an ambush behind Judah, surrounding its soldiers. They cry to God, the priests sound trumpets, and Judah wins. The account attributes the victory to their reliance on the LORD.

After Abijah's death, Asa removes foreign altars and sacred images, strengthens towns and calls Judah to follow God's law. When Zerah attacks with a large army, Asa prays for help. Judah defeats the invaders, pursues them and takes plunder. Encouraged by the prophet Azariah, Asa renews the altar and gathers people from Judah and the northern tribes. They make a public pledge to seek God. The agreement includes a death penalty for anyone who refuses. Asa also removes Maacah as queen mother because of her sacred image, which he destroys.

Later, Baasha of Israel fortifies Ramah to block movement into Judah. Asa pays Ben Hadad of Aram to break his treaty with Baasha and attack Israel. The strategy succeeds, but the prophet Hanani rebukes Asa for relying on a foreign king instead of God. Asa imprisons him and oppresses some of the people. Near the end of his reign, Asa develops a severe foot disease. The text says he consults physicians without seeking the LORD. He dies after forty-one years as king and receives an honored burial.

stories.title: Jehoshaphat
stories.summary:
Jehoshaphat strengthens Judah's defenses and sends officials, priests and Levites through its towns to teach God's law. The account describes his growing wealth, military forces and tribute from neighboring peoples. He then allies with Ahab of Israel and agrees to join an attack on Ramoth Gilead. Before fighting, he asks for a message from the LORD.

Ahab's prophets predict success, but Micaiah describes Israel scattered without a shepherd. He also reports a heavenly vision in which a spirit receives permission to deceive Ahab's prophets. Ahab imprisons him and goes to battle in disguise. Jehoshaphat narrowly escapes attack, while an arrow strikes Ahab, who dies that evening. Back in Jerusalem, Jehoshaphat receives a prophetic rebuke for helping Ahab. He later appoints judges and tells them to reject favoritism and bribes.

When forces from Moab, Ammon and Mount Seir approach, Jehoshaphat calls a fast. Families gather at the temple, where he admits that Judah lacks the strength to face the enemy. Jahaziel announces that God will fight for them. Jehoshaphat sends singers ahead of the army. As they sing, the opposing forces turn against one another until none survive. Judah gathers plunder for three days, gives thanks and returns to Jerusalem with music.

The account credits God with the peace that follows, but notes that local worship sites remain and the people's loyalty is incomplete. It closes with Jehoshaphat joining Ahaziah of Israel in a shipbuilding venture. A prophet condemns the alliance, and the ships are wrecked before they sail.

stories.title: Jehoram, Ahaziah, Athaliah and Joash
stories.summary:
After succeeding Jehoshaphat, Jehoram kills his brothers and some of Judah's leaders. He follows the ways of Ahab's family, whose daughter he has married. Edom and Libnah rebel, and a letter from Elijah announces punishment for his violence and religious practices. Invaders carry away royal wealth and members of his family. Jehoram later dies from a severe bowel disease, without the honors given to earlier kings.

His youngest son Ahaziah takes the throne and follows the counsel of Ahab's family. While visiting Israel's wounded king, he becomes caught in Jehu's attack on that royal house. Jehu's men capture and kill him. Ahaziah's mother Athaliah then kills royal heirs and takes power. Jehoshabeath, Ahaziah's sister and the priest Jehoiada's wife, rescues the young Joash and hides him in the temple for six years.

Jehoiada gathers supporters, places guards around Joash and has him crowned. Athaliah hears the celebration and cries treason, but guards take her outside the temple and kill her. The people renew their commitment to the LORD, destroy Baal's temple and kill its priest. Joash later arranges repairs to God's temple. Contributions collected in a chest pay skilled workers, and the remaining money funds temple vessels.

After Jehoiada dies, Joash listens to Judah's leaders and turns to other worship. When Jehoiada's son Zechariah condemns this change, Joash orders him stoned in the temple court. An Aramean force later defeats Judah and leaves Joash badly wounded. His own servants kill him in retaliation for the bloodshed against Jehoiada's family. His son Amaziah becomes king.

stories.title: Amaziah, Uzziah and Jotham
stories.summary:
Amaziah executes his father's killers but spares their children, following the law that each person bears responsibility for their own wrongdoing. Before attacking Edom, he dismisses hired Israelite soldiers after a prophet warns against using them. Judah defeats Edom and throws captured men from a cliff. The dismissed soldiers meanwhile raid Judah's towns. Amaziah brings home Edom's gods and worships them, then silences a prophet who objects. He challenges Israel's king Joash and suffers defeat. Joash captures him, breaks part of Jerusalem's wall and takes treasure and hostages. Amaziah later flees a conspiracy but is killed at Lachish.

Uzziah succeeds him and gains strength through military victories, building projects and farming. He equips his army and installs devices on Jerusalem's defenses to shoot arrows and stones. The account says his success leads to pride. He enters the temple to burn incense, and priests confront him because that task belongs to them. While arguing with them, he develops a skin disease on his forehead. He leaves the temple and lives separately until his death. His son Jotham manages the royal household and governs the people.

As king, Jotham follows practices the account praises, without repeating his father's intrusion into the temple. He builds defenses and defeats the Ammonites, who pay tribute. The text credits his strength to his conduct before God, while noting that the people still act corruptly. After his death, his son Ahaz takes the throne.

stories.title: Ahaz and Hezekiah's Reforms
stories.summary:
Ahaz makes images for Baal, burns his children in fire and worships at local shrines. The account presents attacks by Aram and Israel as judgment against him. Israel takes many women and children captive, but the prophet Oded condemns this treatment of their own people. Leaders stop the army from keeping the captives. They clothe, feed and care for them, then return them to their relatives at Jericho. Ahaz seeks Assyrian help, but his payments bring no relief. He sacrifices to the gods of Damascus, damages temple vessels and closes the temple doors.

His successor Hezekiah reopens and repairs the doors in his first year. Priests and Levites cleanse the building and restore its furnishings. Hezekiah gathers the leaders for sacrifices, music and worship. He then invites people throughout Israel and Judah to celebrate Passover in Jerusalem. They hold it in the second month because the priests and people were not ready earlier. Some northern communities ridicule the invitation, but others come.

Many participants have not completed the required cleansing. Hezekiah asks God to pardon those who sincerely seek him, and the account says God hears and heals the people. The assembly extends the celebration for another week. Afterward, participants destroy altars and sacred images in Judah and parts of Israel. Hezekiah organizes the priests and Levites and provides for regular offerings. The people contribute produce and livestock in abundance, and officials store and distribute the gifts to support temple workers and their families.

stories.title: Sennacherib's Invasion and Hezekiah's Pride
stories.summary:
Sennacherib of Assyria invades Judah and attacks its fortified towns. Expecting an assault on Jerusalem, Hezekiah blocks water sources outside the city, repairs walls and prepares weapons. He appoints commanders and encourages the people to trust that God will help them. Sennacherib sends messengers from Lachish who challenge that trust. They claim that Jerusalem's God cannot save it any more than other nations' gods saved them. They shout in the people's own language to frighten those on the wall.

Hezekiah and the prophet Isaiah pray. The account says God sends an angel who destroys the Assyrian army's leading warriors and commanders. Sennacherib returns home in disgrace and is later killed by his own sons in his god's temple. Hezekiah receives gifts and honor after Jerusalem's deliverance.

The narrative also describes Hezekiah's severe illness and God's answer to his prayer. He responds with pride rather than gratitude, bringing divine anger on himself and Judah. He and Jerusalem's people then humble themselves, and punishment is delayed beyond his lifetime. The account lists his wealth, storehouses and work redirecting the waters of Gihon. It also says God tests him when Babylonian envoys arrive to ask about a sign. Hezekiah receives an honored burial, and Manasseh succeeds him.

stories.title: Manasseh's Repentance and Josiah's Reforms
stories.summary:
Manasseh rebuilds shrines his father removed, sets foreign altars and an image in the temple, practices divination and burns his children in fire. He and the people ignore God's warnings. Assyrian officers take him captive to Babylon, where he humbles himself and prays. The account says God restores him to Jerusalem. He removes foreign gods, repairs the LORD's altar and commands Judah to worship there. His son Amon later returns to image worship and is killed by his servants. The people execute the conspirators and make Josiah king.

Josiah begins seeking God while young and removes sacred images and altars throughout Judah and parts of Israel. During temple repairs, the priest Hilkiah discovers a book of God's law. Shaphan reads it to the king, who tears his clothes in distress. The prophet Huldah announces disaster because the people have abandoned God. She also says Josiah's humility has been heard and that he will not live to see that disaster. Josiah gathers the people, reads the book aloud and renews their commitment to its commands.

Josiah arranges a large Passover celebration, providing animals and organizing priests, Levites, singers and gatekeepers. The account says no comparable Passover had occurred since Samuel's time. Later, Egypt's king Neco marches toward Carchemish. Josiah goes out against him despite Neco's warning that God has ordered his journey. Josiah disguises himself for battle at Megiddo, where archers wound him. His servants carry him to Jerusalem, and he dies. Judah mourns, and Jeremiah composes a lament for him.

stories.title: The Fall of Judah and Cyrus's Decree
stories.summary:
After Josiah's death, the people make Jehoahaz king, but Egypt's ruler removes him after three months and takes him to Egypt. His brother Eliakim becomes king under the new name Jehoiakim. Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon later attacks, binds Jehoiakim and carries temple vessels to Babylon. Jehoiachin succeeds him briefly before being taken away as well. Nebuchadnezzar appoints Zedekiah, who rejects Jeremiah's warnings and rebels against Babylon.

The account describes priests and people defiling the temple and repeatedly rejecting God's messengers. It presents the coming destruction as judgment after those warnings go unheard. Babylonian forces kill people without sparing the young, old or weak. They remove temple and palace treasures, burn the temple and palaces, and break Jerusalem's wall. Survivors are taken to Babylon and serve its rulers until Persia takes power. The text links the land's desolation to Jeremiah's words and describes seventy years in which it receives its neglected Sabbath rest.

The book ends with a change under Cyrus of Persia. Stirred by the LORD, Cyrus issues a written proclamation saying that God has charged him to build a temple in Jerusalem. He invites God's people to go up there and calls for God to be with them.

stories.title: Cyrus's Decree and the Return
stories.summary:
Cyrus, king of Persia, announces that Israel's God has charged him to rebuild the temple in Jerusalem. He permits members of God's people to return and asks their neighbors to support them with goods, animals, silver, and gold. The account presents his proclamation as fulfilling the word spoken through Jeremiah. Family leaders, priests, and Levites prepare to leave, while those around them contribute supplies.

Cyrus also releases the temple vessels that Nebuchadnezzar had taken to Babylon. These are counted out to Sheshbazzar, who brings them with the returning exiles. A detailed register names families, towns, priests, singers, gatekeepers, and temple servants among the returnees. Some cannot establish their ancestry. Priestly families without records are excluded from priestly privileges pending a decision through sacred means.

The assembly numbers 42,360, besides servants and additional singers. On reaching Jerusalem, some family heads donate to rebuilding the temple according to their resources. The returnees then settle in their towns, establishing the community from which the rebuilding will proceed.

stories.title: Rebuilding the Altar and Foundation
stories.summary:
In the seventh month, the returned people gather in Jerusalem. Jeshua, Zerubbabel, and their associates rebuild the altar on its former base, despite their fear of surrounding peoples. Morning and evening sacrifices begin before the temple foundation is laid. They celebrate the Festival of Booths and resume the appointed offerings.

The community pays stoneworkers and carpenters and supplies food, drink, and oil to obtain cedar from Lebanon. In the second year after their arrival, they appoint Levites to supervise construction. When the foundation is laid, priests with trumpets and Levites with cymbals lead praise according to David's directions. The people respond with loud shouts of thanksgiving.

Not everyone reacts in the same way. Older priests, Levites, and family heads who remember the first temple weep at the sight of the new foundation. Their crying mingles with the joyful shouting until the sounds cannot be distinguished. The celebration and grief are heard far away.

stories.title: Opposition and Delay
stories.summary:
People described as Judah and Benjamin's adversaries offer to help rebuild the temple, saying they also worship Israel's God. Zerubbabel, Jeshua, and the family heads refuse their participation, citing Cyrus's authorization for their own community to build. The surrounding people then discourage the workers and hire advisers to obstruct the project.

The chapter also records opposition during the reigns of Ahasuerus and Artaxerxes. In a letter to Artaxerxes, officials accuse Jerusalem of rebellion and warn that rebuilt walls will threaten royal revenue and control. They ask him to consult earlier records. After a search, the king orders work on the city stopped until he gives further permission. The officials enforce that order by armed force.

These letters concern Jerusalem and its walls, alongside the chapter's account of temple opposition. The closing verse returns to the temple's stalled construction. Work on God's house remains suspended until the second year of King Darius.

stories.title: The Temple Completed
stories.summary:
With encouragement from the prophets Haggai and Zechariah, Zerubbabel and Jeshua resume building the temple. Governor Tattenai and his associates ask who authorized the work and request the leaders' names. The builders explain that Cyrus permitted the rebuilding and returned the temple vessels. Work continues while the officials send their report to Darius.

A search of the royal archives uncovers Cyrus's decree at Achmetha. Darius orders the officials to leave the builders alone and pay construction expenses from regional royal revenues. He also requires daily supplies for sacrifices, so the priests can pray for the king and his sons. Severe penalties are announced for anyone who alters the decree.

The elders complete the temple in Darius's sixth year. Priests, Levites, and the returned community dedicate it with sacrifices, including twelve goats representing Israel's tribes. They organize temple service according to the law of Moses. The passage ends with Passover and seven days of joyful celebration, joined by others who have separated themselves to seek Israel's God.

stories.title: Ezra Comes to Jerusalem
stories.summary:
Ezra, a priest and skilled teacher of Moses' law, travels from Babylon to Jerusalem during the reign of Artaxerxes. He has committed himself to studying, practicing, and teaching the law. The king authorizes willing Israelites and temple workers to accompany him and provides gifts for temple worship. His letter also permits regional funding, exempts temple personnel from taxes, and empowers Ezra to appoint judges and teach the law.

At the river Ahava, Ezra reviews the travelers and discovers that no Levites are present. He sends representatives to recruit Levites and temple servants. The company then fasts and asks God for protection during the journey. Ezra explains that he was ashamed to request an armed escort after speaking of God's protection.

He weighs the silver, gold, and sacred vessels and entrusts them to selected men for delivery. The travelers reach Jerusalem safely, which Ezra attributes to God's care. There the valuables are weighed again and recorded. The returnees offer sacrifices and deliver the king's orders to local officials, who support the people and temple.

stories.title: Ezra and Mixed Marriages
stories.summary:
Leaders tell Ezra that members of the returned community, including priests and officials, have married women from neighboring peoples. They describe these marriages as a breach of the community's obligations to God. Ezra tears his clothing, pulls out hair, and sits appalled until the evening offering. In prayer, he confesses communal wrongdoing and fears that renewed disobedience will endanger the surviving community.

As a weeping crowd gathers, Shecaniah proposes an agreement to send away the foreign wives and their children. Ezra requires an oath from the leaders and people. A proclamation orders all returned exiles to assemble in Jerusalem within three days, threatening confiscation and exclusion for anyone absent.

Gathered in heavy rain, the men agree to Ezra's demand for separation. They ask for scheduled hearings because the cases are numerous and cannot be settled outdoors at once. The text names several people who oppose the arrangement. Ezra and appointed family heads examine the cases over the following months. The account closes with a list of men involved, including priests, Levites, and other Israelites, and notes that some marriages include children.

stories.title: Nehemiah's Prayer and Commission
stories.summary:
At the palace in Susa, Nehemiah hears that Jerusalem's survivors are in distress, its wall is broken, and its gates are burned. He weeps, fasts, and prays for several days. His prayer confesses Israel's failures, including his own family's wrongdoing, and recalls God's promise to gather those who return to him. As the king's cupbearer, he asks for favor before his royal employer.

When Artaxerxes notices his sadness, Nehemiah is frightened but explains that the city of his ancestors' graves lies ruined. Asked what he wants, he prays and requests permission to rebuild Jerusalem. The king approves the journey after asking when he will return.

Nehemiah also receives letters allowing passage through the provinces and timber for gates, walls, and his residence. He attributes the king's response to God's favor. Accompanied by army officers and horsemen, he delivers the letters to the governors. The passage closes with Sanballat and Tobiah deeply displeased that someone has come to help the Israelites.

stories.title: Rebuilding the Wall
stories.summary:
After three days in Jerusalem, Nehemiah quietly inspects the ruined walls at night with a few companions. He then invites the community to rebuild, describing God's help and the king's support. The people agree, while Sanballat, Tobiah, and Geshem ridicule the project and accuse them of rebellion.

The account records the workers section by section around Jerusalem. Priests, local rulers, craftspeople, merchants, and families repair gates and walls. Shallum's daughters join him, while the nobles of Tekoa refuse to help. The wall reaches half its height because the people keep working.

Opposition grows into plans for an attack. Nehemiah prays, posts guards, and stations armed families at vulnerable places. Exhausted workers also face mounting rubble and repeated warnings of danger. When the plot becomes known, construction resumes under protection.

Some men work while others stand guard. Builders carry swords, and burden bearers keep weapons ready. A trumpeter stays beside Nehemiah to summon workers scattered along the wall. People lodge inside Jerusalem to guard at night and labor by day. The passage ends with Nehemiah and his companions remaining dressed and armed.

stories.title: Debt Relief
stories.summary:
Families complain to Nehemiah that hunger, royal taxes, and debt are consuming their livelihoods. Some have mortgaged fields, vineyards, and houses to obtain grain. Others have borrowed to pay taxes, and their children are being forced into servitude. They cannot recover their children because their property belongs to others.

Angered by these reports, Nehemiah confronts the nobles and officials before an assembly. He contrasts their lending practices with efforts to redeem fellow Jews sold abroad. Acknowledging that he and his associates also lend money and grain, he calls for the charges to stop. He demands the immediate return of property and the amounts being charged.

The creditors promise to restore what they have taken and demand nothing further. Nehemiah has them swear before the priests, and the people carry out the agreement. He then describes his own twelve years as governor. He has declined the governor's allowance, bought no land, continued the wall work, and fed many people at his table. He ends by asking God to remember what he has done for the community.

stories.title: The Wall Completed
stories.summary:
As Jerusalem's wall nears completion, Sanballat and Geshem repeatedly invite Nehemiah to meet outside the city. He believes they intend harm and refuses to leave the work. An open letter then accuses him of planning rebellion and seeking kingship. Nehemiah rejects the accusations and prays for strength.

Shemaiah urges him to hide inside the temple because assassins are coming. Nehemiah refuses and concludes that Tobiah and Sanballat hired Shemaiah to frighten him into wrongdoing and disgrace. He asks God to remember those trying to intimidate him.

The wall is finished in fifty-two days. According to the account, surrounding enemies lose confidence because they recognize God's help. Yet Tobiah maintains close ties with Judah's nobles, who praise him to Nehemiah and relay Nehemiah's words back to him. His threatening letters continue.

After installing the gates, Nehemiah appoints leaders and guards and gives orders for opening and securing the city. Jerusalem remains spacious but sparsely populated, with houses still unbuilt. He decides to register the people by family and finds the record of the first returnees.

stories.title: Ezra Reads the Law
stories.summary:
The people gather near Jerusalem's Water Gate and ask Ezra to bring the law of Moses. He reads from morning until midday before men, women, and others able to understand. Levites explain the reading so the assembly can grasp its meaning. When the people weep, their leaders tell them that this holy day calls for celebration and sharing food with those who have none.

Further study reveals the command to live in temporary shelters during the seventh-month festival. The people gather branches and make shelters on roofs, in courtyards, and in public spaces. They celebrate with great joy, hearing the law daily throughout the feast.

Later that month, the Israelites assemble with fasting and signs of mourning. They confess their own sins and their ancestors' failures. A long prayer recalls creation, Abraham, the escape from Egypt, wilderness provision, and settlement in the land. It contrasts repeated disobedience with God's patience and repeated rescue.

The prayer ends in the community's present hardship: foreign kings control the land's produce, their bodies, and their livestock. In response, the leaders, Levites, and priests commit themselves to a written agreement and seal it.

stories.title: The Dedication of Jerusalem’s Wall
stories.summary:
Levites and singers are summoned from their towns and villages for the dedication of Jerusalem's wall. The celebration is prepared with thanksgiving, singing, cymbals, harps, and other stringed instruments. Priests and Levites purify themselves, the people, the gates, and the wall.

Nehemiah brings Judah's leaders onto the wall and organizes two large thanksgiving processions. Ezra leads one group along its route, accompanied by leaders, priests with trumpets, and musicians. Nehemiah follows the other group with the remaining leaders and people. The account traces their movement past the city's gates, towers, and stairs.

Both groups take their places at the temple, where priests sound trumpets and the singers raise their voices under their director. Great sacrifices accompany the celebration. Women and children join the rejoicing, which the account attributes to God. The passage ends with Jerusalem's joyful noise carrying far beyond the city.

stories.title: Nehemiah's Reforms
stories.summary:
A public reading of Moses' law leads the community to exclude people of foreign ancestry from its assembly. The chapter then recounts problems Nehemiah finds after returning from a visit to the king. Eliashib has given Tobiah a large temple storeroom. Nehemiah throws out Tobiah's belongings, orders the rooms purified, and restores the temple supplies.

He also discovers that unpaid Levites and singers have returned to their fields. He confronts the officials, restores the workers, and appoints trusted supervisors to distribute contributions. Finding trade and farm work continuing on the Sabbath, he orders Jerusalem's gates closed for that day. He warns merchants camping outside and appoints Levites to guard the gates.

Nehemiah next confronts men married to women of Ashdod, Ammon, and Moab. Their children speak other languages rather than the language of Judah. He curses the men, strikes some, pulls out their hair, and requires an oath against such marriages. He also drives away a priestly family member married into Sanballat's family.

The account closes with the restoration of priestly duties, wood offerings, and firstfruits. Throughout these measures, Nehemiah asks God to remember him favorably.

stories.title: Vashti Deposed
stories.summary:
King Ahasuerus displays his wealth and royal splendor before officials and nobles from his vast kingdom. After these celebrations, he gives a seven-day feast for everyone in the citadel of Susa. Queen Vashti holds a separate banquet for the women in the palace.

On the final day, while merry with wine, the king sends seven attendants to bring Vashti wearing her royal crown. He wants to show her beauty to the assembled guests. She refuses to come. The passage gives no explanation for her refusal, but describes the king's intense anger.

He consults advisers about the legal response. Memucan argues that Vashti's conduct will encourage women throughout the empire to disregard their husbands. He proposes permanently excluding her from the king's presence and giving her position to another woman.

The king accepts this advice. Letters go out in the languages and scripts of the provinces, declaring that every man should rule his household. The chapter ends with a domestic dispute at court transformed into an empire-wide decree.

stories.title: Esther Becomes Queen
stories.summary:
After the king's anger over Vashti subsides, his attendants suggest gathering young women so he can choose a new queen. Esther, also called Hadassah, is among those taken into the royal household at Susa. She is Jewish and has been raised by her cousin Mordecai after her parents' deaths. Following his instructions, she does not reveal her ancestry.

Esther gains the favor of Hegai, the official responsible for the women. He provides special care, attendants, and quarters, while Mordecai visits the courtyard daily to learn how she is doing. After the prescribed preparations, she goes to the king, taking only what Hegai recommends. The king favors her above the other women and crowns her queen. A banquet, holiday, and gifts mark the occasion.

Meanwhile, Mordecai discovers a plot by two royal doorkeepers to attack the king. He tells Esther, who reports it in his name. An investigation confirms the accusation, the conspirators are executed, and Mordecai's action is entered in the royal records.

stories.title: Haman's Plot
stories.summary:
The king promotes Haman above the other officials and commands his servants to bow before him. Mordecai refuses. When Haman learns that Mordecai is Jewish, he decides to destroy all Jews in the empire rather than punish Mordecai alone. A lot is cast to select the appointed date.

Haman tells the king that a scattered people follows different laws and does not obey royal commands. The king gives him authority and his signet ring. Orders are sent throughout the provinces to kill all Jews on one day, including women and children, and seize their property. While the king and Haman drink, Susa is bewildered and Jewish communities mourn.

Through a messenger, Mordecai urges Esther to appeal to the king. She explains that entering his presence uninvited can mean death, unless he extends his golden scepter. Mordecai warns that her royal position will not protect her and asks whether it has brought her to this moment.

Esther requests three days of fasting from the Jews of Susa. She and her attendants will also fast. Then she will approach the king despite the danger, accepting that she may die.

stories.title: Esther's Banquets
stories.summary:
Esther enters the royal court, and the king extends his golden scepter, allowing her to approach. Rather than immediately stating her full request, she invites him and Haman to a banquet. There she asks them to return for another banquet the next day. Haman leaves delighted, but Mordecai's refusal to honor him renews his anger. At his wife's and friends' suggestion, he prepares a tall gallows for Mordecai.

That night, the sleepless king has the royal records read aloud. Hearing how Mordecai uncovered an assassination plot, he learns that no reward was given. He asks Haman how to honor a favored man. Assuming the honor is his, Haman proposes royal clothing and a public procession on the king's horse. The king orders him to give those honors to Mordecai.

At the second banquet, Esther asks for her life and her people's lives, identifying Haman as their enemy. The king leaves in anger. Haman begs Esther for mercy and falls onto her couch. Returning, the king interprets this as an assault.

An attendant points out the gallows Haman prepared for Mordecai. The king orders Haman executed there, and his anger subsides.

stories.title: The Jews Delivered and Purim
stories.summary:
The king gives Haman's estate to Esther and his signet ring to Mordecai. Esther again pleads for her people, because the earlier destruction decree remains in force. The king says a sealed royal decree cannot be revoked, but authorizes a new one. Mordecai issues orders allowing Jews to assemble and defend themselves on the appointed day. The decree permits killing opposing forces, including women and children, and taking their property.

Couriers carry the order throughout the empire. Jewish communities celebrate, while officials support them because they fear Mordecai's growing power. When the appointed day arrives, the Jews defeat those seeking to harm them. In Susa, they kill five hundred men and Haman's ten sons.

At Esther's request, the king permits another day of action in Susa and the public hanging of Haman's sons. Three hundred more men are killed there. Across the provinces, the account reports seventy-five thousand enemies killed. It repeatedly notes that the Jews do not take plunder.

Mordecai and Esther establish Purim as an annual commemoration of the reversal from danger and mourning to relief and celebration. Its observance includes feasts, gifts of food, and gifts to the poor. The book ends with Mordecai second to the king, working for his people's welfare.

stories.title: Job's Testing
stories.summary:
Job is introduced as an upright, prosperous man who avoids evil and offers sacrifices for his children. In a heavenly gathering, God points to his integrity. Satan questions whether Job's loyalty would survive the loss of God's protection and blessings. God permits an attack on Job's possessions but not his person.

Messengers arrive in rapid succession. Raiders have taken livestock and killed servants, fire has destroyed sheep, and a powerful wind has collapsed a house on Job's children. Job tears his robe, shaves his head, and mourns. He blesses God's name rather than accusing God of wrongdoing.

In another heavenly encounter, Satan argues that bodily suffering will break Job's loyalty. God permits him to afflict Job while sparing his life. Covered with painful sores, Job sits among ashes and scrapes himself with broken pottery. His wife urges him to renounce God and die. Job answers that receiving good from God does not mean refusing hardship.

Three friends come to comfort him. They barely recognize him, weep, and share his mourning. For seven days and nights, they sit silently beside him because his suffering is so great.

stories.title: Elihu Speaks
stories.summary:
Job's three companions stop answering him, and the younger Elihu becomes angry with both sides. He objects that Job has justified himself rather than God. He also objects that the friends have condemned Job without answering him. Until now, Elihu has waited because the others are older.

Elihu explains that he expected age and experience to bring wisdom. Yet he now argues that understanding comes from the spirit God gives, not simply from years. He has listened closely and believes none of the three has refuted Job. He will therefore offer his own answer rather than repeat their arguments.

Comparing his pent-up words to wine ready to burst its container, Elihu says he must speak to find relief. He promises not to favor anyone or use flattery, because he answers to his maker. He closes his introduction by warning that his maker would punish him for flattering others.

stories.title: God Answers from the Whirlwind
stories.summary:
God addresses Job from a whirlwind and challenges him with questions rather than an account of his suffering. Where was Job when the earth's foundations were laid and boundaries set for the sea? Can he command dawn, explore death's depths, direct storms, or govern the stars? The questions move through a world beyond Job's knowledge and control.

The speech then considers animals living beyond human management: lions, ravens, mountain goats, wild donkeys, wild oxen, and birds. It describes their food, reproduction, freedom, strength, and habits. Job is asked whether these creatures depend on his wisdom or power.

When God calls for an answer, Job says he is of little account and will speak no further. God challenges him again, asking whether he would condemn God to justify himself. Job is invited to display the power needed to bring down the proud and save himself.

The final sections describe Behemoth and Leviathan in vivid detail. Behemoth possesses immense strength, while Leviathan resists capture and weapons and is portrayed with smoke and flame. The passage ends with Leviathan's fearlessness and supremacy among the proud.

stories.title: Job Restored
stories.summary:
Job answers God by acknowledging that God's purposes cannot be prevented. He says he has spoken about things beyond his understanding. His earlier knowledge was hearsay, but he now describes a direct encounter and responds in dust and ashes.

God then addresses Eliphaz and the other two friends. Unlike Job, they have not spoken rightly about God. They must bring sacrifices, and Job will pray for them. They follow these instructions, and God accepts Job's prayer.

Job's fortunes are restored as he prays for his friends. Relatives and former acquaintances come to share a meal, console him, and give him money and gold. The account lists livestock totaling twice his earlier holdings. He also has seven sons and three daughters. His daughters are named, praised for their beauty, and given an inheritance alongside their brothers.

Job lives another 140 years and sees four generations of descendants. The book closes with his death at an old age, after a long life.

stories.title: Isaiah's Call
stories.summary:
In the year King Uzziah dies, Isaiah sees the Lord enthroned above the temple, with the robe's train filling the building. Six-winged heavenly beings called seraphim proclaim God's holiness and glory. Their voices shake the thresholds, and smoke fills the house.

Isaiah fears that he is ruined because he has seen the king while belonging to a people of unclean speech. One of the seraphim brings a burning coal from the altar and touches his mouth. The being declares his guilt removed and his sin forgiven.

When the Lord asks whom to send, Isaiah volunteers. His commission is severe: he must speak to people who hear without understanding and see without perceiving. The command describes hearts becoming unresponsive, preventing a return that would bring healing.

Isaiah asks how long this will last. The answer points to ruined cities, empty houses, and a devastated land whose inhabitants have been removed. Even a remaining tenth will face further destruction. The vision ends with an image of a felled tree's stump, identified as a holy seed.

stories.title: Ahaz and the Sign of Immanuel
stories.summary:
Judah's king Ahaz and his people are terrified by an alliance between Syria and Israel. God sends Isaiah and his son Shearjashub to meet Ahaz. Isaiah tells the king to remain calm: the allied rulers' plan to overthrow Judah and install another king will fail. He warns that Ahaz must trust if he is to stand firm.

Ahaz is invited to request a sign but refuses, saying he will not test God. Isaiah responds that the Lord will give a sign anyway: a woman will bear a son named Immanuel. Before the child knows how to reject wrong and choose right, the lands of the two feared kings will be abandoned.

The message then turns from the failed alliance to a greater threat. Assyria will bring unprecedented trouble upon Ahaz, his family, and Judah. Images of swarming insects and a hired razor portray invasion and humiliation.

The chapter ends with changes to the land. Surviving people will live on curds and honey, while valuable vineyards and cultivated hills become thorn-covered ground used by grazing animals.

stories.title: Sennacherib's Threat and Hezekiah
stories.summary:
After capturing Judah's fortified cities, Sennacherib sends a senior Assyrian officer with a large force to Jerusalem. The officer mocks Judah's reliance on Egypt and on God. Ignoring a request to speak privately in Aramaic, he addresses the people on the wall in their own language. He urges surrender and argues that no nation's gods have stopped Assyria.

Hezekiah's officials report the speech, and the king enters the temple in mourning. He sends representatives to Isaiah, who promises that the Assyrian king will return home and die there. Another threatening message arrives. Hezekiah spreads it before God and asks for deliverance, distinguishing Israel's God from the manufactured gods Assyria has destroyed.

Isaiah sends a response condemning Sennacherib's arrogance. The message promises that Jerusalem will not be entered or besieged successfully, and that Judah's survivors will take root again.

The account reports that God's angel strikes 185,000 men in the Assyrian camp. Sennacherib returns to Nineveh. Later, while worshiping in his god's temple, he is killed by two sons, who flee. Another son, Esar Haddon, succeeds him.

stories.title: Hezekiah's Illness
stories.summary:
Hezekiah becomes gravely ill, and Isaiah tells him to put his affairs in order because he will die. The king turns toward the wall, prays, and weeps. God sends Isaiah back with a different message: Hezekiah will receive fifteen more years, and Jerusalem will be defended against Assyria. As a sign, the shadow on Ahaz's sundial moves backward ten steps.

Hezekiah's written reflection describes the terror of dying before his life is complete. He compares his life to a tent being removed and fabric cut from a loom. After recovering, he gives thanks for deliverance and promises praise with music in the temple. The account also records Isaiah's instruction to apply a cake of figs to the boil.

When envoys from Babylon bring letters and a gift, Hezekiah shows them his treasures, stores, and weapons. Isaiah questions him and announces that these possessions will one day be carried to Babylon. Some of his descendants will serve as eunuchs in its royal palace. Hezekiah accepts the word, commenting that there will be peace and stability in his own days.

stories.title: Jeremiah's Call
stories.summary:
Jeremiah, a priest's son from Anathoth, receives God's word during King Josiah's reign. The introduction places his ministry across the reigns that lead to Jerusalem's exile. God tells him that he was known and appointed as a prophet to the nations before birth. Jeremiah objects that he is too young and does not know how to speak.

God answers that he must go wherever he is sent and speak whatever he is commanded. Touching Jeremiah's mouth, God declares that the words have been placed there. His work will involve both destruction and renewal: uprooting and tearing down, but also building and planting.

Jeremiah sees an almond branch, which God connects with watching over the divine word. He then sees a boiling pot tipping from the north. God explains that disaster will come from that direction against Judah and Jerusalem because the people have worshiped other gods.

Jeremiah must speak without fear before kings, officials, priests, and people. They will fight him, but God promises to make him like a fortified city and rescue him.

stories.title: The Potter's House and the Broken Jar
stories.summary:
God sends Jeremiah to watch a potter at work. When a clay vessel is spoiled, the potter reshapes it into another form. God compares Israel to clay in a potter's hands. Announced disaster may be withdrawn if a nation changes its conduct, while promised good may be withdrawn if it turns to evil. Judah is urged to change, but the people insist on following their own plans.

Opponents plot against Jeremiah and refuse to listen. He recalls pleading for them before God, then asks for judgment against those seeking his life.

God next tells him to buy a pottery jar and take elders and priests to the valley of Hinnom. There he condemns the shedding of innocent blood and the burning of children as offerings to Baal. He announces slaughter, siege, and hunger so severe that people will eat their own children.

Jeremiah is instructed to shatter the jar before those gathered with him. Unlike the workable clay, the broken vessel cannot be restored, picturing the announced destruction of the people and city. Returning to the temple court, he repeats that disaster is coming because the people refuse to hear.

stories.title: Jeremiah and Pashhur
stories.summary:
Pashhur, a priest and senior temple official, hears Jeremiah's prophecy, strikes him, and places him in stocks at the temple gate. On his release the next day, Jeremiah announces a new name for Pashhur: Terror on Every Side. He predicts Babylonian conquest, the removal of Jerusalem's treasures, and Pashhur's exile and death in Babylon. He also accuses Pashhur of prophesying falsely to his friends.

Jeremiah then speaks directly to God about his own distress. His messages of violence and destruction have made him a daily target of ridicule. He wants to stop speaking in God's name, yet the message feels like fire trapped inside his bones. He cannot hold it in. Even familiar companions watch for an opportunity to denounce him.

His words move between confidence and despair. He declares that God stands beside him, asks to see judgment against his persecutors, and calls for praise. Then he curses the day of his birth and the messenger who announced it. The chapter ends with his unresolved question about why he was born to experience sorrow and shame.

stories.title: Hananiah's False Prophecy
stories.summary:
In the temple, before priests and people, Hananiah announces that God has broken Babylon's domination. He promises that within two years the temple vessels, King Jeconiah, and the other exiles will return. Jeremiah responds that he hopes this will happen. Yet he reminds the listeners that earlier prophets often announced war and disaster. A prophet promising peace must be tested by whether that promise comes true.

Hananiah removes the wooden yoke from Jeremiah's neck and breaks it. He repeats that Babylon's power over the nations will be broken within two years. Jeremiah leaves without answering further.

Later, God's word sends Jeremiah back. Breaking the wooden yoke has only replaced it with an iron one: the nations will still serve Nebuchadnezzar. Jeremiah tells Hananiah that God has not sent him and that he has led the people to trust a falsehood. He announces that Hananiah will die that year for urging rebellion against God. The account closes with Hananiah's death in the seventh month.

stories.title: The Scroll Burned
stories.summary:
God tells Jeremiah to record the messages he has received concerning Israel, Judah, and the nations. The stated hope is that hearing the warnings will lead Judah to change and receive forgiveness. Jeremiah dictates the words to Baruch. Unable to enter the temple himself, he sends Baruch to read the scroll publicly during a fast.

Officials hear about the reading and summon Baruch to repeat it. Alarmed, they ask how the scroll was written and advise Baruch and Jeremiah to hide. They then report its contents to King Jehoiakim.

The king sits beside a fire in his winter residence as Jehudi reads the scroll aloud. After every few columns, the king cuts off the section and throws it into the fire. He ignores appeals to preserve it and orders the arrest of Jeremiah and Baruch, but the account says God hides them.

God commands Jeremiah to prepare another scroll and announces judgment against the king, his household, and his servants. Baruch again writes Jeremiah's dictated words, replacing everything destroyed. The passage ends by noting that many similar words are added.

stories.title: Jeremiah in the Cistern
stories.summary:
During Zedekiah's reign, Babylon's army briefly withdraws from Jerusalem because Egyptian forces are approaching. Jeremiah warns that the Egyptians will return home and Babylon will come back to burn the city. When he tries to leave for Benjamin, a guard accuses him of desertion. Officials beat and imprison him despite his denial.

Zedekiah secretly consults Jeremiah, who again predicts his capture. At Jeremiah's request, the king transfers him to the guard's courtyard and provides bread while supplies last. Officials later demand Jeremiah's death because his calls for surrender discourage the defenders. With the king's permission, they lower him into a waterless cistern, where he sinks into mud.

Ebedmelech, an Ethiopian palace official, protests that Jeremiah will die there. The king authorizes a rescue. Ebedmelech lowers ropes and worn clothing to cushion Jeremiah's arms, and the men pull him out.

In another private meeting, Jeremiah urges Zedekiah to surrender so he and the city can survive. The king fears mistreatment by Judean defectors and insists that their conversation remain secret. Jeremiah gives officials the explanation the king prescribed. He remains in the guard's courtyard until Jerusalem falls.

stories.title: The Fall of Jerusalem and Flight to Egypt
stories.summary:
Babylonian forces break into Jerusalem after a long siege. Zedekiah flees but is captured near Jericho. His sons and Judah's nobles are killed before him; he is then blinded and taken away in chains. The city is burned, its walls demolished, and many inhabitants deported. Some poor people remain and receive fields and vineyards.

Jeremiah is protected by Babylonian orders and chooses to stay with Gedaliah, the appointed governor, at Mizpah. The passage also records God's promise to spare Ebedmelech. Gedaliah encourages the remaining people to serve Babylon and gather the harvest. He refuses to believe warnings that Ishmael plans to kill him.

Ishmael murders Gedaliah, others at Mizpah, and many visiting mourners. He takes the survivors captive, but Johanan pursues him and recovers them. Ishmael escapes to Ammon. Fearing Babylonian retaliation, Johanan's group prepares to leave for Egypt.

They ask Jeremiah for God's guidance and promise to obey. After ten days, he tells them to remain in Judah, warning that war and famine will follow them into Egypt. They reject his message and take the community, including Jeremiah and Baruch, to Tahpanhes. There Jeremiah places stones by Pharaoh's residence as instructed. He announces that Nebuchadnezzar will establish his throne there, conquer Egypt, and burn its temples.

stories.title: Ezekiel's Vision and Commission
stories.summary:
Among the exiles by the river Chebar, Ezekiel sees the heavens open. A storm cloud approaches with fire and brightness, revealing four living creatures. Each has four faces and four wings, with wheels beside it that move in concert with the creatures. Above them are a shining expanse, a throne, and a humanlike figure surrounded by radiance. Ezekiel identifies the appearance as the likeness of God's glory and falls facedown.

The Spirit raises him to his feet. God sends him to rebellious Israel and commands him to speak whether people listen or refuse. Ezekiel receives a scroll covered with words of lament and sorrow. He eats it as commanded, finding it sweet as honey.

Carried back to the exiles, he sits overwhelmed for seven days. God then appoints him as a watchman, responsible for passing on warnings. If he withholds a warning, he bears responsibility for the unwarned person's death. If he delivers it faithfully, the listener remains responsible for the response.

Another encounter with God's glory follows in the plain. Ezekiel is told to shut himself inside his house. He will be bound and unable to speak freely, but God will open his mouth when giving him a message.

stories.title: The Glory Leaves the Temple
stories.summary:
While elders sit with Ezekiel in exile, a vision carries him to Jerusalem's temple. He is shown an offensive image, elders offering incense before pictures of creatures and idols, women mourning Tammuz, and men worshiping the sun. God connects these acts with the violence filling the land and announces judgment.

A figure with writing equipment is ordered to mark those who grieve over the city's wrongdoing. Armed figures then kill those without the mark, beginning at the sanctuary. Ezekiel falls facedown and asks whether all Israel's survivors will be destroyed. The response emphasizes the land's bloodshed and injustice.

The vision turns to the winged beings and wheels Ezekiel saw by the Chebar. Burning coals are taken to scatter over the city. God's glory moves from the temple threshold to the beings and then to the eastern gate. Ezekiel condemns leaders who give harmful counsel; one dies as he prophesies.

Alongside judgment comes a promise to the scattered people. God will gather them, give them a new spirit, and replace their stony hearts with responsive hearts. Finally, the divine glory leaves the city and rests on the mountain to its east. Ezekiel returns in the vision to the exiles and tells them what he has seen.

stories.title: The Death of Ezekiel's Wife
stories.summary:
God tells Ezekiel that the person he treasures will be taken from him suddenly. He is commanded not to perform the usual public acts of mourning. He must keep his head covering and sandals on, refrain from covering his lips, and not eat the food associated with mourning.

Ezekiel speaks to the people in the morning, and his wife dies that evening. The following morning he follows the instructions. The people ask what his conduct means for them.

He explains that God will allow the sanctuary they cherish to be desecrated, and the sons and daughters left behind will die by the sword. Their response will resemble his own: instead of customary mourning, they will waste away in their wrongdoing and groan to one another. Ezekiel's bereavement and behavior are presented as a sign of their coming loss.

The passage ends with a promise concerning a survivor who will bring news. When that person arrives, Ezekiel's mouth will be opened, and he will no longer remain silent.

stories.title: The Valley of Dry Bones
stories.summary:
God's Spirit places Ezekiel in a valley filled with very dry bones. Asked whether they can live, he answers that God knows. He is commanded to speak to them. As he does, the bones come together and are covered with sinews, flesh, and skin, but they still lack breath.

Ezekiel then calls for breath from the four winds. The bodies come alive and stand as a vast army. God explains that the bones represent Israel, whose people say their hope is gone. He promises to open their graves, put his Spirit within them, and bring them back to their land.

A second sign follows. Ezekiel writes Judah's name on one stick and Joseph's, representing Ephraim and its companions, on another. He joins the sticks before the people. God explains that the divided kingdoms will become one nation under one ruler.

The promise includes cleansing from wrongdoing, obedience to God's commands, and a king described as God's servant David. The people and their descendants will live in their land. An enduring covenant of peace and God's sanctuary among them complete the vision of restored communal life.

stories.title: Ezekiel Is Shown the Temple in a Vision
stories.summary:
In the twenty-fifth year of exile, fourteen years after Jerusalem's fall, Ezekiel describes being carried to Israel in a vision. God places him on a very high mountain. To the south, he sees a structure resembling a city.

A man with a bronze-like appearance stands at its gate, holding a linen cord and a measuring reed. He tells Ezekiel to watch carefully, listen closely, and attend to everything he is about to see. Ezekiel has been brought there to receive this vision and report it to the people of Israel. The man prepares him to observe what will be shown, rather than beginning the measurements immediately.

stories.title: Daniel and His Friends in Babylon
stories.summary:
After Nebuchadnezzar besieges Jerusalem, young men from Judah's royal and noble families are brought into Babylonian court training. They are to learn the language and literature of the Chaldeans and receive royal food and wine for three years. Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah are among them and receive new names: Belteshazzar, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego.

Daniel resolves not to defile himself with the assigned food and wine. The chief official treats him kindly but fears punishment if the young men look less healthy than their peers. Daniel therefore proposes a ten-day trial to their steward, requesting vegetables and water.

At the trial's end, the four look healthier than those eating the royal food, so the steward continues their different diet. The account credits God with giving them learning and wisdom, and Daniel a particular understanding of visions and dreams.

When the king examines the trainees, he finds none equal to these four. They enter royal service, and their answers surpass those of the kingdom's other specialists. The chapter closes by noting that Daniel continues until Cyrus's first year.

stories.title: Nebuchadnezzar's Dream of the Statue
stories.summary:
A troubling dream leaves Nebuchadnezzar unable to sleep. He demands that his advisers tell him both the dream and its meaning. They protest that no human can meet that demand. Furious, he orders Babylon's wise men killed, putting Daniel and his companions in danger.

Daniel asks for time and urges his friends to seek God's mercy. The mystery is revealed to him in a night vision. After giving thanks, he asks that the wise men be spared and goes before the king. He credits God, rather than his own wisdom, with revealing the secret.

The dream features a vast statue with a golden head, silver chest and arms, bronze middle, iron legs, and feet mixing iron and clay. A stone cut without human hands strikes its feet. The whole statue crumbles and blows away, while the stone becomes a mountain filling the earth.

Daniel identifies Nebuchadnezzar as the golden head and describes succeeding kingdoms, including a divided kingdom combining strength and weakness. God will establish a kingdom that destroys the others and endures forever. The king honors Daniel, praises his God, and appoints him over Babylon's province and wise men. At Daniel's request, his three companions also receive provincial responsibilities.

stories.title: The Fiery Furnace
stories.summary:
Nebuchadnezzar sets up a large golden image and summons his officials to its dedication. Everyone must bow when the music sounds, under threat of death in a furnace. Some officials report that Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego refuse to worship the image or serve the king's gods.

The king confronts them and offers another opportunity to comply. They answer that their God can rescue them, but even if rescue does not come, they will not worship the image. Enraged, he orders the furnace heated far beyond its usual level. The men are bound and thrown in. The heat kills the soldiers carrying out the order.

Nebuchadnezzar then sees four figures walking freely in the fire. He describes the fourth as resembling a divine being. He calls the three men out, and the assembled officials find their bodies and clothing unharmed, without even the smell of fire.

The king praises their God for sending an angel and rescuing them. He issues a harsh decree against anyone who speaks against that God, threatening destruction of both offenders and their houses. The account ends with the three men promoted in Babylon.

stories.title: Nebuchadnezzar's Humbling
stories.summary:
Nebuchadnezzar recounts a disturbing dream in a proclamation about the Most High God's power. He sees an immense tree feeding and sheltering living creatures. A heavenly watcher orders it cut down, leaving its bound stump. The command shifts to a person who will live among animals with an animal's mind for seven periods of time.

Daniel is troubled by the dream but explains that the tree represents the king and his power. Nebuchadnezzar will lose human society and eat grass until he acknowledges God's rule over kingdoms. The surviving stump means his kingdom can be restored. Daniel urges him to practice righteousness and show mercy to the poor.

Twelve months later, the king boasts about Babylon and his own achievement. A heavenly voice announces the judgment. He is driven away, eats grass, and lives exposed to the weather, with hair and nails growing long.

At the end of the appointed time, he looks toward heaven and his understanding returns. He praises God's enduring rule. His counselors seek him out, his royal authority is restored, and his greatness increases. He closes by acknowledging that God can humble those who act proudly.

stories.title: Belshazzar's Feast
stories.summary:
During a great royal banquet, Belshazzar orders the vessels taken from Jerusalem's temple brought out for drinking. The king and his guests use them while praising gods made from precious metals, wood, and stone. Suddenly, fingers appear and write on the palace wall. Terrified, the king offers rich rewards and high office to anyone who can explain the writing. His advisers cannot do so.

The queen recommends Daniel, recalling his ability to interpret difficult matters. Daniel declines the rewards as a condition of speaking. He reminds Belshazzar that Nebuchadnezzar lost his power through pride and recovered only after recognizing God's rule. Although Belshazzar knew this, Daniel says, he has dishonored the God who holds his life.

Daniel explains the written words as a judgment: God has numbered the kingdom's days and ended it; the king has been weighed and found deficient. His kingdom will be divided and given to the Medes and Persians.

Belshazzar nevertheless orders Daniel clothed in purple, given a gold chain, and proclaimed third ruler. That same night, Belshazzar is killed. The account ends with Darius the Mede receiving the kingdom.

stories.title: Daniel in the Lions' Den
stories.summary:
Darius appoints Daniel as one of three senior administrators and considers placing him over the whole kingdom. Other officials cannot find misconduct in his work, so they target his religious practice. They persuade the king to prohibit petitions to any god or person except himself for thirty days. Violators must be thrown to lions, and the signed decree cannot be changed.

Knowing the decree, Daniel continues kneeling in prayer three times daily with his windows open toward Jerusalem. His opponents report him. The distressed king tries to save him but is pressed to enforce the law. Daniel is placed in the lions' den, and its entrance is sealed.
