After a sleepless night, Darius rushes to the den and calls to Daniel. Daniel answers that God sent an angel to shut the lions' mouths. He says he has been found innocent before God and has done the king no harm. He is lifted out without injury.

Darius orders Daniel's accusers, together with their wives and children, thrown into the den, where the lions kill them. He then proclaims reverence for Daniel's God as a living ruler and rescuer. Daniel prospers during the reigns of Darius and Cyrus.

stories.title: Daniel's Visions
stories.summary:
Daniel records a series of visions across several reigns. First, four beasts rise from a turbulent sea, representing earthly kings and kingdoms. A boastful horn persecutes God's holy people. In a heavenly court, the Ancient of Days judges, and a humanlike figure receives an enduring kingdom. The interpretation promises that the holy people will ultimately receive the kingdom after oppression.

A later vision shows a ram defeated by a goat. Gabriel identifies them with Media and Persia, and Greece. The goat's great horn breaks, four replace it, and another destructive power attacks the sanctuary and stops regular offerings. Its rule has a limit, but the vision leaves Daniel exhausted and troubled.

Reading Jeremiah's account of Jerusalem's seventy years of desolation, Daniel prays with fasting and confession. He asks for mercy upon the ruined city and sanctuary. Gabriel announces seventy weeks concerning the people and city, describing restoration, an anointed figure's removal, renewed destruction, and the interruption of sacrifice.

After three weeks of mourning, Daniel receives another revelation beside a river. A heavenly messenger strengthens him and describes conflict involving the princes of Persia and Greece, with Michael providing help. The message traces wars, alliances, betrayal, and rivalry between northern and southern kings. It includes the desecration of the sanctuary, persecution of the wise, and an arrogant ruler's eventual end.

The closing vision describes unprecedented distress, Michael's intervention, and deliverance for those recorded in the book. Many who sleep in the dust awake, some to enduring life and others to disgrace. Daniel hears time periods but does not fully understand. He is told to seal the words until the appointed end and continue his way. He will rest and finally receive his allotted inheritance.

stories.title: Hosea's Marriage to Gomer
stories.summary:
God commands Hosea to take a wife associated with sexual unfaithfulness, presenting the marriage as a sign of Israel's abandonment of God. Hosea marries Gomer, daughter of Diblaim. The passage follows the births of three children whose names carry messages of judgment.

The first son is named Jezreel. God connects the name with bloodshed at Jezreel, announces punishment upon Jehu's dynasty, and declares that Israel's kingdom and military strength will end. Gomer next bears a daughter, named Lo-Ruhamah, meaning not shown mercy. God says Israel will no longer receive mercy, while Judah will be delivered without reliance on weapons or armies.

After the daughter is weaned, another son is born. He is named Lo-Ammi, meaning not my people. The name accompanies a declaration that the relationship between God and Israel has been broken. The final declaration tells Israel that the people no longer belong to God and that he will not be theirs.

stories.title: Amaziah Opposes Amos
stories.summary:
Amaziah, the priest at Bethel, sends a report to King Jeroboam accusing Amos of conspiracy. He says Amos has announced the king's death by the sword and Israel's exile. Amaziah then orders Amos to leave for Judah, earn his living there, and stop prophesying at Bethel because it is the king's sanctuary.

Amos answers by describing his work as a herdsman and a grower of sycamore figs. He says his commission did not arise from belonging to a prophetic profession or family. God took him from tending the flock and sent him to speak to Israel.

In response to Amaziah's demand for silence, Amos delivers a judgment against him. His wife will become a prostitute, his children will be killed, and his land will be divided. Amaziah himself will die in a foreign land described as unclean. The passage ends by repeating the warning that Israel will be taken into exile.

stories.title: Jonah Flees and Is Swallowed
stories.summary:
God sends Jonah to speak against Nineveh's wrongdoing, but Jonah boards a ship from Joppa toward Tarshish instead. A violent storm threatens the vessel. The sailors pray to their gods and throw cargo overboard, while Jonah sleeps below. The captain wakes him and urges him to pray.

The sailors cast lots, which identify Jonah as connected with their danger. He says he worships the God who made sea and land and admits he is fleeing. He tells them to throw him overboard so the storm will stop. They first try to row ashore, but the sea grows worse. After asking God not to hold them guilty for his death, they cast Jonah into the water. The storm immediately ceases, and they offer worship and vows.

God appoints a great fish to swallow Jonah, who remains inside for three days and nights. His prayer describes sinking beneath the waters, remembering God, and receiving deliverance from death. He promises thanksgiving and fulfillment of his vows. At God's command, the fish vomits him onto dry land.

stories.title: Nineveh Repents
stories.summary:
God gives Jonah a second command to go to Nineveh and proclaim the message entrusted to him. This time Jonah obeys. Entering the great city, he announces that it will be overthrown in forty days.

The people believe the warning and begin fasting. People of every social rank put on rough mourning clothes. When the news reaches the king, he leaves his throne, removes his royal robe, dresses in mourning clothes, and sits in ashes.

The king and nobles issue a decree extending the fast even to the city's animals. People must call urgently upon God and abandon their evil conduct and violence. The king does not claim that these actions guarantee safety. He hopes God may turn from anger so the city will survive.

God sees that the people have changed their conduct. The chapter closes with God withdrawing the announced disaster and leaving Nineveh undestroyed.

stories.title: Jonah's Anger
stories.summary:
Jonah is deeply angry that God has shown mercy. In prayer, he says this is why he originally fled toward Tarshish: he knew God was compassionate and might withdraw disaster. He asks to die rather than continue living. God asks whether his anger is right.

Jonah goes east of the city and builds a shelter to watch what will happen. God provides a plant that shades his head, bringing him great pleasure. The next morning, a worm attacks the plant and it withers. A hot east wind and the beating sun leave Jonah faint, and he again asks to die.

God questions his anger over the plant. Jonah insists that his anger is justified, even to death. God points out that Jonah cares about something he neither grew nor worked for, which lasted only briefly.

The book ends with God's unanswered question: should he not care about Nineveh, with its many people unable to distinguish right from left, and its many animals?

stories.title: The Birth of Jesus and the Magi
stories.summary:
Matthew begins with Joseph discovering that Mary, his promised wife, is pregnant before they have lived together. He plans a quiet separation rather than publicly disgrace her. An angel appears in a dream and tells him that the child comes from the Holy Spirit. Joseph is to name him Jesus because he will save his people from their sins. Matthew connects the birth with a prophetic promise of Immanuel, meaning God with us. Joseph follows the instruction and names the child Jesus.

After the birth in Bethlehem, visitors from the east arrive in Jerusalem seeking the newborn king of the Jews. They have seen his star and come to honor him. Herod is troubled and consults religious scholars, who identify Bethlehem from a prophetic passage. He privately asks the visitors when the star appeared and requests a report about the child.

The star leads them to the house where Jesus is with Mary. They bow before him and present gold, frankincense, and myrrh. Warned in a dream against returning to Herod, they leave for their own country by another route.

stories.title: Flight to Egypt and Return to Nazareth
stories.summary:
After the eastern visitors leave, an angel warns Joseph in a dream that Herod intends to kill Jesus. Joseph takes the child and Mary to Egypt during the night. They remain there until Herod dies. Matthew connects this departure and eventual return with the words about God calling his son out of Egypt.

Herod realizes that the visitors have not returned to him. Furious, he orders the killing of boys aged two and younger in Bethlehem and its surrounding area. The age limit follows the information he received about the star. Matthew describes the grief through Jeremiah's image of Rachel mourning her children.

After Herod's death, another dream tells Joseph that the people seeking the child's life are dead. He brings Mary and Jesus back toward Israel. Learning that Herod's son Archelaus rules Judea, Joseph fears settling there. A further warning directs him to Galilee, where the family makes its home in Nazareth. Matthew closes by linking this settlement with Jesus being called a Nazarene.

stories.title: The Baptism and Temptation of Jesus
stories.summary:
John preaches in the Judean wilderness, calling people to turn from wrongdoing because the kingdom of heaven is near. Crowds confess their sins and receive baptism in the Jordan River. When Pharisees and Sadducees arrive, John demands conduct that shows genuine change, rather than reliance on descent from Abraham. He announces someone stronger, who will baptize with the Holy Spirit and separate people like grain from chaff.

Jesus comes from Galilee for baptism. John objects, but Jesus asks him to proceed as the proper fulfillment of righteousness. As Jesus rises from the water, the heavens open, God's Spirit descends like a dove, and a heavenly voice identifies him as God's beloved Son.

The Spirit then leads Jesus into the wilderness, where he fasts for forty days and nights. The devil challenges him to turn stones into bread, throw himself from the temple, and gain the world's kingdoms through worshiping him. Jesus answers each demand with scripture, rejecting the tests and insisting that worship belongs to God alone. The devil leaves, and angels come to attend him.

stories.title: Calling the First Disciples
stories.summary:
When Jesus learns that John has been arrested, he withdraws to Galilee and moves from Nazareth to lakeside Capernaum. Matthew connects this setting with Isaiah's image of light reaching people who live in darkness. Jesus begins announcing that the kingdom of heaven is near and calling people to change their lives.

Beside the Sea of Galilee, he sees the brothers Simon Peter and Andrew casting their fishing net. He invites them to follow him and learn to gather people. They leave their nets immediately. Farther along, James and John are repairing nets in a boat with their father Zebedee. They also respond at once, leaving both boat and father to follow Jesus.

Jesus travels throughout Galilee, teaching in synagogues, announcing the kingdom, and healing people with illnesses and other afflictions. News spreads into Syria, and people bring those experiencing pain, paralysis, seizures, and conditions described as demon possession. Large crowds follow from Galilee and neighboring regions, including Jerusalem, Judea, and the area beyond the Jordan.

stories.title: Healings and Calming the Storm
stories.summary:
As crowds follow Jesus, he cleanses a man with leprosy and sends him to a priest. In Capernaum, a Roman officer asks for his paralyzed servant's recovery. The officer trusts that Jesus can heal without visiting, and Jesus praises his faith. He also heals Peter's mother-in-law and many others. Before crossing the lake, he warns would-be followers about the demands of accompanying him.

A violent storm strikes while Jesus sleeps in the boat. His frightened disciples wake him, and he stills the wind and water. Across the lake, two men described as demon-possessed approach from the tombs. The demons enter pigs, which rush into the sea. Local people ask Jesus to leave.

Back across the lake, Jesus forgives a paralyzed man's sins and heals him amid objections from religious scholars. He calls Matthew from his tax office and defends eating with people labeled sinners. Questions about fasting prompt comparisons with a wedding, new cloth, and fresh wineskins.

A woman with prolonged bleeding touches his clothing and is healed. Jesus then takes a dead girl's hand, and she rises. He restores two blind men's sight and enables a man described as demon-possessed to speak. Reactions divide between amazement and accusations. Seeing the crowds as troubled sheep without a shepherd, Jesus urges his disciples to pray for more workers.

stories.title: Sending Out the Twelve
stories.summary:
Jesus gathers his twelve disciples and gives them authority to expel unclean spirits and heal illness. Matthew then names the group entrusted with this work. Simon Peter and his brother Andrew appear first, followed by James and John, the sons of Zebedee. The list continues with Philip, Bartholomew, Thomas, Matthew the tax collector, James son of Alphaeus, and Thaddaeus. Simon the Zealot and Judas Iscariot complete the twelve. The narrator identifies Judas as the one who later betrays Jesus.

Jesus sends this group out with instructions. In the opening direction included here, he tells them not to travel among Gentiles or enter a Samaritan town. The cited passage ends at that restriction, before the rest of the mission instructions.

stories.title: Jesus and John the Baptist
stories.summary:
From prison, John hears about Jesus' deeds and sends disciples to ask whether he is the expected one. Jesus directs them to report the healings they witness, the raising of the dead, and good news reaching the poor. He adds a blessing for those who do not reject him.

After the messengers leave, Jesus speaks to the crowd about John. He describes him as more than a prophet and identifies him with the messenger preparing God's way. He also associates John with the expected return of Elijah. Jesus compares his generation to dissatisfied children: they reject John's austere life and criticize Jesus for eating with tax collectors and sinners.

Jesus then condemns towns where many of his mighty works occurred without producing repentance. He says other condemned cities would have responded differently and will face a more tolerable judgment. Turning to prayer, he thanks the Father for revealing these things to the childlike rather than the learned. He speaks of the unique knowledge shared between Father and Son. The passage closes with his invitation to burdened people to come, learn his gentle way, and find rest.

stories.title: Sabbath Controversies and the Sign of Jonah
stories.summary:
Pharisees challenge Jesus when his hungry disciples pick grain on the Sabbath. He answers with examples involving David and temple priests, emphasizes mercy, and calls himself lord of the Sabbath. In a synagogue, he heals a man's disabled hand despite another challenge. His opponents begin planning his destruction, and he withdraws while continuing to heal people. Matthew connects this quieter work with Isaiah's description of God's servant.

After Jesus heals a blind man who cannot speak, some people wonder whether he is David's promised descendant. Pharisees instead attribute his power to the ruler of demons. Jesus argues that a divided kingdom cannot survive. He presents his actions as evidence of God's kingdom and warns against speaking against the Holy Spirit. He also teaches that words reveal a person's inner character and carry consequences at judgment.

When religious scholars request a sign, Jesus points to Jonah's time inside the great fish and compares it with his own coming burial. He contrasts their response with people who listened to Jonah and Solomon. A warning about a returning unclean spirit follows. When his mother and brothers seek him, Jesus identifies those who do his Father's will as his family.

stories.title: Feeding the Five Thousand and Walking on Water
stories.summary:
Herod hears about Jesus and thinks John the Baptist has risen. Matthew recounts how Herod imprisoned John after criticism of his marriage. At a birthday feast, Herod promises Herodias's daughter a gift. Prompted by her mother, she requests John's head. Herod orders the execution, and John's disciples bury him and tell Jesus.

Jesus withdraws by boat, but crowds follow on foot. Moved by compassion, he heals their sick. As evening approaches, the disciples suggest sending everyone away for food. Jesus instead takes five loaves and two fish, blesses them, and distributes them through the disciples. About five thousand men eat, besides women and children, and twelve baskets of pieces remain.

Jesus sends the disciples across the lake while he prays alone. During the night, he approaches their storm-battered boat across the water. They fear a ghost, but he reassures them. Peter steps onto the water at Jesus' invitation, then becomes afraid and begins sinking. Jesus catches him and questions his doubt. Once they enter the boat, the wind stops, and the disciples acknowledge him as God's Son. At Gennesaret, people bring the sick, who are healed by touching his clothing.

stories.title: Peter's Confession and the Transfiguration
stories.summary:
Near Caesarea Philippi, Jesus asks what people say about his identity. Peter calls him the Messiah and Son of the living God. Jesus credits this recognition to the Father and speaks of Peter, the foundation of his community, and the kingdom's keys. He then predicts suffering, death, and resurrection. When Peter objects, Jesus sharply rebukes him and teaches that following him means accepting self-denial and the cross.

Six days later, Peter, James, and John accompany Jesus up a mountain. His face shines and his clothes become brilliant. Moses and Elijah appear, and Peter proposes shelters for the three. A voice from a bright cloud calls Jesus God's beloved Son and commands the disciples to listen. Jesus reassures the frightened men. As they descend, he tells them to keep the vision private until his resurrection and links Elijah's coming with John the Baptist.

Jesus next heals a suffering boy whom the disciples could not help, then discusses their lack of faith. Another prediction of his death leaves them deeply distressed. In Capernaum, a question about the temple tax prompts a discussion of royal children and outsiders. Jesus directs Peter to obtain a coin from a fish's mouth and pay for them both.

stories.title: The Rich Young Man
stories.summary:
In Judea, Jesus answers a challenge about divorce by appealing to the creation account and the joining of husband and wife. He discusses exceptions and unmarried life, then welcomes children whom the disciples try to turn away. A wealthy young man asks what he must do to gain eternal life. After naming commandments, Jesus tells him to sell his possessions, give to the poor, and follow. The man leaves grieving because he owns much.

Jesus describes wealth as a great obstacle to entering God's kingdom. When the disciples ask who can be saved, he says that what is impossible for people is possible for God. He promises a future place for those who have followed him. A vineyard story follows: workers hired at different hours receive equal wages, provoking complaints from those who worked longest. The owner defends his generosity.

On the journey to Jerusalem, Jesus predicts his condemnation, crucifixion, and resurrection. The mother of James and John requests places of honor for her sons. Jesus speaks instead of suffering and service, saying he came to give his life for many. Near Jericho, two blind men keep calling despite the crowd's objections. Jesus restores their sight, and they join him.

stories.title: The Triumphal Entry and Temple Cleansing
stories.summary:
Approaching Jerusalem, Jesus sends two disciples for a donkey and her colt. Matthew connects his entrance with a prophetic picture of a humble king. Crowds spread clothing and branches on the road and acclaim him as David's son. People in the stirred-up city ask who he is.

At the temple, Jesus drives out buyers and sellers and overturns trading tables. He contrasts a house of prayer with a robbers' den. He heals blind and disabled people while children praise him, angering the chief priests and religious scholars. After spending the night in Bethany, he curses a fruitless fig tree, which immediately withers. He uses the disciples' astonishment to teach about faith and prayer.

Back in the temple, leaders question his authority. He asks whether John's baptism came from heaven or people, and their refusal to answer leaves their challenge unanswered. Jesus tells stories about two sons responding differently to their father and tenants who kill a vineyard owner's servants and son. He connects the stories with rejected messengers, failed obedience, and judgment. The chief priests and Pharisees recognize themselves as his targets. They want to arrest him but fear the crowd, which regards him as a prophet.

stories.title: The Last Supper and Gethsemane
stories.summary:
Jesus predicts crucifixion as religious leaders plan his arrest. At Bethany, a woman pours costly perfume on his head. The disciples object to the expense, but Jesus interprets her action as preparation for burial. Judas then arranges to betray him for thirty silver pieces.

During the Passover meal, Jesus announces that one of the twelve will betray him. He shares bread as his body and a cup as his covenant blood, poured out for the forgiveness of sins. After a hymn, they leave for the Mount of Olives. Jesus predicts that the disciples will scatter and that Peter will deny knowing him three times before the rooster crows. Peter and the others insist they will remain loyal.

In Gethsemane, Jesus takes Peter, James, and John aside while he prays in deep distress. He asks that the coming suffering pass, while submitting to his Father's will. Three times he prays, repeatedly finding his companions asleep.

Judas arrives with an armed crowd and identifies Jesus with a kiss. One companion cuts off the high priest's servant's ear. Jesus orders the weapon put away, saying violence is not the way to resist this arrest. He connects events with the fulfillment of scripture. All the disciples abandon him and flee.

stories.title: Trial, Crucifixion and Burial
stories.summary:
Jesus is brought before Caiaphas and the council, where witnesses accuse him over words about the temple. Asked whether he is the Messiah, he answers with a vision of the Son of Man in heavenly authority. The council condemns him, and he is beaten and mocked. Outside, Peter denies knowing him three times. A rooster's call brings Jesus' warning to mind, and Peter leaves in tears.

Judas returns the betrayal money in remorse and dies by suicide. The priests use the money to buy a burial field. Before Pilate, Jesus faces accusations while largely remaining silent. The crowd demands Barabbas's release and Jesus' crucifixion. Pilate publicly washes his hands, then orders Jesus flogged and delivered for execution. Soldiers dress him as a mock king and abuse him.

Simon of Cyrene is forced to carry the cross. Jesus is crucified between two robbers at Golgotha amid public taunts. Darkness covers the land, and Jesus cries out about being forsaken before dying. Matthew describes the temple curtain tearing, an earthquake, and opened tombs. The account also describes raised holy people appearing after his resurrection. Soldiers watching him respond with fear and acknowledge him as God's Son.

Joseph of Arimathea places the body in his own new tomb while women watch. At the leaders' request, the tomb is sealed and guarded against the removal of Jesus' body.

stories.title: The Resurrection and the Great Commission
stories.summary:
Mary Magdalene and the other Mary visit the tomb as the first day of the week dawns. An earthquake accompanies an angel's descent, and the angel rolls aside the stone. The guards collapse in fear. The angel tells the women that Jesus has risen and invites them to see where he lay. They must tell the disciples to meet him in Galilee.

The women leave with fear and joy. Jesus meets them, and they grasp his feet and worship him. He repeats the instruction to send his brothers to Galilee. Meanwhile, some guards report what happened to the chief priests. The leaders pay them to say that disciples stole the body while they slept and promise to protect them from the governor.

The eleven disciples go to the appointed mountain in Galilee. They worship Jesus, though some doubt. He declares that all authority in heaven and on earth has been given to him. He commissions them to make disciples among all nations, baptize them, and teach them to observe his commands. Matthew ends with his promise to remain with them through the end of the age.

stories.title: John the Baptist and the Baptism of Jesus
stories.summary:
Mark opens by announcing good news about Jesus and citing prophetic words about a messenger preparing the Lord's way. John appears in the wilderness, calling for repentance and offering baptism connected with the forgiveness of sins. People from Jerusalem and Judea come to the Jordan, where they confess wrongdoing and are baptized. John wears camel-hair clothing and a leather belt, and eats locusts and wild honey.

He tells the crowds that someone stronger is coming after him. John considers himself unworthy even to loosen that person's sandals. His own baptism uses water, but the coming figure will baptize with the Holy Spirit.

Jesus arrives from Nazareth and receives baptism from John. As he emerges from the river, he sees the heavens opening and the Spirit descending like a dove. A heavenly voice addresses him as the beloved Son. The Spirit immediately drives him into the wilderness. Mark briefly describes forty days of temptation by Satan, the presence of wild animals, and angels attending Jesus.

stories.title: Calling the Disciples and Healing in Capernaum
stories.summary:
After John's arrest, Jesus announces in Galilee that God's kingdom is near and calls people to repent and believe the good news. At the lakeshore, he summons Simon and Andrew from their fishing nets. James and John also follow, leaving their father Zebedee in the boat with hired workers.

In Capernaum's synagogue, listeners are struck by Jesus' authority. A man with an unclean spirit cries out, identifying him as God's Holy One. Jesus silences the spirit and commands it to leave. At Simon and Andrew's home, he takes Simon's feverish mother-in-law by the hand and helps her up. Her fever ends, and she serves them. That evening, crowds bring people needing healing or relief from demons.

Before dawn, Jesus leaves to pray alone. When Simon finds him, Jesus says they must move on to preach in other towns. Later, he touches and cleanses a man with leprosy. He orders him to remain quiet and present himself to a priest with the required offering. Instead, the man spreads the news widely. Jesus can no longer enter towns openly and stays outside, where people continue coming to him.

stories.title: The Paralytic and Controversies
stories.summary:
A crowded house in Capernaum prevents four people from bringing a paralyzed man directly to Jesus. They open the roof and lower his mat. Jesus first declares his sins forgiven, provoking objections from religious scholars who consider this God's authority alone. He then tells the man to rise and carry his mat home. The man does so before the astonished crowd.

Jesus calls Levi from a tax office and later eats with tax collectors and people labeled sinners. When critics object, he compares his work to a physician treating the sick. Questions about his disciples' lack of fasting lead to a comparison with wedding guests celebrating while the bridegroom remains. He adds images of new cloth tearing an old garment and new wine bursting old skins.

Another dispute begins when the disciples pick grain on the Sabbath. Jesus recalls David eating sacred bread and says the Sabbath was made for people. In a synagogue, opponents watch whether he will heal a man's disabled hand. Jesus asks whether the day permits doing good or harm, but receives no answer. Grieved and angry at their resistance, he restores the hand. Pharisees then join Herod's supporters in planning his destruction.

stories.title: Parables and Calming the Storm
stories.summary:
Jesus teaches from a boat while a large crowd listens from shore. He describes seed falling on a path, rocky ground, thorny ground, and good soil. Only the last produces a lasting harvest. Privately, he explains that these settings represent different responses to the message. Opposition, shallow commitment, worries, and desires for wealth prevent some listeners from bearing fruit.

Other comparisons concern a lamp meant to shine, the responsibility of attentive listening, and seed growing beyond a farmer's understanding. Jesus likens God's kingdom to a tiny mustard seed that becomes a large plant sheltering birds. Mark distinguishes his public teaching through stories from the explanations he gives his disciples in private.

That evening, they cross the lake. A fierce storm sends waves into the boat while Jesus sleeps on a cushion in the stern. The disciples wake him and ask whether he cares that they may die. He commands the wind and water to become quiet, and the storm stops. Jesus questions their fear and lack of faith. They remain awed, asking who he can be if even the wind and sea obey him.

stories.title: The Gadarene Demoniac, Jairus and the Woman
stories.summary:
Across the lake, Jesus meets a man living among tombs whom no chains can restrain. The account describes him as tormented by many unclean spirits, which identify themselves as Legion. Jesus permits them to enter a nearby herd of pigs. About two thousand pigs rush into the sea and drown. Local people find the man clothed and calm but ask Jesus to leave. Jesus sends the restored man home to tell what has happened.

Back across the lake, the synagogue leader Jairus begs Jesus to help his dying daughter. As they move through a crowd, a woman with twelve years of bleeding touches Jesus' clothes. Treatment has exhausted her resources without helping. She immediately feels healed. Jesus asks who touched him, and she comes forward trembling. He acknowledges her faith and sends her away in peace.

Messengers then report that Jairus's daughter has died. Jesus tells her father not to fear. At the house, he takes only the parents and Peter, James, and John into the girl's room. He holds her hand and tells her to rise. The twelve-year-old stands and walks. Jesus asks that she receive food and strictly tells those present not to publicize what happened.

stories.title: Feeding the Multitude
stories.summary:
The apostles return to Jesus and describe their work and teaching. Because the constant crowds leave little time even to eat, he invites them away to rest. They depart by boat, but people run ahead and arrive first. Jesus sees them as sheep without a shepherd and begins teaching.

Late in the day, the disciples suggest sending the crowd to buy food. Jesus tells them to provide it themselves, then asks what supplies they have. Five loaves and two fish are brought. He seats the people in groups on the grass, gives a blessing, and distributes the food through his disciples. Five thousand men eat their fill, and twelve baskets of pieces remain.

Jesus sends the disciples ahead by boat and goes up a mountain to pray. During the night, he sees them struggling against the wind and approaches across the water. They think he is a ghost, but he reassures them and enters the boat. The wind stops. Mark says they remain astonished because they have not understood the feeding. After landing at Gennesaret, they encounter more crowds bringing sick people. Those who touch Jesus' clothing are healed.

stories.title: Peter's Confession and the Transfiguration in Mark
stories.summary:
On the road near Caesarea Philippi, Jesus asks the disciples who they think he is. Peter identifies him as the Messiah. Jesus orders silence, then openly predicts rejection, death, and resurrection. Peter protests, and Jesus rebukes him for thinking in human rather than divine terms. Addressing the crowd, he describes discipleship as denying oneself and carrying a cross.

Six days later, Jesus takes Peter, James, and John up a mountain. His appearance changes, his clothing shines intensely, and Elijah and Moses speak with him. Frightened and unsure what to say, Peter proposes three shelters. A cloud surrounds them, and a voice calls Jesus God's beloved Son and commands them to listen. The companions suddenly see only Jesus. He tells them to keep the event private until his resurrection, a saying they struggle to understand.

They return to a dispute over a boy whom the other disciples could not heal. His father describes destructive seizures attributed to an unclean spirit. When Jesus speaks about belief, the father asks for help with his unbelief. Jesus commands the spirit to leave. The boy appears dead, but Jesus raises him by the hand. Privately, he tells the disciples that this kind requires prayer and fasting.

stories.title: Blind Bartimaeus
stories.summary:
As Jesus leaves Jericho with his disciples and a large crowd, a blind beggar sits beside the road. Mark names him Bartimaeus, the son of Timaeus. Hearing that Jesus of Nazareth is passing, he repeatedly calls him David's son and asks for mercy.

People nearby tell Bartimaeus to be quiet, but he calls out more loudly. Jesus stops and asks them to bring him over. Their words now change to encouragement: Jesus is calling him. Bartimaeus throws aside his cloak, jumps up, and approaches.

Jesus asks what he wants him to do. Bartimaeus answers that he wants his sight restored. Jesus tells him that his faith has made him well and that he may go. His sight returns immediately. Rather than remaining beside the road, he follows Jesus along it.

stories.title: Triumphal Entry and the Temple
stories.summary:
Near Jerusalem, Jesus sends two disciples to fetch a young donkey that has never been ridden. They answer the bystanders as instructed and bring it to him. People spread clothing and branches along the road, praising the coming kingdom of David. Jesus enters the temple, looks around, and returns to Bethany because it is late.

The next day, he approaches a leafy fig tree but finds no fruit, though Mark notes it is not fig season. He declares that nobody will eat from it again. In Jerusalem, he drives traders from the temple, overturns tables, and prevents people carrying goods through it. He contrasts a house of prayer for all nations with a robbers' den. Religious leaders seek his death but fear his influence over the crowd.

The following morning, Peter notices that the fig tree has withered from its roots. Jesus teaches about trust in God, prayer, and forgiving others. Back at the temple, leaders demand to know the source of his authority. Jesus asks them first to identify the source of John's baptism. Unable to answer without facing objections, they claim ignorance. Jesus then declines to answer their question.

stories.title: The Last Supper and Gethsemane in Mark
stories.summary:
Religious leaders seek a discreet way to kill Jesus before Passover. In Bethany, a woman breaks a jar of costly perfume and pours it over his head. Some object that the money could have helped the poor. Jesus defends her action as preparation for his burial. Judas then offers to hand him over, and the priests promise money.

Two disciples follow Jesus' instructions to prepare a furnished upstairs room for Passover. At the meal, he announces that one of the twelve will betray him. He gives them bread as his body and shares a cup as his covenant blood, poured out for many. After singing, they leave for the Mount of Olives. Jesus predicts their desertion and tells Peter that he will deny him three times before the rooster crows twice.

In Gethsemane, Jesus prays in anguish, asking his Father to remove the coming suffering while accepting the Father's will. Peter, James, and John repeatedly fall asleep instead of keeping watch. Judas arrives with an armed group and identifies Jesus with a kiss. Someone nearby cuts off the high priest's servant's ear. Jesus challenges the manner of his arrest and points to scripture's fulfillment. His followers flee, including a young man who escapes naked when his linen covering is seized.

stories.title: Trial, Crucifixion and Burial in Mark
stories.summary:
At the high priest's residence, conflicting testimony fails to establish a case against Jesus. Asked whether he is the Messiah and God's Son, he answers affirmatively and speaks of heavenly authority. The council condemns him for blasphemy, and people strike and mock him. In the courtyard, Peter denies any connection with Jesus three times. The second rooster call reminds him of Jesus' prediction, and he weeps.

The council hands Jesus to Pilate. Although Jesus gives little answer to the accusations, the crowd demands his execution and the release of Barabbas. Pilate orders him flogged and crucified. Soldiers dress him in purple, crown him with thorns, and mock him as king. Simon of Cyrene is forced to carry his cross.

Jesus is crucified at Golgotha between two robbers. Bystanders and leaders taunt him, and darkness covers the land. He cries out about God's abandonment and then dies with a loud cry. The temple curtain tears from top to bottom. The Roman officer watching him identifies him as God's Son, while women followers observe from a distance.

Before the Sabbath, Joseph of Arimathea requests the body. Pilate confirms the death with the officer and grants permission. Joseph wraps Jesus in linen and places him in a rock-cut tomb. Two women note its location.

stories.title: The Empty Tomb
stories.summary:
After the Sabbath, Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome buy spices to anoint Jesus' body. They reach the tomb shortly after sunrise on the first day of the week. On the way, they wonder who will move the very large stone from its entrance. When they look up, they find it already rolled aside.

Inside, they see a young man in a white robe seated on the right. He tells the alarmed women that Jesus of Nazareth, who was crucified, has risen and is not there. He points to the place where the body had been laid.

The women are instructed to tell the disciples, especially Peter, that Jesus is going ahead to Galilee. They will see him there, as he promised. The women flee, overwhelmed by trembling and astonishment. This passage ends with their fear and their silence: they say nothing to anyone.

stories.title: The Births of John and Jesus
stories.summary:
The priest Zechariah and his wife Elizabeth are elderly and childless. While Zechariah burns incense in the temple, Gabriel announces that Elizabeth will bear a son named John. He will prepare people for the Lord in Elijah's spirit. Zechariah questions the promise and loses his speech until its fulfillment. Elizabeth becomes pregnant.

Gabriel later visits Mary in Nazareth. Though a virgin, she will conceive through the Holy Spirit and bear Jesus, who will inherit David's throne and reign without end. Mary accepts the message and visits Elizabeth. Elizabeth's child moves at her greeting, and she blesses Mary. Mary praises God for raising the lowly, feeding the hungry, and remembering mercy toward Israel.

When Elizabeth gives birth, relatives expect the child to receive his father's name. Zechariah writes that his name is John, and his speech returns. He praises God and describes his son's future work of preparing the way. John grows and lives in the wilderness until his public appearance.

An imperial registration brings Joseph and the pregnant Mary to Bethlehem. Jesus is born there and laid in a feeding trough because there is no room in the lodging place. Angels announce the birth to shepherds, who find the child as described. They spread the report and return praising God, while Mary keeps these events in her thoughts.

stories.title: Presentation and the Boy Jesus in the Temple
stories.summary:
Eight days after his birth, the child is circumcised and named Jesus, as the angel instructed. His parents later bring him to Jerusalem for the presentation and purification required by the law. They offer the prescribed birds. In the temple, Simeon takes Jesus in his arms and praises God. The Spirit had promised that he would see the Messiah before death. He describes the child as salvation for Israel and a light for other nations.

Simeon also warns Mary of opposition, division, and personal grief. Anna, an elderly prophet devoted to worship in the temple, gives thanks and speaks about Jesus to others awaiting Jerusalem's redemption. The family returns to Nazareth, where Jesus grows in wisdom.

At twelve, Jesus accompanies his parents to Jerusalem for Passover but remains behind when they depart. After searching, they find him in the temple among teachers, listening, asking questions, and giving remarkable answers. Mary describes their anxious search. Jesus replies that he must be in his Father's house, but they do not understand. He returns to Nazareth and obeys them. Mary remembers these events as he continues to grow.

stories.title: Rejection at Nazareth
stories.summary:
Jesus returns to Galilee and teaches in synagogues, gaining widespread praise. In Nazareth, where he grew up, he attends the Sabbath gathering and reads from Isaiah. The passage announces good news for the poor, freedom for captives, sight for the blind, and the Lord's favor. Jesus sits down and tells the attentive congregation that the scripture is being fulfilled before them.

The listeners marvel at his words while identifying him as Joseph's son. Jesus anticipates a demand to perform at home the deeds reported from Capernaum. He says prophets are not accepted in their hometowns. He recalls Elijah helping a widow outside Israel during famine and Elisha cleansing Naaman, a Syrian, rather than Israel's many sufferers.

The congregation becomes furious at these examples. They drive Jesus out of town and lead him to the edge of the hill on which it stands, intending to throw him down. He passes through the crowd and leaves. Luke does not describe any further confrontation in this passage.

stories.title: The Miraculous Catch
stories.summary:
A crowd presses around Jesus at the lake of Gennesaret to hear God's word. Nearby fishermen are washing their nets beside two boats. Jesus gets into Simon's boat and asks him to move a short distance offshore. From there, he sits and teaches the people.

When the teaching ends, Jesus tells Simon to move into deeper water and lower the nets. Simon explains that they worked all night without catching anything, but agrees to try at Jesus' word. The catch is so large that the nets begin to break. They signal their partners, who help fill both boats until the vessels begin sinking.

Overwhelmed, Simon Peter falls at Jesus' knees and asks him to leave because he is a sinful man. His partners James and John share his astonishment. Jesus reassures Simon and tells him that his work will now involve gathering people. After bringing the boats ashore, they leave everything and follow him.

stories.title: The Centurion and the Widow's Son
stories.summary:
In Capernaum, a Roman officer has a valued servant who is close to death. He sends local Jewish elders to ask Jesus for help. They urge Jesus to come, pointing to the officer's support for their people and his building of their synagogue. As Jesus approaches, friends arrive with another message. The officer does not consider himself worthy of a visit and believes a command alone can heal his servant.

He compares Jesus' authority with his own experience of giving and receiving military orders. Jesus expresses amazement and tells the crowd that he has not found such faith in Israel. The messengers return and find the servant well.

Soon afterward, Jesus reaches Nain as a funeral procession leaves the town. The dead man is a widow's only son. Moved by compassion, Jesus tells her not to weep and touches the bier, stopping its bearers. He commands the young man to rise. The man sits up and speaks, and Jesus gives him back to his mother. The crowd responds with awe and praise, calling Jesus a great prophet. Reports spread throughout the region.

stories.title: The Sinful Woman Anoints Jesus
stories.summary:
Jesus accepts a meal invitation from Simon, a Pharisee. A local woman known as a sinner enters with a jar of perfume. Weeping at Jesus' feet, she wets them with tears, wipes them with her hair, kisses them, and applies the perfume. Simon privately reasons that a prophet would recognize her reputation and reject her touch.

Jesus responds with a story about two people whose debts are canceled. One owes ten times as much as the other. Simon agrees that the person forgiven more would show greater love. Jesus then contrasts the woman's actions with Simon's reception. Simon supplied no water for his feet, welcoming kiss, or oil for his head; the woman has offered abundant care.

Jesus connects her great love with the forgiveness of her many sins. He directly assures her that her sins are forgiven. Other guests question who can make such a declaration. Jesus addresses the woman again, telling her that her faith has saved her and sending her away in peace.

stories.title: The Good Samaritan and Mary and Martha
stories.summary:
A legal expert tests Jesus by asking how to inherit eternal life. Jesus directs him to the law, and the man answers with commands to love God and one's neighbor. When he asks who counts as a neighbor, Jesus tells a story. A traveler is robbed, beaten, and abandoned on the road from Jerusalem to Jericho. A priest and a Levite each pass without helping.

A Samaritan stops in compassion, dresses the man's wounds, and carries him on his animal to an inn. He pays for continuing care and promises to cover further expenses. Jesus asks which traveler acted as a neighbor. The legal expert identifies the one who showed mercy, and Jesus tells him to act likewise.

In another village, Martha welcomes Jesus into her home. Her sister Mary sits at his feet listening while Martha becomes overwhelmed by serving. Martha asks Jesus to make Mary help her. He responds that Martha is troubled by many concerns, while Mary has chosen the good part. He will not take that choice away from her.

stories.title: The Lost Sheep, Coin and Son
stories.summary:
When religious critics complain that Jesus welcomes and eats with sinners, he tells three stories. A shepherd searches for one missing sheep and celebrates its recovery with friends. A woman carefully searches her house for a lost coin and likewise shares her joy. Jesus connects both celebrations with heaven's joy when a sinner turns back.

The third story concerns two sons. The younger asks for his inheritance, travels away, and wastes it. A famine leaves him hungry and tending pigs. Remembering that his father's hired workers have enough food, he decides to return, confess his wrongdoing, and ask for work. His father sees him approaching, runs to embrace him, and orders fine clothing and a feast. He describes his lost son as found and alive again.

The older son returns from the fields and refuses to join the celebration. He protests that years of obedience have earned him no comparable party. His father comes outside and assures him that everything remaining is his. Yet the brother's return calls for celebration. The story ends with this appeal, without saying whether the older son enters the house.

stories.title: The Rich Man and Lazarus
stories.summary:
Jesus tells of a wealthy man who dresses magnificently and feasts every day. At his gate lies Lazarus, a poor man covered in sores who longs for scraps from the table. Dogs lick his wounds. Both men die, but their situations are reversed: angels carry Lazarus to Abraham, while the rich man experiences torment.

Seeing Lazarus beside Abraham, the rich man asks that Lazarus bring a little water to cool his tongue. Abraham reminds him of their contrasting earthly lives. He also explains that a great divide prevents anyone from crossing between their places.

The rich man then asks Abraham to send Lazarus to warn his five brothers, so they may avoid the same suffering. Abraham answers that they already have Moses and the prophets to guide them. The rich man insists that someone returning from death would make them repent. Abraham concludes that those who refuse to listen to scripture would not be persuaded even by a resurrection.

stories.title: Zacchaeus
stories.summary:
As Jesus passes through Jericho, a wealthy chief tax collector named Zacchaeus tries to see him. Because he is short and the crowd blocks his view, he runs ahead and climbs a sycamore tree. When Jesus reaches the spot, he looks up, calls Zacchaeus by name, and says he must stay at his house that day.

Zacchaeus comes down quickly and welcomes Jesus with joy. Onlookers complain that Jesus is staying with someone they regard as a sinner. Zacchaeus addresses Jesus and declares that he gives half his possessions to the poor. He also says that anyone he has cheated will receive four times the amount in repayment.

Jesus announces that salvation has reached this household and identifies Zacchaeus as a son of Abraham. He closes by describing the Son of Man's purpose as seeking and saving what was lost. The encounter moves from Zacchaeus's effort to see Jesus to a public welcome and a declaration about his place among God's people.

stories.title: The Road to Emmaus
stories.summary:
Two followers walk toward Emmaus, discussing Jesus' death and the reports that his tomb is empty. Jesus joins them, but they do not recognize him. One, Cleopas, explains their sorrow: they had hoped Jesus would redeem Israel, yet their leaders handed him over for crucifixion. Women from their group have reported angels announcing that he is alive, but others found only the empty tomb.

Jesus challenges their difficulty believing the prophets. Beginning with Moses, he interprets scripture as pointing to the Messiah's suffering and glory. As they near the village, he appears ready to continue, but they invite him to stay because evening is approaching.

At the meal, Jesus blesses bread, breaks it, and gives it to them. They recognize him, and he disappears from their sight. They recall how deeply his explanation of scripture affected them during the walk. Immediately, they return to Jerusalem. There they find the eleven and others gathered, declaring that the Lord has appeared to Simon. The two add their own account of the journey and recognition at the meal.

stories.title: The Ascension
stories.summary:
While the followers are discussing the reported appearances, Jesus stands among them and offers peace. They are frightened, thinking they see a spirit. He shows his hands and feet and invites them to touch him, insisting that he has flesh and bones. As they struggle with joy and disbelief, he asks for food and eats before them.

Jesus reminds them that scripture's words about him must be fulfilled. He opens their understanding of the law of Moses, the prophets, and the psalms. He describes the Messiah's suffering and resurrection, followed by the proclamation of repentance and forgiveness to all nations. That work is to begin in Jerusalem, and they are its witnesses. He tells them to remain in the city until they receive the power promised by his Father.

Jesus leads them toward Bethany, raises his hands, and blesses them. While blessing them, he is carried into heaven. They worship him and return joyfully to Jerusalem. Luke closes with the followers regularly praising God in the temple.

stories.title: The First Disciples and the Wedding at Cana
stories.summary:
John identifies Jesus as God's Lamb, prompting two of his disciples to follow Jesus and spend the day with him. One is Andrew, who finds his brother Simon and announces that they have found the Messiah. Jesus gives Simon the name Cephas, rendered Peter. The next day, Jesus calls Philip, who brings Nathanael despite his doubts about Nazareth. Jesus' knowledge of Nathanael beneath a fig tree leads Nathanael to acknowledge him as God's Son and Israel's king. Jesus promises greater things ahead.

At a wedding in Cana, Jesus' mother tells him that the wine has run out. He responds that his hour has not yet come, but she tells the servants to follow his instructions. Jesus has them fill six stone purification jars with water and take a sample to the feast's steward.

The steward tastes wine and praises the bridegroom for keeping the best until this point. He does not know its source, though the servants do. John presents this as Jesus' first sign, revealing his glory and strengthening his disciples' belief. Jesus then spends a few days in Capernaum with his family and disciples.

stories.title: Cleansing the Temple and Nicodemus
stories.summary:
At Passover in Jerusalem, Jesus finds livestock sellers and money changers in the temple. He makes a cord whip, drives out the animals, scatters coins, and overturns tables. He tells the dove sellers to stop turning his Father's house into a market. Challenged to provide a sign of his authority, he speaks of raising a destroyed temple in three days. His listeners understand the building, but John explains that he means his body.

Many people respond to his signs, though Jesus does not entrust himself to them. Nicodemus, a Pharisee and leader, visits at night and recognizes him as a teacher sent by God. Jesus says that seeing God's kingdom requires a new birth. Nicodemus takes this physically, and Jesus explains birth through water and Spirit, comparing the Spirit's activity to wind.

The discussion turns to the Son of Man being lifted up, as Moses once raised the serpent in the wilderness. The passage presents God's gift of the Son as an expression of love for the world and a means of life through belief. It closes by contrasting those who avoid the light to hide wrongdoing with those who come into it.

stories.title: The Woman at the Well
stories.summary:
Traveling from Judea to Galilee, Jesus stops beside Jacob's well near Sychar in Samaria. His disciples go to buy food, and he asks a Samaritan woman for water. She is surprised that a Jewish man would ask her. Jesus offers living water that becomes a source of eternal life. She initially understands this as water that would end her repeated trips to the well.

Jesus speaks accurately about her five former husbands and her present relationship. Recognizing him as a prophet, she asks about competing places of worship. He describes worship of the Father in spirit and truth, beyond the choice between Jerusalem and the local mountain. When she mentions the expected Messiah, he identifies himself.

The disciples return, surprised by the conversation. Leaving her jar, the woman invites the townspeople to meet someone who knows her life. Jesus tells his disciples that doing his Father's work is his food and compares their work to gathering an approaching harvest.

Many Samaritans believe because of the woman's report and ask Jesus to stay. After two days, more believe through hearing him directly. They tell her that their conviction now rests on their own encounter and call him the world's Savior.

stories.title: Healing at Bethesda
stories.summary:
During a visit to Jerusalem, Jesus comes to the pool of Bethesda, where many sick and disabled people gather. He notices a man who has been ill for thirty-eight years and asks whether he wants to recover. The man explains that nobody helps him into the water before others arrive. Jesus tells him to rise, pick up his mat, and walk. He immediately does so.

Because it is the Sabbath, religious opponents challenge the man for carrying his mat. He initially cannot identify his healer. Jesus later finds him in the temple and warns him against further sin. The man then names Jesus, and opposition grows over his Sabbath activity. Jesus says that he is working as his Father works, intensifying objections to his claims about God.

Jesus explains that the Son acts in unity with the Father, who gives him authority to grant life and judge. He speaks of the dead hearing his voice and of resurrection leading to life or judgment. He names witnesses supporting his mission: John, his deeds, the Father, and scripture. The passage ends with a challenge to opponents who study Moses yet refuse the one Jesus says Moses described.

stories.title: Bread of Life
stories.summary:
Near Passover, a large crowd follows Jesus across the Sea of Galilee. Philip sees no practical way to feed them, while Andrew points out a boy with five barley loaves and two fish. Jesus gives thanks and distributes the food. About five thousand men eat, and twelve baskets of pieces remain. When the crowd wants to make him king by force, he withdraws alone. That night, he approaches his disciples' boat across the rough water and reassures them.

The crowd finds Jesus in Capernaum the next day. He challenges their interest in food that merely fills them and speaks instead of food that gives lasting life. They recall the wilderness manna. Jesus identifies himself as the bread from heaven, promising life and resurrection to those who believe.

His listeners object to his heavenly origin and struggle with his language about eating his flesh and drinking his blood. He connects this language with sharing his life and remaining in him. Many disciples find the teaching intolerable and stop following. When Jesus asks whether the twelve also wish to leave, Peter says that he has the words of eternal life. Jesus then warns that one of the twelve will betray him, and John identifies Judas.

stories.title: The Woman Caught in Adultery
stories.summary:
After spending the night on the Mount of Olives, Jesus returns to the temple and begins teaching. Religious scholars and Pharisees interrupt by placing a woman before him. They say she has been caught committing adultery and ask whether she should be stoned under the law of Moses. The narrator explains that their question is intended to provide grounds for accusing Jesus.

Jesus bends down and writes on the ground. When they keep questioning him, he says that the person among them without sin should throw the first stone. He then resumes writing. The passage does not say what he writes.

The accusers leave one by one, starting with the oldest. Jesus asks the woman whether anyone remains to condemn her. She answers that nobody does. He says that he does not condemn her either and tells her to leave and no longer sin. The encounter ends without a punishment being carried out.

stories.title: The Man Born Blind
stories.summary:
Jesus encounters a man blind from birth. His disciples ask whether the man's condition results from his own sin or his parents'. Jesus rejects that choice and speaks of God's work becoming visible through him. He applies mud to the man's eyes and sends him to wash in Siloam. The man returns able to see.

Neighbors dispute his identity before bringing him to the Pharisees. Because the healing happened on the Sabbath, the religious authorities disagree about Jesus. They question the man's parents, who confirm his lifelong blindness but avoid explaining the recovery. John says they fear exclusion from the synagogue.

Under repeated questioning, the healed man insists on the change he knows: he was blind and now sees. His refusal to condemn Jesus leads to insults. He argues that such a deed points to God's support, and the authorities expel him.

Jesus finds him and identifies himself as the one in whom he should believe. The man responds with belief and worship. Jesus then speaks of a reversal between those who see and those who do not. When nearby Pharisees challenge the comparison, he says their claim to see leaves them responsible for their sin.

stories.title: Jesus at the Feast of Dedication
stories.summary:
During the winter Feast of Dedication, Jesus walks in Solomon's porch at the Jerusalem temple. People surround him and demand a plain statement about whether he is the Messiah. He answers that he has already told them and that his works in his Father's name bear witness. He compares his followers to sheep who recognize his voice, receive eternal life, and remain secure in his and his Father's care.

When Jesus declares his unity with the Father, opponents pick up stones. He asks which good work has prompted this response. They answer that the issue is blasphemy: they understand him to be making himself God. Jesus appeals to scripture's use of divine language for others and defends calling himself God's Son.

He urges them to examine his works even if they reject his words, presenting those works as evidence of his relationship with the Father. Another attempt to seize him fails. Jesus withdraws beyond the Jordan, where John had previously baptized. Many people visit, recall John's testimony about him, and believe.

stories.title: The Raising of Lazarus
stories.summary:
Mary and Martha send word that their brother Lazarus is ill. Jesus remains where he is for two days, then decides to return to Judea despite the danger there. He first describes Lazarus as sleeping, then plainly tells the disciples that he has died. By the time Jesus reaches Bethany, Lazarus has been in the tomb four days.

Martha meets him and says her brother would not have died if he had been present. Jesus speaks of resurrection and identifies himself as resurrection and life. Martha acknowledges him as the Messiah and God's Son. Mary then comes with mourners and voices the same grief. Jesus is deeply troubled and weeps.

At the tomb, Martha objects to removing the stone because of the time since death. Jesus asks her to trust his promise, thanks the Father aloud, and calls Lazarus out. Lazarus emerges still wrapped in burial cloths. Jesus tells those present to release him.

Many witnesses believe, while others report the event to the Pharisees. Leaders fear that Jesus' growing following will provoke Roman intervention. Caiaphas argues that one man's death is preferable to national destruction. They begin planning to kill Jesus. He withdraws to Ephraim as Passover approaches and authorities seek information about his whereabouts.

stories.title: Anointing and Triumphal Entry
stories.summary:
Six days before Passover, Jesus attends a meal in Bethany with Lazarus. Martha serves, and Mary anoints Jesus' feet with costly perfume, wiping them with her hair. Judas objects that it could have been sold for the poor. John attributes his objection to theft from the shared funds. Jesus defends Mary and connects the perfume with his burial. Leaders also plan to kill Lazarus because his restoration draws believers to Jesus.

The next day, a crowd carrying palm branches welcomes Jesus toward Jerusalem as Israel's king. He rides a young donkey, fulfilling words the disciples understand only later. Reports about Lazarus help draw the crowd.

Some Greek visitors ask to see Jesus. He announces the hour of his glorification and compares his approaching death to a grain that produces fruit by dying. Troubled, he asks the Father to glorify his name, and a heavenly voice responds. Jesus speaks about being lifted up and drawing people to himself.

The passage then reflects on continued unbelief despite his signs, citing Isaiah. Some leaders believe privately but fear exclusion and loss of approval. Jesus' closing words present him as light sent to save, while warning that rejection of his message will have consequences at judgment.

stories.title: Jesus Washes the Disciples' Feet
stories.summary:
During supper, Jesus rises, removes his outer clothing, and wraps a towel around himself. Knowing that he will return to the Father, he begins washing his disciples' feet. Peter initially refuses, but Jesus says that accepting the washing is necessary to share in him. Peter then asks for a more complete washing. Jesus explains that those already bathed need only their feet washed, while hinting that not everyone present is clean.

Afterward, he explains the example: if their teacher and lord serves them this way, they should serve one another. He then announces that one of them will betray him. At Peter's prompting, the beloved disciple asks who. Jesus gives Judas a dipped piece of bread and tells him to act quickly. Judas leaves into the night. The others misunderstand his departure as an errand or charitable duty.

Jesus tells the remaining disciples that he will soon leave them and gives a new command to love one another as he has loved them. This love will identify them as his disciples. Peter insists that he is ready to die for Jesus. Jesus replies that, before the rooster crows, Peter will deny him three times.

stories.title: Arrest, Trial and Crucifixion
stories.summary:
Judas brings armed officers and soldiers to a garden where Jesus meets his disciples. Jesus identifies himself and asks that his followers be released. Peter cuts off the servant Malchus's ear, but Jesus orders him to put away his sword. Taken first to Annas, Jesus defends the openness of his teaching. Annas then sends him to Caiaphas. Meanwhile, Peter denies being his disciple three times before a rooster crows.

Before Pilate, Jesus describes a kingdom unlike earthly kingdoms and a mission of bearing witness to truth. Pilate says he finds no basis for a charge, but the crowd demands Barabbas. Pilate has Jesus flogged, and soldiers mock him. Pilate repeats that he finds no basis for a charge. Pressure then grows around Jesus' claims to divine sonship and kingship. Pilate finally hands him over for crucifixion.

Jesus carries his cross to Golgotha and is executed between two others. Pilate's inscription calls him king of the Jews. Soldiers divide his clothing, while Jesus entrusts his mother and the beloved disciple to one another. After receiving sour wine, he declares his work finished and dies.

Soldiers find him already dead and leave his legs unbroken, but one pierces his side. John connects these details with scripture. Joseph of Arimathea obtains the body, and Nicodemus brings burial spices. They wrap Jesus in linen and place him in a nearby, unused garden tomb before the Sabbath.

stories.title: The Resurrection Appearances
stories.summary:
Before daylight, Mary Magdalene finds the stone removed from Jesus' tomb and tells Peter and the beloved disciple that the body is missing. They run there and inspect the burial cloths. The beloved disciple sees and believes, though they have not yet understood the scripture about resurrection.

Mary remains outside weeping. After speaking with two angels, she sees Jesus but mistakes him for the gardener. When he calls her by name, she recognizes him. He sends her to tell the disciples about his coming ascent to the Father. That evening, Jesus appears among them behind locked doors, shows his wounds, and commissions them. He breathes on them and speaks of receiving the Holy Spirit and forgiving sins.

Thomas was absent and refuses to believe without seeing and touching the wounds. Eight days later, Jesus appears again and invites him to examine them. Thomas addresses him as his Lord and God. Jesus blesses those who believe without seeing.

John closes this passage by acknowledging that many signs have not been recorded. The selected ones, he explains, are written to support belief that Jesus is the Messiah and God's Son, and life through that belief.

stories.title: Breakfast by the Sea of Tiberias
stories.summary:
Seven disciples spend a fruitless night fishing on the Sea of Tiberias. At daybreak, Jesus stands onshore, but they do not recognize him. He tells them to cast their net on the right side of the boat. The catch is so large that they cannot haul it in. The beloved disciple recognizes Jesus, and Peter jumps into the water while the others bring the boat and net ashore.

They find a charcoal fire with fish and bread. Peter brings in the net, holding 153 large fish without tearing. Jesus invites them to breakfast and shares the food. John identifies this as his third appearance to the gathered disciples after rising.

After the meal, Jesus asks Peter three times whether he loves him. Each reply brings an instruction to care for his sheep. Jesus then describes Peter's future loss of freedom, which the narrator connects with his death, and calls him to follow.

Peter asks about the beloved disciple's future. Jesus redirects him to his own calling. The narrator corrects a resulting rumor that this other disciple would never die. The closing lines identify his testimony behind the account and acknowledge that Jesus did far more than the book can contain.

stories.title: The Ascension and the Replacement of Judas
stories.summary:
Acts opens by recalling Jesus' appearances during the forty days after his suffering. He speaks about God's kingdom and tells the apostles to wait in Jerusalem for the promised Holy Spirit. When they ask about restoring Israel's kingdom, he says the timing belongs to the Father. Their role will be to bear witness from Jerusalem through Judea and Samaria to the ends of the earth.

Jesus is taken up, and a cloud hides him from view. Two men in white tell the watching disciples that he will return as they have seen him go. They return from the Mount of Olives to Jerusalem and gather for prayer with women followers, Jesus' mother, and his brothers.

Among about 120 believers, Peter raises the need to replace Judas. The account describes Judas's connection with the arrest, his fatal fall, and the field associated with his betrayal money. Peter cites psalms to support choosing another witness. The replacement must have accompanied Jesus' ministry from John's baptism through the ascension. Joseph Barsabbas and Matthias are proposed. After prayer, lots are drawn, and Matthias joins the eleven apostles.

stories.title: Pentecost
stories.summary:
At Pentecost, Jesus' followers gather in one place when a sound like a powerful wind fills the house. Forms resembling flames appear over them. Filled with the Holy Spirit, they speak in other languages. A crowd of Jewish residents and visitors from many regions hears God's deeds described in their own languages. Some are amazed, while others accuse the speakers of drunkenness.

Peter rejects that accusation and explains the event through Joel's promise that God will pour out the Spirit on people of different ages and stations. He then speaks about Jesus' public deeds, execution, and resurrection. Drawing on David's psalms, he argues that the risen Jesus is the Messiah and has poured out the Spirit.

Deeply moved, listeners ask what to do. Peter calls them to repent and receive baptism in Jesus' name for forgiveness and the gift of the Spirit. About three thousand people are baptized that day.

The new community devotes itself to the apostles' teaching, shared meals, fellowship, and prayer. Members sell property and distribute proceeds according to need. They meet in the temple and in homes, sharing food with gladness. The account closes with continued growth in the community.

stories.title: The Lame Man Healed and Arrest of Peter and John
stories.summary:
Peter and John enter the temple for afternoon prayer. At the Beautiful Gate, a man unable to walk since birth asks for money. Peter offers healing in Jesus' name instead and helps him stand. The man walks and leaps into the temple, praising God. People recognize him and gather in amazement.

Peter denies that their own power produced the recovery. He attributes it to Jesus, whom he describes as rejected and killed but raised by God. He calls his hearers to repent and connects Jesus with promises made through Moses and the prophets. Temple authorities interrupt and imprison the apostles because of their resurrection teaching.

The next day, the council asks whose authority enabled the healing. Peter again names Jesus and declares salvation through him. The leaders are struck by the men's confidence and cannot deny the healed man's presence. They threaten Peter and John and order them to stop speaking about Jesus. Both answer that they cannot keep silent about what they have witnessed.

Released without punishment, they report to their companions. The community prays for courage rather than freedom from all opposition. Their meeting place shakes, and they are filled with the Holy Spirit, continuing to speak boldly.

stories.title: Ananias and Sapphira
stories.summary:
The believers share their possessions so that nobody among them lacks necessities. Those selling land or houses bring the proceeds to the apostles for distribution. Barnabas, a Levite from Cyprus, is named as one who sells a field and gives the money.

Ananias and his wife Sapphira also sell property, but they keep some proceeds while presenting the remainder misleadingly. Peter confronts Ananias, saying he has lied to the Holy Spirit. He emphasizes that the land was his to keep and the money remained under his control after sale. The charge concerns deception, not an obligation to surrender everything. Ananias collapses and dies, and young men carry him out for burial.

About three hours later, Sapphira arrives without knowing what happened. Peter asks whether the stated amount was the full sale price, and she confirms it. He accuses the couple of conspiring to test the Lord's Spirit and announces that her husband's bearers will carry her too. She dies immediately and is buried beside him. The account ends with fear spreading through the community and everyone hearing the report.

stories.title: Stephen
stories.summary:
As the community grows, Greek-speaking believers complain that their widows are being overlooked in daily food distribution. The apostles ask the community to select seven trusted men to supervise this work while they concentrate on prayer and teaching. Stephen is among those chosen. His signs and persuasive speech provoke opponents, who bring accusations concerning Moses, the law, and the temple before the council.

Stephen answers with a long account of Israel's past. He begins with Abraham's call, then describes Joseph's rejection and later rescue of his family. Moses likewise meets rejection before leading Israel out of Egypt. Stephen recalls the people's resistance in the wilderness, their worship of the golden calf, and warnings of exile. He traces the sanctuary from the traveling tent to Solomon's temple, while insisting that God cannot be confined to a human building.

He then accuses his hearers of repeating their ancestors' resistance to the Holy Spirit. They have betrayed and killed the righteous one announced by the prophets, he says. The council reacts furiously. Stephen reports seeing heaven open and Jesus at God's right hand.

His opponents drag him outside the city and stone him. Their garments are left with a young man named Saul. Stephen asks Jesus to receive his spirit and prays that the killing not be held against them before he dies.

stories.title: Philip and the Ethiopian
stories.summary:
Following Stephen's death, persecution scatters believers from Jerusalem, while Saul searches homes and imprisons followers. Those who flee continue spreading their message. Philip goes to Samaria, where his teaching and healings bring joy and many baptisms. Simon, previously admired for sorcery, also believes. When Peter and John arrive, they pray and lay hands on the new believers, who receive the Holy Spirit. Simon offers money for this ability. Peter rebukes him, and Simon asks for prayer.

An angel then directs Philip to the road from Jerusalem toward Gaza. There he encounters an Ethiopian court official returning from worship in Jerusalem. The man, a eunuch responsible for the queen's treasury, is reading Isaiah in his chariot. At the Spirit's direction, Philip approaches and asks whether he understands.

The official invites him aboard and asks whom Isaiah describes as a sufferer led like a sheep to slaughter. Philip begins with that passage and explains the good news about Jesus. When they reach water, the official requests baptism. They stop, enter the water, and Philip baptizes him. The Spirit then takes Philip away. The official continues joyfully, while Philip appears at Azotus and preaches along the coast toward Caesarea.

stories.title: Saul's Conversion
stories.summary:
Saul obtains authority to arrest followers of Jesus in Damascus and bring them to Jerusalem. Near the city, a heavenly light surrounds him, and he falls to the ground. A voice asks why he is persecuting Jesus and directs him into Damascus. His companions hear the sound but see nobody. Blinded, Saul must be led into the city, where he spends three days without food or drink.

In a vision, Jesus sends a disciple named Ananias to him. Ananias objects because of Saul's violent reputation, but Jesus describes Saul as chosen to carry his name before nations, rulers, and Israel. Ananias visits, calls Saul his brother, and lays hands on him. Saul's sight returns, and he receives baptism and food.

Saul immediately begins proclaiming Jesus as God's Son in the synagogues. His changed message amazes listeners and eventually provokes a murder plot. Followers lower him through the city wall in a basket at night. In Jerusalem, believers initially fear him, but Barnabas introduces him to the apostles and explains his experience. Further threats lead the community to send him to Tarsus. The passage closes with peace and growth among the churches of Judea, Galilee, and Samaria.

stories.title: Peter, Cornelius and the Gentiles
stories.summary:
Cornelius, a Roman officer in Caesarea, is known for prayer and generosity. An angel tells him to send for Peter in Joppa. Meanwhile, Peter has a rooftop vision of animals lowered in a sheet and hears a command to kill and eat. He objects that he has never eaten forbidden food. The voice tells him not to call unclean what God has cleansed. This happens three times.

The Spirit directs Peter to accompany Cornelius's messengers. At Caesarea, Peter refuses Cornelius's gesture of worship and explains that God has taught him not to treat people as unclean. Cornelius describes his vision, and Peter announces that God shows no favoritism. He recounts Jesus' ministry, death, and resurrection, offering forgiveness through belief in him.

While Peter is speaking, the Holy Spirit comes upon the listeners. His Jewish companions hear them speaking other languages and praising God. Peter orders their baptism, reasoning that those who received the same Spirit cannot be denied water.

Back in Jerusalem, critics object that Peter ate with uncircumcised people. He recounts the visions, the visit, and the Spirit's arrival. His listeners accept the explanation and praise God for granting Gentiles repentance leading to life.

stories.title: Peter's Escape and Herod's Death
stories.summary:
King Herod attacks the community and executes James, John's brother. Seeing approval for this action, he also imprisons Peter during the festival period.
